cm.n: Henry notes that hand-washing itself "was a cleanly custom, and no harm in it" — the real problem wasn't the practice but the Pharisees making it a binding religious law rather than a matter of personal choice.

On the Syrophoenician woman, Henry stresses just how far outside Israel's covenant she stood — "a stranger to the commonwealth of Israel, an alien to the covenant of promise," with no claim on Jesus by nationality or religion. Her persistence despite that, he suggests, is exactly what makes her faith so striking.

Ryle frames the central lesson plainly: 'the heart is the chief source of defilement and impurity in God's sight. Moral purity does not depend on washing or not washing — touching things or not touching them, eating things or not eating them, as the Scribes and Pharisees taught.' He commends anyone who, like the psalmist, prays 'teach me thy statutes' rather than resting…

set: This chapter moves through Gentile Decapolis territory (feeding four thousand), Dalmanutha on the western shore, Bethsaida, and finally north to Caesarea Philippi at the base of Mount Hermon — a city built around pagan shrines to the god Pan, a strikingly idol-filled backdrop for Peter's confession that Jesus is the Christ.

his.t: A pagan city by a spring, with a shrine to the god Pan.
Condemned men carried their own crossbeam, so the image was grim.

cus.t: A little leaven spreads through all the dough, standing for hidden influence.
Saliva was a folk remedy, though Jesus needed no such help.

cu: Rabbis typically taught by citing a chain of earlier authorities behind their interpretation. "Leaven" as a teaching image drew on something every listener understood physically — a small amount works through an entire batch of dough, exactly how Jesus describes corrupting influence spreading quietly through a whole community.

ot.n: The Davidic covenant behind the title "Christ" Peter uses in his confession.
"Having eyes, do you not see?" — a phrase Jesus draws directly from this Old Testament pattern of spiritual blindness.
The suffering servant's death as divine necessity — background for Jesus' "must suffer" language in His first passion prediction.

im.c: Get Thee Behind Me, Satan, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry notices Jesus doesn't simply repeat His earlier method: with five loaves He fed five thousand, but rather than reasoning "five fed five thousand, so four should feed four thousand," He takes all seven loaves available this time and uses every bit of them — teaching, in Henry's words, that we should "take things as they are, and accommodate ourselves to them; use what we…

Henry credits the crowd's devotion directly: many had come from far away and their food had long since run out, "yet they continued with Christ, and did not speak of leaving him till he spoke of dismissing them" — true zeal, he notes, makes nothing of hardship in the pursuit of what it values.

Ryle points to 'the strange mixture of grace and infirmity which may be found in the heart of a true Christian' in Peter's sudden turn — the very man who had just made such a noble confession, moments later presuming to rebuke his own Master for speaking of His coming death.

Lewis does not comment on Mark 8, but his chapter "The Shocking Alternative" in Mere Christianity is an extended answer to Jesus' question to the disciples in verse 29, "Who do you say that I am?" He says the one thing we must not say is that He was a great human teacher and nothing more.

set: The unnamed mountain is traditionally linked to Mount Tabor, though many scholars favor Mount Hermon, near Caesarea Philippi where the previous chapter's events took place.

his.t: Many expected Elijah to return before the Messiah, as Malachi said.
Gehenna was the Hinnom Valley south of Jerusalem, once a place of child sacrifice.

cus.t: Peter's offer to build shelters recalls the booths of the Feast of Tabernacles.
Salt preserved food and sealed covenants, so "have salt" meant staying faithful.

cu: Peter's offer to build three shelters (v.5) draws on the Feast of Tabernacles tradition of temporary booths — a natural, if premature, response to standing before Moses, Elijah, and a transfigured Jesus at once.

ot.n: Moses' face shining after meeting with God — the visual precedent for Jesus' transfiguration.
The promise of Elijah's return before the Day of the Lord, discussed directly by Jesus and the disciples in v.11-13.
"Their worm never dies, and the fire is never quenched" — quoted directly by Jesus in v.48.

im.c: The Transfiguration, by Gustave Doré (1866)
im.k: Public domain — Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry notes the one real distinguishing feature of this particular case: the spirit had possessed the boy since early childhood, "and that strengthened his interest, and confirmed his hold" — much like a chronic disease made harder to cure the longer it's allowed to take root.

The early church father Chrysostom reads "this kind" as referring to an especially powerful, obstinate class of demon, requiring prayer and fasting specifically because these disciplines "lift men up from the flesh to God" — not a magic formula, but a genuine spiritual reorientation that made the disciples capable of what mere technique could not accomplish.

Writing on this same Transfiguration scene, Ryle draws a sharp contrast between Jesus and the two great figures beside Him: 'however great Moses and Elijah might be, there stood One before him far greater than they. They were but servants; He was the King's Son. They were but stars; He was the Sun. They were but witnesses; He was the Truth.'

set: The chapter opens in Judea beyond the Jordan (the region of Perea, under Herod Antipas) and closes at Jericho, one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, about fifteen miles northeast of Jerusalem along a steep, dangerous pilgrim road climbing roughly 3,300 feet.

his.t: Jesus travels through Judea and across the Jordan toward Jerusalem as Passover nears.
Rabbis disagreed on grounds, and Herod Antipas' marriage had already cost John his life.

cus.t: A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or captive.
Teachers were often given children to bless, though disciples tried to block them.

cu: A formal certificate of divorce (Deuteronomy 24:1-4) was a real, legally binding Jewish practice; papyrus examples from this era have survived. Rabbis of the period actively debated how liberally that provision could be applied — Jesus bypasses the debate entirely by returning to the creation account itself.

ot.n: The creation account Jesus quotes directly as the foundation for His teaching on marriage.
The Mosaic divorce provision the Pharisees cite, which Jesus reframes as a concession to hardness of heart rather than the created ideal.
The suffering servant bearing the guilt of "many" — closely echoed in Jesus' description of His own coming death as a ransom.

im.c: Christ and the Rich Young Ruler, by Heinrich Hofmann
im.k: Public domain — Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry emphasizes something easy to rush past: "Jesus, beholding him, loved him" — Christ's genuine affection for the rich young man is stated plainly even though Henry knows the story ends in the man walking away. He reads it as proof that "Christ particularly loves to see young people, and rich people, asking the way to heaven," regardless of how the individual case turns out.

Clarke notes the small but telling detail in Bartimaeus's name itself: the Syriac word "bar" simply means "son," so "Bartimaeus" is literally "son of Timaeus" — Mark preserves both the Aramaic patronymic and its meaning together, the kind of small linguistic detail that shows genuine familiarity with the local language and culture.

Ryle cites a startling rabbinical example, via Lightfoot's research into Jewish sources, of just how loosely divorce was practiced in Jesus' day: 'the school of Hillel saith, If the wife cooks her husband's food ill by over-salting it, or over-roasting it, she is to be put away.' Against that backdrop, Jesus' insistence on marriage's permanence was a genuinely radical…

set: Passover week, when Jerusalem's population swelled several times over with pilgrims. Jesus enters from the east, crossing the Mount of Olives through Bethphage and Bethany — a route soaked in messianic expectation, since pilgrims approaching from that direction were already primed to look for a king.

his.t: Crowds filled the city, eager to cheer a king.
Buying and selling filled the Court of the Gentiles, the only place nations could pray.

cus.t: Spreading cloaks and leafy branches on the road honored a king.
A king on a donkey came in peace, not on a war horse.

cu: Spreading cloaks and branches on the road was a recognized way to honor entering royalty. Money-changers in the temple exchanged ordinary coinage for the special Tyrian shekels required for temple offerings, and dove-sellers supplied birds for the poor's sacrifices — legitimate services in principle, but ones Jesus judged had become exploitative and profit-driven.

ot.n: The King coming "righteous and having salvation, gentle and riding on a donkey" — directly fulfilled in Jesus' entry.
The exact pilgrim psalm the crowd is quoting when they shout "Hosanna" and "blessed is he who comes."
The two prophecies Jesus quotes together in His rebuke of the temple's commerce.

im.c: Christ's Entry into Jerusalem, by Gustave Doré (1866)
im.k: Public domain — Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry reads the fig tree's curse as "the reverse of the first blessing, Be fruitful" — a deliberate echo of Genesis, turning God's original command to creation into its opposite for a tree that only pretended fruitfulness through its leaves. He treats it as a type of the Jewish religious establishment: full of impressive outward show, but no actual fruit for Christ to find.

Henry notes Mark deliberately splits the fig tree story into two halves, wrapping the temple cleansing inside it — the cursing happens on one morning, the withering is discovered the next, with the temple incident sitting between them.

Ryle calls the fig tree episode 'a parable in deeds, as full of meaning as any of our Lord's parables in words' — rich in the leaves of a formal religion, but barren of any actual fruit, standing as a living warning to 'the Jewish Church' of that very generation.

set: Likely the Wednesday of Passion Week, in the temple courts. Mark groups the Pharisees, Herodians, Sadducees, and scribes together in quick succession — normally rival factions, momentarily united in trying to trap Jesus in His own words.

his.t: A priestly group who denied resurrection and accepted only the Torah.
Many Jews hated paying tax to Caesar, so the question was a trap.

cus.t: Landowners often leased vineyards, collecting a share of the fruit.
The smallest coins in use, worth a fraction of a day's wage.

cu: A Roman denarius bore Caesar's image and an inscription calling him "son of the divine Augustus" — many Jews viewed carrying the coin at all as a compromise with idolatry, which is exactly what makes Jesus' question about whose image it bears so pointed. The Sadducees' hypothetical draws on a real legal practice, levirate marriage, requiring a man to marry his deceased brother's childless widow.

ot.n: The original vineyard image for Israel, which Jesus' parable directly draws on and escalates.
The two commandments Jesus names as greatest — combining them this way was itself a notable move.
"The Lord said to my Lord" — quoted directly by Jesus to press the scribes on the Messiah's true identity.

im.c: The Widow's Mite, by Gustave Doré (1866)
im.k: Public domain — Project Gutenberg

cm.n: Henry defends the widow against an objection readers might raise on her behalf: why give away money she could barely spare, rather than keeping it for herself? His answer is that Christ Himself settled the question by commending her — proof, in Henry's view, that giving according to ability, even out of real scarcity, is accepted "as if they had been two pounds" rather than…

Poole works out the actual value of the widow's gift in real terms: Mark tells us two mites made one quadrans, and a denarius (a full day's wage for a laborer) was worth far more than that — her total offering, by any reasonable estimate, came to a small fraction of a single day's pay.

Gill works out the exact value of the widow's two mites: a quadrans, the fourth part of a Roman as, itself already the smallest coin in common circulation — making her gift, in strict monetary terms, about as small a sum as existed. Its worth to Jesus, he notes, was measured by what it cost her, not by what it was worth to anyone else.

t: The Return of the Son of Man
set: Seated on the Mount of Olives directly across the Kidron Valley from the temple, Jesus can see the very buildings He has just predicted will be leveled — a detail that gives His words unusual visual weight for the four disciples listening.

his.t: Its white stone and gold made its fall seem unthinkable.
Rome burned the temple in AD 70, about forty years later.

cus.t: Roofs were living space with outside stairs, so fleeing meant not going back in.
Roman time divided night into four watches, and servants stayed alert.

cu: Fleeing to rooftops or leaving a field in progress reflects real first-century Judean village life, where houses had external staircases to flat roofs and fields lay just outside town — Jesus' warnings assume His listeners' actual physical surroundings.

ot.n: The three passages behind Jesus' phrase "abomination of desolation," which He tells His hearers to go read themselves.
Earlier prophetic images of cosmic upheaval — darkened sun, falling stars — echoed directly in v.24-25.
The Son of Man receiving everlasting dominion and glory — directly quoted in Jesus' description of His own return.

im.c: The Prophecy of the Destruction of the Temple, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry notices the disciples trying to draw Jesus back into admiring the temple He'd just left in disgust — "how apt many of Christ's own disciples are to idolize things that look great." His response, Henry notes, shows "how little Christ values external pomp, where there is not real purity": impressive architecture offers no protection when what it houses has gone rotten.

Ancient historians record that when Roman forces under Titus burned the temple in AD 70, gold decoration melted and ran into the cracks between the stones — leading soldiers to pry apart literally every stone in the search for it. Whatever the original intent behind Jesus' words, "not one stone left upon another" was fulfilled with striking, almost accidental literalness.

Gill notes a small geographical detail: the disciples sat with Jesus 'over against the temple' on the Mount of Olives specifically because the temple's eastern wall was lower than the rest, giving them a genuinely full, unobstructed view of the massive Herodian structure they were admiring.

set: Bethany, an upper room in Jerusalem, and finally the olive grove of Gethsemane at the foot of the Mount of Olives — "Gethsemane" itself means "oil press," and ancient olive trees still growing there today may descend from trees present in the first century.

his.t: Leaders wanted a quiet arrest before the Passover crowds could riot.
The Sanhedrin of seventy elders and priests met under the high priest.

cus.t: Guests reclined at the table, so those beside Jesus shared the same dish.
Abba was the family word for father, used in prayer with tenderness.

cu: Pure nard was imported from India and worth roughly a year's wages — breaking the alabaster jar meant the whole flask had to be used at once, since it couldn't be resealed, making the woman's gift total and irreversible. The Passover meal required a lamb sacrificed at the temple and eaten in a properly prepared room, which is exactly what the disciples are sent ahead to arrange.

ot.n: Moses sprinkling covenant-ratifying blood on the people at Sinai — directly echoed in Jesus' words over the cup.
"I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered" — quoted directly by Jesus to predict the disciples' coming collapse.
The suffering servant who "did not open His mouth" — echoed in Jesus' silence before His accusers.

im.c: Judas Betrays Jesus with a Kiss, by Gustave Doré
im.k: Public domain — Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry notices a pattern running through Jesus' whole ministry: "Christ never rode in triumph into Jerusalem, but when he came thither to suffer; nor had ever his head anointed, but for his burial." Even His moments of honor turn out to be tied directly to His coming death, not separate from it.

Henry speculates on how Judas may have rationalized his betrayal to himself — reasoning that since Jesus Himself had repeatedly said He must be betrayed, surely acting it out couldn't really be counted against him, "for who hath resisted his will?" He treats this as a warning about how easily people twist God's foreknowledge into an excuse for their own choices.

Ryle traces Judas's ruin to a single root cause: 'the love of money was the cause of this unhappy man's ruin. That same grovelling covetousness, which enslaved the heart of Balaam, and brought on Gehazi a leprosy, was the destruction of Iscariot's soul.' He treats it as one recurring pattern across Scripture, not an isolated case.

set: Jesus is tried before Pontius Pilate, Roman governor of Judea from AD 26-36, then taken to Golgotha — "the Place of the Skull" — traditionally identified with the site beneath the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, just outside the first-century city walls.

his.t: Pilate governed Judea from AD 26 to 36 and was known for harshness.
Rome crucified rebels publicly to frighten others into obedience.

cus.t: Prisoners were beaten before crucifixion, often weakening them.
A written charge was fixed above the condemned person on the cross.

cu: Pilate's custom of releasing a prisoner at the feast isn't independently attested outside the Gospels, but fits a plausible pattern of Roman provincial governance aimed at keeping restless populations calm during high-tension festivals.

ot.n: "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me" — quoted word for word as Jesus' cry from the cross.
Soldiers casting lots for a sufferer's garments, written roughly a thousand years before the event it describes.
The suffering servant given "a grave with the rich" — echoed in Joseph of Arimathea's wealthy, honorable tomb.

im.c: Crucifixion of Jesus, by Gustave Doré (1866)
im.k: Public domain — Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry connects Jesus being bound directly to Psalm 118:27's language of sacrifices bound with cords — "Christ was bound, to make bonds easy to us." He also cites Cicero's own description of crucifixion, teterrimum supplicium, "a most tremendous punishment," noting Christ met death in its most extreme, deliberately shameful form — the death reserved for slaves and the worst…

On Pilate releasing Barabbas, Henry notes the irony sharply: Pilate released "the scandal and plague of their nation" while condemning "the glory and blessing of their nation" — not from conviction, but simply to keep the crowd quiet, "willing to content the people." Political expedience, not justice, decided who lived and who died that day.

Ryle calls Barabbas's release 'a vivid emblem of the manner in which God pardons and justifies the ungodly' — a guilty man walking free while an innocent one dies in his place, the exact shape of the exchange at the center of the gospel itself.

Lewis does not comment on Mark 15, but "The Perfect Penitent" in Mere Christianity is a reflection on what the cross is for. He says that the central Christian belief is that Christ's death put us right with God and gave us a fresh start, and that how it works is less important than the fact.

set: The tomb near Golgotha, at first light on the Sunday following Passover — the women arrive with spices to complete the burial anointing that had to be rushed before the Sabbath began at sundown on the day of Jesus' death.

his.t: Rome often let families bury the crucified, and Pilate released Jesus' body.
Jerusalem was still crowded with pilgrims, and soldiers kept order.

cus.t: Spices honored the dead and eased the smell, they did not preserve the body.
Work stopped from Friday sunset, so the women waited until Sunday.

cu: Completing a body's anointing after burial was standard Jewish practice when death occurred too close to the Sabbath for full preparation — exactly the situation Mark 15:42 describes. A woman's testimony carried little legal weight in the culture of the time, which makes Mark's choice to have women be the first witnesses to the empty tomb an unusual, and by most reckonings unlikely, detail to have simply invented.

ot.n: "You will not abandon me to Sheol" — read by the early church as anticipating the resurrection.
Three days in the great fish, which Jesus Himself pointed to as a sign of His own coming three days in the tomb.
The Feast of Firstfruits, observed on the day after the Sabbath during Passover week — the same day tradition places the resurrection.

im.c: The Angel at the Sepulcher, by Gustave Doré (1866)
im.k: Public domain — Project Gutenberg

cm.n: Henry marks the day itself as a turning point in history: "this sabbath is over, and the first day of the week is the first day of a new world." He describes the women's visit to the tomb as "not a superstitious one, but a pious one" — genuine devotion, not empty ritual, bringing them there before dawn.

On the angel's gentle "be not affrighted," Henry notes that angels don't only rejoice over a sinner's conversion, but over a believer's comfort too — the point of the announcement wasn't just information, but genuine consolation for people who had every reason to still be afraid.

Ryle points to the courage the errand itself required: visiting a grave in the dim light of dawn would try any woman, but to do so for someone executed as a common criminal, whom their own nation had despised, was 'a mighty boldness indeed' — the kind of act, he says, that shows the real difference between weak faith and strong faith.

t: Two Promised Births: John and Jesus
set: The chapter moves between three places: the temple in Jerusalem during the reign of Herod the Great, the Galilean village of Nazareth, and a town in the hill country of Judah, traditionally identified as Ein Karem a few miles west of Jerusalem.

his.t: Herod the Great rules as Rome's client king and is still rebuilding the temple.
Roughly 400 years had passed since the last Old Testament prophet.

cus.t: Priests drew lots for the rare honor of burning incense in the holy place.
Boys were named at circumcision on day eight, and neighbors expected the family name.

cu: Priests were divided into twenty-four divisions (1 Chronicles 24), each serving at the temple for a week at a time, and Zechariah belonged to the division of Abijah. The honor of burning incense in the holy place was assigned by lot, and later Jewish tradition says a priest who had done it was passed over until everyone else had taken a turn — so for Zechariah it may well have been the one time in his life.

ot.n: The promise of an Elijah-like messenger who will turn hearts before the Lord comes — applied to John in verse 17.
Hannah's song after the birth of Samuel, which Mary's Magnificat closely echoes.
God's promise of an everlasting throne for David's line, behind Gabriel's words in verses 32-33.
The promise of a child to elderly, childless Abraham and Sarah — a pattern repeated with Zechariah and Elizabeth.
Gabriel's earlier appearance to Daniel to explain the timeline of the coming anointed ruler.

im.c: The Annunciation, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry reads Zechariah's muteness as a sign that was also a fair penalty: "If thou wilt have a sign for the support of thy faith, it shall be such a one as shall be also the punishment of thine unbelief." He notes the word covers deafness as well as dumbness, since the neighbors later had to make signs to Zechariah (v.62), and he stresses that man's unbelief does not cancel…

On "in the spirit and power of Elijah," Gill lists how much John and Elijah shared: both lived much in the wilderness, both were austere in how they lived and dressed, and both came as restorers of religion when it was low and decayed.

Guzik compares Mary's question with Zechariah's: nearly the same words, but Zechariah asked "in skeptical unbelief" and Mary "in wonder-filled faith" — "the same words can flow from very different hearts." He also counts at least twelve other Old Testament allusions in the Magnificat beyond its resemblance to Hannah's song.

Lewis did not write a commentary on Luke, but his argument in Miracles (chapter 14, "The Grand Miracle") bears directly on this chapter. He calls the Incarnation — God becoming man — the central miracle of Christianity, and holds that every other miracle either prepares for it, shows it, or follows from it.

t: The Birth of Jesus and the Boy in the Temple
set: The chapter moves from Nazareth to Bethlehem, the town of David a few miles south of Jerusalem, where the shepherds keep their flocks in nearby fields. It then shifts to the temple courts in Jerusalem for the presentation and for the Passover visit when Jesus is twelve, before returning to Nazareth.

his.t: Augustus rules the Mediterranean world, and Herod the Great governs Judea as Rome's client king.
Taxes and a census made foreign rule felt, keeping hopes for a Messiah alive.

cus.t: Luke's word can mean a guest room, so a crowded family home fits.
Poorer families offered two birds instead of a lamb.

cu: Luke's word for "inn" (kataluma) can also mean a guest room, which is how the same word is used for the room of the Last Supper, so some readers picture a crowded family home rather than a roadside lodging. Newborns were wrapped in strips of cloth, and a manger was a feeding trough.

ot.n: The prophecy that the ruler of Israel would come from Bethlehem.
A servant given as a light to the nations — the background to Simeon's words in verse 32.
The law of purification after childbirth and the offering of two birds, followed in verses 22-24.
The consecration of every firstborn male to the Lord, quoted in verse 23.
The boy Samuel growing in favor with the Lord and with people, echoed in verse 52.

im.c: The Angel and the Shepherds, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry observes that the shepherds were not shaken by the poverty they found: "The poverty and meanness in which they found Christ the Lord were no shock to their faith, who themselves knew what it was to live a life of comfortable communion with God in very poor and mean circumstances." He adds that just as the cross later became a stumbling-block to some, so the manger did…

In The Everlasting Man, Chesterton notes that the Bethlehem cave was an ordinary stable used by the hill herdsmen. He reads the shepherds as the common people who had always been the makers of myths, and the Magi as the philosophers, so that both strands of the ancient world arrive at the same manger. His line: "The shepherds had found their Shepherd."

Preaching on verse 49, Spurgeon notes these are the first recorded words of Jesus and tells his hearers to "write that 'MUST' in capital letters." He hears surprise in the reply — Jesus is astonished they did not realize that God is His Father — and says of the boy that other things did not interest Him, but this thing absorbed Him.

Lewis does not comment on Luke 2, but in Miracles his chapter "The Grand Miracle" treats the birth in the manger as the center of Christian belief. He calls the Incarnation the miracle on which the others depend, and pictures a descent so deep that God goes down into the human world, and takes it back up with Him.

t: John the Baptist, the Baptism, and the Genealogy of Jesus
set: John preaches in the wilderness and "all the region around the Jordan," the rift valley that runs from the Sea of Galilee down to the Dead Sea. Luke opens by naming six rulers across Judea, Galilee, and the territories to the north and east, tying the scene to the wider political map of the Roman East.

his.t: Luke names Tiberius, Pilate, Herod and the high priests to fix the date near AD 29.
Antipas ruled Galilee and later jailed John for criticizing his marriage.

cus.t: Farmers tossed grain into the wind so the wheat fell and the chaff blew away.
They collected for Rome and often took extra, so John's advice to them is specific.

cu: Ritual washing was familiar in Jewish life, but John's call was unusual: he asked people who already counted themselves God's people to be immersed as a sign of repentance, much as a convert might be. His farming picture was familiar to everyone listening: a winnowing fork tossed threshed grain into the wind so the wheat fell to the floor and the light chaff blew away to be burned.

ot.n: The voice in the wilderness preparing the way of the Lord, quoted in full in verses 4-6.
"You are My Son" — the royal declaration echoed by the voice at the baptism.
The Servant in whom God delights — the second half of the heavenly voice.
The line from Adam through Seth to Noah, which Luke's genealogy traces in reverse.

im.c: John the Baptist Baptizes Jesus, by Gustave Doré
im.k: Public domain — Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry reads John's answers to each group as a pattern: those who profess repentance "must show it by reformation, according to their places and conditions." He notes soldiers in particular are "cautioned against the temptations of their employments." On the genealogy, he says Matthew shows Jesus as son of Abraham and heir to David's throne, while Luke shows Him as the Seed of…

Ryle stresses that John "exposes the uselessness of a repentance which is not accompanied by fruits in the life," and puts it plainly: "Doing is the very life of repentance." He also draws a sober lesson from the way Luke closes John's story with his imprisonment: the reward of God's servants is often not in this world.

JFB observes that the fruits John asks for are simply resistance to the sins that most tempt each group — tax collectors to extortion, soldiers to violence. On the genealogy, they lay out the long-running question: is this Joseph's line or Mary's?

t: Tested in the Wilderness, Rejected at Nazareth
set: The chapter begins in the barren wilderness of Judea, then moves to Nazareth, a small hill village in lower Galilee, and finally to Capernaum, a fishing town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee.

his.t: Many Jews longed for an anointed deliverer to free them from foreign rule.
It sat on a busy trade route near the border of Herod Antipas' territory.

cus.t: A reader stood to read, and the teacher sat down to speak, as Jesus does here.
The "year of the Lord's favor" echoes Jubilee, when debts were erased and slaves freed.

cu: In a synagogue service the reader stood to read from the scroll, and the one who taught sat down, which is why Luke notes that Jesus sat before speaking. The "year of the Lord's favor" echoes the Jubilee of Leviticus 25, when debts were canceled, slaves freed, and land returned to its families. Luke's word for Peter's mother-in-law's "high fever" is a medical term, a detail often connected to Luke being a physician.

ot.n: "Man shall not live on bread alone" — Jesus' first answer, spoken to Israel after its time in the wilderness.
Worship God only, and do not test Him — Jesus' second and third answers.
The anointed one who brings good news to the poor, the passage Jesus reads at Nazareth.
The Jubilee year of release behind the phrase "the year of the Lord's favor."
Elijah and the widow of Zarephath, and Elisha and Naaman — the two outsiders Jesus names in verses 25-27.

im.c: The Temptation of Christ, by Ary Scheffer (1854)
im.k: Public domain — Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry observes that being led into the wilderness gave the tempter an advantage, since Jesus was alone, with no one by whose prayers and advice He might be helped. "He who knew his own strength might give Satan advantage; but we may not, who know our own weakness." He also notes that Satan found nothing in Christ for his "fiery darts to fasten upon," and that Christ conquered…

Ryle points out that the verb for "led" is the same one used of the Spirit's guidance of believers, so Jesus "did not seek conflict with the devil, but was 'led' to it." He draws two warnings from the scene: that the devil can quote Scripture when it suits his purpose, and that the acts he suggests are often trifling in appearance while the principle behind them is rebellion…

Guzik reads "the acceptable year of the Lord" as the Old Testament Jubilee, when slaves were set free, debts canceled, and everything given a new start, so Jesus' announcement at Nazareth is that the Jubilee has arrived in His own person. On the first temptation, he stresses that Jesus reminded Satan that "every word of God is more important than the very bread we eat."

t: Fishers of Men, a Leper, a Paralytic, and a Tax Collector
set: The opening scene is on the shore and waters of the Lake of Gennesaret, another name for the Sea of Galilee, where fishing was the main industry. The rest takes place in towns nearby, most likely Capernaum, where excavated houses have flat roofs, which fits the roof scene.

his.t: Fishing was a major Galilean trade, with crews working in partnership.
Rome let locals collect taxes and keep extra, so tax men were widely despised.

cus.t: A leper lived apart and was ritually unclean, so Jesus' touch broke a strong taboo.
Roofs were beams covered with branches and clay, so a crowd could open one.

cu: A leper was ritually unclean and kept apart (Leviticus 13), so Jesus' touch breaks a strong social taboo, and His instruction to show himself to the priest follows Leviticus 14. Flat roofs in Galilean houses were reached by an outside stair and could be opened up and repaired.

ot.n: "Woe to me... I am a man of unclean lips" — Isaiah's reaction to seeing the Lord, echoed in Peter's words.
God sending fishers and hunters to gather His people — the background to "catch men."
The laws for diagnosing leprosy and for cleansing a person who was healed, followed in verses 12-14.
God as the One who forgives all sins and heals all diseases, behind the paralytic's story.
God as bridegroom to His people, which lies behind Jesus' image of the bridegroom in verse 34.

im.c: The Miraculous Draught of Fishes, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry takes Peter's "Depart from me" gently: given how much reason sinful people have to tremble before the holy Lord, "Peter may well be excused." But he says we must go the other way: "We must all own ourselves sinful men, and that therefore Jesus Christ might justly depart from us; but we must therefore fall down at his knees, to pray him that he would not depart; for woe…

Ryle notes that Peter's cry shows "how much a sense of God's presence abases man and makes him feel his sinfulness," and adds that at a later point in life Peter "would, doubtless, have said, 'Abide with me,' and not, 'depart.'" He also points to the paralytic's friends as a picture of "what pains men will take about an object when they are in earnest," carrying the man up an…

Ellicott notes that the saying about old wine in verse 39 is peculiar to Luke. He reads the old wine as the religion that animated a person's former life, and the new wine as "the freer, nobler life-power of the gospel," so it is no surprise that people used to the older system hesitate over the new, much as the Pharisees "were shrinking from the freedom of which our Lord set…

Lewis does not comment on Luke 5, but "The Shocking Alternative" in Mere Christianity turns on verses 20-24, where Jesus tells the paralytic his sins are forgiven. Lewis points out that we can only forgive wrongs done to ourselves, so a man who forgives every sin is claiming to be the one against whom all sin is committed.

t: Lord of the Sabbath and the Sermon on the Plain
set: The chapter moves through Galilean grainfields and a synagogue, up a mountain for the night of prayer, and then down to "a level place," where a crowd from Judea, Jerusalem, and the coast of Tyre and Sidon gathers. The mix of people from Jewish and non-Jewish regions fits Luke's interest in the reach of Jesus' message.

his.t: Crowds came from Judea and the Tyre and Sidon coast, Jews and Gentiles alike.
Pharisees and scribes watched Jesus closely, since a popular teacher threatened their influence.

cus.t: Pharisees counted rubbing grain by hand as work, which the Sabbath forbade.
The cloak was the outer garment, so giving both layers meant giving nearly everything.

cu: Plucking heads of grain to eat was permitted for a traveler under the Law (Deuteronomy 23:25), but the Pharisees counted rubbing the grain in the hands as a form of threshing, a type of work. David's eating of the consecrated bread (1 Samuel 21:1-6) was the example Jesus chose. A man's cloak was his outer garment and his tunic the inner one, so giving both was giving nearly everything.

ot.n: David and his men eating the consecrated bread — the example Jesus gives in verses 3-4.
The blessings and curses at the start of Israel's life in the land, a pattern behind the blessings and woes.
The two ways of the righteous and the wicked, behind the closing images of the tree and the two builders.
A warning to the comfortable and well-fed, close in spirit to the woes.
The command to love one's neighbor as oneself, which Jesus stretches to cover enemies.

im.c: The Sermon on the Mount, by Gustave Doré (1866)
im.k: Public domain — Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: On "Lord of the Sabbath," Ryle insists the words do not mean Jesus was altering or letting down the fourth commandment. They mean He delivers the Sabbath from Jewish traditions, protects it from superstitious views of how to keep it, and shows its true spirit.

Wesley notes that the Greek for Jesus' night of prayer is singular and emphatic, implying "an extraordinary and sublime devotion." On verse 38, he explains "into your bosom" as an allusion to the mantles the Jews wore, which could hold a large quantity of grain, and adds: "Amazing goodness! So we are permitted even to carve for ourselves...

Henry takes the woes as a warning to those who are tempted to "set their hearts upon a smiling world" and say to their souls, "take thine ease." Of the woe on those whom all men speak well of, he says it would be a bad sign if a preacher spoke so that nobody was ever disturbed, since the task is to tell people the truth.

Lewis does not comment on Luke, but in Mere Christianity (Book III, chapter 7, "Forgiveness") he reads "love your enemies" through "love your neighbor as yourself." We do not love ourselves because we find ourselves likable, so loving an enemy does not mean feeling fond of him.

t: The Centurion, the Widow's Son, John's Question, and the Woman Who Loved Much
set: The chapter opens in Capernaum, where excavation has revealed a first-century basalt foundation under the later limestone synagogue, which fits the elders' remark that the centurion "has built our synagogue." Jesus then travels to Nain, a small town on the slope of the hill of Moreh overlooking the Jezreel Valley, some miles…

his.t: Centurions led about 100 soldiers, and this Gentile had won over Capernaum's Jewish elders.
John asked from prison, where Herod Antipas had locked him up for rebuking him.

cus.t: The dead were carried on an open bier and buried the same day, followed by mourners.
Guests reclined at meals with feet to the side, so the woman could reach Jesus' feet.

cu: Burial took place the same day, and the body was carried outside the town on an open bier, with mourners and flute players going before it. Touching a bier made a person ritually unclean, which makes Jesus' act in verse 14 notable (Numbers 19:11). At a dinner, guests reclined on couches with their feet away from the table, which is how the woman could stand behind Jesus at His feet.

ot.n: Elijah raising a widow's son at Zarephath — the earlier miracle the crowd at Nain would have had in mind.
The blind see, the lame walk, the deaf hear — the promised signs Jesus lists in His answer to John.
Good news preached to the poor, the same passage Jesus read at Nazareth in Luke 4.
The messenger sent to prepare the way, which Jesus applies to John in verse 27.
The ritual uncleanness that came from touching a dead body, relevant to Jesus touching the bier.

im.c: The Resurrection of the Widow's Son at Nain, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Ryle draws three things from the centurion: his kindness to a servant, his humility, and his faith. He urges that "all believers ought to strive to be clothed with humility." Of the widow at Nain, he writes that Jesus "saw the weeping mother, and knew well what her feelings must have been, for He had been born of a woman Himself," and on the woman at Simon's house, that "a…

Henry notes a reversal in the centurion's story: he did not think himself worthy to visit Christ, "yet Christ thought him worthy to be visited by him; for those that humble themselves shall be exalted." At Nain, he says Christ's "eye affected his heart," and He told the widow not to weep, which shows He has concern for mourners.

Gill takes up the question of why John sent his disciples with "Are You the One who was to come?" He argues it was "not that he doubted that Jesus was the Messiah," and not so much for his own satisfaction as "for theirs; and to remove all doubt and hesitation from them about Christ." Other readers hear real doubt in the question, and Gill's reading is one side of an old…

t: The Sower, the Storm, Legion, and Jairus' Daughter
set: The chapter moves across Galilean towns and villages, out onto the Sea of Galilee, and across it to the region of the Gerasenes on the eastern shore, a mostly Gentile area of the Decapolis where a steep bank runs down to the water. The best-known candidate for the site is Kursi, where the shore is steep.

his.t: Women supporting a rabbi was unusual, and Joanna's husband served Herod's household.
Their region was mostly Gentile, which explains the herd of pigs.

cus.t: Seed was scattered by hand before plowing, so some landed on paths, rock and thorns.
Her bleeding made her ritually unclean, so touching Jesus' cloak was a bold risk.

cu: Sowing was done by hand-scattering seed before plowing, so some seed inevitably fell on the footpaths that crossed a field, on thin rocky soil, and among thorn roots, exactly as the parable says. Women traveling with a rabbi and supporting him from their own means was unusual, and Luke notes that one of them, Joanna, was the wife of an official in Herod's household.

ot.n: The prophet's commission to speak to people who hear without understanding, quoted in verse 10.
God's word as rain and seed that does not return empty, the background to the sower.
The Lord stilling the storm for sailors in distress.
The laws on a woman's bleeding, behind the woman's fear and secrecy in verses 44-47.
Elijah and Elisha restoring children to their parents, which prepares for Jairus' daughter.

im.c: Jesus Calming the Tempest, by Gustave Doré
im.k: Public domain — Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Ryle takes the parable as a series of cautions, the first being "to beware of the devil when we hear the word," since for some hearers the seed is plucked away almost as soon as it is sown. He warns that "we may be warm admirers of favorite preachers" and yet remain stony-ground hearers, and that "open sin is not the only thing that ruins souls," since the thorns of care and…

Henry treats the disciples' cry "Master, Master, we perish!" as a lesson in what to do with fear: "The way to have our fears silenced is to bring them to Christ, and lay them before him." On Jesus' word to Jairus, he writes that our faith in Christ "should be bold and daring, as well as our zeal for him," and in his shorter commentary observes that "in perfect faith there is…

Spurgeon notes that Jesus, after He began to preach, gave up carpentry and gave His whole being to the work, so He was fed and cared for by the kindness of the godly women who "were glad to minister unto him of their substance." On Jairus, he lingers over the instruction to "believe only": "What a depth lies in those two words!"

Lewis does not comment on Luke, but the preface to The Screwtape Letters speaks to the Gerasene man's story. He says there are "two equal and opposite errors" about devils: to disbelieve in them, or to believe and take an excessive, unhealthy interest in them, and that they are equally pleased by both.

t: The Twelve Sent, the Five Thousand Fed, and the Road to Jerusalem
set: The chapter begins with the Twelve traveling Galilean villages, moves to the grasslands near Bethsaida for the feeding of the five thousand, then to a place of private prayer and a high mountain, which Luke does not name, traditionally Mount Tabor or Mount Hermon.

his.t: Herod Antipas had beheaded John and wondered if Jesus was John raised again.
Many expected a conquering Messiah, so talk of a cross shocked the disciples.

cus.t: Shaking dust off the feet marked leaving non-Jewish land, so here it was a pointed warning.
Sitting in groups of fifty matched the orderly pattern of a pilgrim meal.

cu: Shaking dust off one's feet was a gesture pious Jews made when leaving non-Jewish territory, so applied to a town that rejects the message it is a pointed sign of separation. Groups of fifty on the grass are the orderly arrangement of a pilgrim meal. Peter's "three shelters" are the booths of the Feast of Tabernacles.

ot.n: The cloud on Sinai and Moses entering it, behind the cloud on the mountain in verses 34-35.
The promise of a prophet like Moses whom the people must heed, echoed in "Listen to Him!"
Elijah calling down fire on a king's soldiers, which James and John recall in verse 54.
Elijah calling Elisha away from his plow, the background to verses 61-62.
Elisha feeding a hundred men with twenty loaves, a smaller precedent for the feeding of the five thousand.

im.c: The Transfiguration, by Gustave Doré (1866)
im.k: Public domain — Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Ryle takes "take up his cross daily" as proof of the absolute need for daily self-denial: "We ought to fight a daily battle, and war a daily warfare," and he asks pointedly, "Where is our daily carrying of the cross?" On the Transfiguration, he stresses that Moses and Elijah were seen alive and in glory, so believers who have died are "not lost, but gone before us," and that…

Henry points out that Moses and Elijah spoke of Jesus' death as His departure, an "exodus," which "made it not formidable" and let Him see it as a move to a better world. He applies the same view to Christians, who may think of death as being "received up" with Christ. On James and John, he writes of Jesus' correction: "Have you not been taught to love your enemies...

Hultgren observes that the Greek term for "departure" in verse 31 is exodus, so Moses and Elijah "speak then of Jesus' exodus from this world through his suffering, death, and resurrection into heaven." He also notes that both men had received revelation on mountains, Moses on Sinai and Elijah on Horeb, and concludes that the Transfiguration shows "the way of God for Jesus…

Lewis does not comment on Luke, but near the end of Mere Christianity he turns Jesus' words about losing one's life into a principle that, he says, "runs through all life." Christ does not ask for a share of our time or money but for us, to put to death the natural self, and he says the way to a real self is to give it up: "lose your life and you will save it." He…

t: The Seventy-Two, the Good Samaritan, and Mary and Martha
set: The mission of the seventy-two takes in towns Jesus planned to visit, including Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum around the Sea of Galilee. The Good Samaritan is set on the road from Jerusalem down to Jericho, which drops about 3,300 feet in roughly seventeen miles through rocky, cave-filled country, famous for robbers.

his.t: Jews and Samaritans were bitter rivals, split over worship and centuries of mistrust.
It drops about 3,300 feet in 17 miles through rocky hills, a known haunt of robbers.

cus.t: A priest or Levite touching a corpse became unclean, which may explain why they avoided him.
Sitting at a teacher's feet was the place of a disciple, usually a man's role.

cu: A priest or Levite who touched what looked like a corpse would become ritually unclean for a time, which may be part of why they "passed by on the other side" of a man left half dead. Samaritans and Jews were enemies, so the hero of the story is the last person Jesus' hearers would have chosen. Oil and wine were everyday first aid, and two denarii, two days' wages, would pay for a long stay at an inn.

ot.n: The table of seventy nations, which the Greek Old Testament counts as seventy-two, behind the number sent out.
"Love the Lord your God with all your heart" — the first half of the lawyer's answer.
"Love your neighbor as yourself" — the second half, and the verse the parable explains.
The fall of the morning star, sometimes linked to Jesus' vision of Satan's fall.
Treading on the lion and the cobra, background to the authority over snakes and scorpions.

im.c: The Good Samaritan, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Ryle notes that Jesus sent the seventy-two "two and two," which he says "deserves remark, and ought to be remembered in modern missionary work." On Martha, he rejects the idea that "one thing is needful" means only one dish of food, since by that logic the "good part" Mary chose would be a good portion of the feast she picked for herself.

Henry reads "the one thing needful" as what Mary chose: "sitting at Christ's feet, to hear his word." Martha "was troubled about many things, when she should have applied herself to one; godliness unites the heart, which the world had divided." Her care and work were good in their proper season, he says, but now she had something unspeakably more needful to do first.

Guzik notes that when the seventy-two came back thrilled by their authority over demons, Jesus pointed them away from what they had done for God and toward what God had done for them, that their names were written in heaven. On the parable, he observes that Jesus "allowed the parable to answer the lawyer's question and guide the application," ending with "Go and do likewise."

t: Teach Us to Pray: Prayer, Beelzebul, Jonah, and Woes
set: Luke does not name the place where Jesus was praying or where the later scenes unfold. The setting is the long journey toward Jerusalem that began in chapter 9, and the final scene is a meal in a Pharisee's house.

his.t: Other Jewish exorcists worked in this era, hence "by whom do your sons cast them out?"
Pharisees were respected for strict purity and tithing, which makes Jesus' woes startling.

cus.t: A village home had one room, so waking for a late guest meant waking the whole family.
Pharisees washed before meals for purity, so Jesus skipping it was noticed.

cu: Village houses were small, with one room for the whole family to sleep, so the neighbor who says he and his children are in bed cannot rise without waking everyone. Bread was baked daily, so a family with a surprise guest at night might have nothing left. Pharisaic tradition required washing before a meal beyond what the Law itself commanded for ordinary people, which is why the host is surprised.

ot.n: The magicians' words "This is the finger of God" — the phrase Jesus uses in verse 20.
Nineveh's repentance at Jonah's preaching, the sign Jesus points to.
The Queen of Sheba coming from far away to hear Solomon's wisdom.
Uncleanness from touching a grave, behind the "unmarked graves" image.
The killing of Zechariah in the temple court, the last martyr Jesus names.

im.c: The Dumb Man Possessed, by Gustave Doré (1866)
im.k: Public domain — Project Gutenberg

cm.n: Henry calls "Lord, teach us to pray" "itself a good prayer, and a very needful one, for it is a hard thing to pray well, and it is Jesus Christ only that can teach us, by his word and Spirit, how to pray." On "ask, and it shall be given," he adds that you will receive "either the thing itself or that which is equivalent; either the thorn in the flesh removed, or grace…

Ryle takes the parable of the friend at midnight as a lesson in "the importance of perseverance in prayer," since if boldness succeeds so well between people, "how much more may we expect it to obtain mercies when used in prayer to God." He notes that the Greek word for importunity is used only here in the New Testament, and warns against hunting for "far-fetched allegorical…

Spurgeon says the disciple's request shows how far Jesus' own prayer lay above anything he had known, and that "if we are to pray aright, we must be taught of God, by his Holy Spirit." We are full of infirmities, and prayer is where we feel them most, but "the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities," so we may breathe this very prayer: "Lord, teach us to pray."

Lewis does not comment on Luke, but in Letters to Malcolm he writes about this prayer. He says that for many years after his conversion he used no ready-made prayers except the Lord's Prayer, and then realized that trying to make it his daily bread meant counting on more mental and spiritual strength than he had.

t: Beware of Greed, Do Not Worry, Be Ready
set: Luke names no place. The chapter is set during the journey toward Jerusalem begun at 9:51, before a crowd so large, "many thousands," that people were trampling one another. The scene continues straight from the hostile dinner at the end of chapter 11.

his.t: Opposition was rising, so His words about fearing those who kill the body were real.
Land was family wealth, and rabbis were often asked to settle inheritance disputes.

cus.t: Sparrows were the cheapest bird sold for food, five for two small coins.
Servants waiting for a master's late return kept their robes tucked up and lamps lit.

cu: Sparrows were the cheapest bird sold for food, and Luke has five sold for two pennies, a small coin worth about one sixteenth of a denarius. Matthew has two for one penny, so in Luke's version the fifth is thrown in free, a detail often noted as heightening the point. Rabbis were commonly asked to settle inheritance disputes, which explains the man's request.

ot.n: A household divided against itself, quoted in verse 53.
God providing food for the ravens, behind "consider the ravens."
The labor of a man who leaves everything to someone else, close to the rich fool's situation.
Do not fear what others fear; regard the Lord as holy and let Him be your fear.
God as the shepherd who gathers His flock, behind "little flock."

im.c: The Foolish Virgins, by James Tissot (1886-1894) — Matthew 25's parable of lamps and readiness, which echoes Luke 12:35-40
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Ryle observes that there is no sin "to which the heart is more prone" than covetousness, and that the man who stores up treasure for himself but is not rich toward God is the one God calls a fool.

Henry sums up the rich man's mistakes, among them that he counts as treasure what is laid up for the body and the present life, and that he takes no care to be "rich in the account of God." On "little flock," he notes that though it is outnumbered and "in danger of being overpowered," Christ's will is that it not be afraid: "see yourselves safe under the protection and conduct…

Spurgeon sets the rich fool beside the penitent thief of the day before: to one Christ said, "Today shalt thou be with me in Paradise," but to the impenitent rich man, "This night thy soul shall be required of thee." On "seek His kingdom," he says you get the spiritual blessing first, and then "the common blessings of life shall be added unto you."

Lewis does not comment on Luke, but in the chapter on hope in Mere Christianity he gives an everyday version of "seek His kingdom, and these things will be added." He argues that the Christians who did most for the present world were those who thought most about the next, and sums it up: aim at heaven and you will get earth "thrown in"; aim at earth and you will get…

t: Repent, the Fig Tree, and the Narrow Door
set: Verse 22 says Jesus is "making His way toward Jerusalem," so everything in this chapter happens on the road, in towns and synagogues, with the city and its coming conflict ahead.

his.t: Pilate killed Galilean worshipers at their sacrifices, shocking the whole region.
Antipas ruled Galilee and had killed John, so a warning about him was no empty threat.

cus.t: Many Jews allowed leading an animal to water on the Sabbath, which Jesus uses in His answer.
Both were everyday items, so small things growing large was easy to picture.

cu: A synagogue leader was responsible for order in the service, so his objection in verse 14 is a real concern for him. Many Jews of the time allowed leading an animal to water on the Sabbath, which is why Jesus' argument in verse 15 lands so hard.

ot.n: God planted Israel as a vineyard and looked for good fruit. The fig tree parable continues the same image.
A great tree in which the birds of the air nest is a biblical picture of a kingdom with wide shelter, which sits behind the mustard seed parable.
Sarah prepares three measures of flour for her heavenly guests, the same amount used in the leaven parable.
"Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity." Jesus uses the psalmist's words in verse 27.
"Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord." The pilgrim song Jesus quotes in verse 35.
God is pictured as an eagle who hovers over its young and spreads its wings, a parallel to the hen and her chicks.

im.c: The Vine Dresser and the Fig Tree, by James Tissot (1886-1894), the parable of Luke 13:6-9
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: On the Galileans and the tower, Henry draws the line that "we cannot judge of men's sins by their sufferings in this world." Jesus does not explain why bad things happen. He turns the news into a question for the listener: if they perished, you deserve the same, so repent. On the fig tree he reads Israel, and every church that enjoys privileges without bearing fruit.

On the narrow door Henry stresses that the word is "strive," not merely "seek," because many will seek and fail. His sharpest warning is for the people who say they ate and drank with Jesus and heard Him teach, yet are not known by Him. "Many are ruined by an ill-grounded hope of heaven" that they never examined.

Gill takes the Galileans of verse 1 to be possibly followers of Judas of Galilee, killed by Pilate while sacrificing, so that their blood was literally mingled with the offering. On the bent woman, he says her condition was "brought upon her by an evil spirit, by Satan" with God's permission, and had lasted so long that it was thought incurable.

Lewis does not comment on Luke 13, but his chapter on hell in The Problem of Pain speaks to the shut door of verses 25-28. He argues that Christ's own words about hell are blunt and that the idea cannot be dropped.

t: The Great Banquet and the Cost of Following
set: Jesus is still on the road to Jerusalem (13:22) and spends a Sabbath meal in the home of a leading Pharisee. The Sabbath dinner was a main social event of the week, and those invited were chosen carefully. The guests are "watching Him closely" (v.1), so what looks like a friendly meal is partly a trap.

his.t: Large crowds followed Jesus toward Jerusalem, so He warns them of the cost.
Herod's building projects made towers and big builds familiar, so counting the cost was concrete.

cus.t: Seats nearest the host were places of honor, and guests competed for them.
A dinner was expected to be repaid, so inviting the poor broke the pattern.

cu: Seating at a banquet followed rank: the places nearest the host were the places of honor, and guests jockeyed for them (v.7). Invitations were an exchange, since a dinner was expected to be repaid with another dinner (v.12).

ot.n: "Do not claim a place among his great men; it is better for him to say to you, 'Come up here.'" The proverb behind Jesus' advice on seats.
The Lord of hosts prepares a banquet for all peoples, the picture behind the man's cry about eating at the feast of God.
God's people were to care for the poor and the stranger, the kind of guests Jesus tells the host to invite.
Honor your father and mother. The call to put Christ first in verse 26 sets this command in its place and does not cancel it.

im.c: The Last Supper, by James Tissot (1886-1894). Used here for the table-fellowship setting of Luke 14, where Jesus teaches at a meal; it does not depict this chapter's events.
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry sees the invited guests who refuse as the Jews who had every offer and turned it down, and the poor gathered from the streets as the Gentiles and the outcasts. His warning is plain: "They that will not have Christ when they may shall not have him when they would." On the host who should invite the poor, he says charity is not a loss, since those who give to the helpless…

On the cost of discipleship, Henry says that Christ wants no one to follow Him blindly, so He lays out the price before anyone starts. The builder and the king show that a half-finished tower or a lost war is worse than never beginning. Henry also stresses that grace is sufficient to finish what is begun.

Gill describes dropsy as a "preternatural collection of serum, or water in some part of the body," and thinks the Pharisees may have placed the man there to see whether Jesus would heal on the Sabbath.

Lewis does not comment on Luke 14, but his chapter "The Great Sin" in Mere Christianity bears on verses 7-11. He calls pride the utmost evil and the sin behind all others, and says it is essentially competitive: the proud person takes pleasure in being above others, not simply in having something.

t: The Lost Sheep, the Lost Coin, and the Lost Sons
set: Jesus is still traveling toward Jerusalem and is surrounded by people whom respectable society kept at a distance. Sharing a meal meant fellowship, so "eats with them" (v.2) is the real complaint.

his.t: Respectable society kept tax collectors and notorious sinners at a distance.
Many Jews lived across the Mediterranean, so a son might wander far into foreign lands.

cus.t: A father rarely divided his estate while alive, so the younger son's request was an insult.
Dignified older men didn't run, so the father's sprint broke every social rule.

cu: A father did not normally divide his estate while alive, and for a son to ask for his share (v.12) was to wish him dead in effect. A dignified older man did not run, so the father's sprint to meet his son (v.20) breaks the social rules. The best robe, a ring, and sandals (v.22) were signs of full sonship, since hired servants and slaves were often barefoot. A "fattened calf" meant a feast for the whole village.

ot.n: God promises to search for His scattered sheep and bring them back, the background for the shepherd who goes after the one.
The Lord as shepherd who leads and restores, the picture behind the shepherd carrying the sheep home.
God as a father whose compassion will not let Israel go, even after rebellion.
Ephraim, God's dear son, whom He still remembers and for whom His heart yearns.
"We all, like sheep, have gone astray," which lies beneath the whole chapter.

im.c: The Return of the Prodigal Son, by James Tissot (1886-1894), Luke 15:20
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry reads the lost sheep as a sinner lost to God, to the flock, and to himself, and notes that "God follows backsliding sinners with the calls of his word and the strivings of his Spirit." Of the coin he says "the soul is silver, of intrinsic worth and value," even when it has fallen into the dirt.

On the prodigal son Henry reads the far country as the world, where sinners take up residence, and notes that "he came to himself" means he had been out of his mind, since sin is "a state of madness and frenzy." On the father running, he writes: "Here were feet of mercy, and those feet quick-paced." On the older brother, he says that those who are "comparatively innocents…

Gill reads the ninety-nine "just persons, which need no repentance" as the scribes and Pharisees who thought themselves righteous, and he insists that real repentance includes faith in Christ and a true leaving of sin. On the coin, he takes the woman as Christ, the lamp as the Gospel, and the sweeping as its preaching.

t: The Shrewd Manager and the Rich Man and Lazarus
set: Jesus is still on the road to Jerusalem. A wealthy landowner with a manager who handles his accounts and debts was a familiar figure, and large estates often rented land to tenants who repaid in oil or grain, as the two debtors do here.

his.t: Wealthy landowners used managers and rented land to tenants who paid in oil or grain.
Luke says the Pharisees loved money, so Jesus' warning struck close to home.

cus.t: Managers often added a commission to debts, which this manager may have cut from his own share.
Lazarus lay at the gate with dogs licking his sores, showing how complete his neglect was.

cu: A manager in this world often added a commission to the debts he recorded. If the manager cut that commission, he gave up his own profit and not the master's money, which would explain the master's praise for his shrewdness. Dogs were unclean scavengers, so their licking Lazarus's sores (v.21) adds to his misery.

ot.n: God commands open-handed generosity to the poor at one's gate, the duty the rich man ignored.
True worship includes sharing food with the hungry and sheltering the poor.
"Whoever oppresses the poor shows contempt for their Maker."
A prophetic warning to the comfortable who lie on couches of ivory and feast while others suffer.
The Mosaic law on divorce, behind Jesus' short teaching in verse 18.

im.c: The Poor Lazarus at the Rich Man's Door, by James Tissot (1886-1894), Luke 16:19-21
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: On the shrewd manager, Henry says we are only stewards of what God owns, so we should spend it on piety and charity, because "we may make to ourselves friends with it." He warns that "God withholds his grace from covetous worldly people more than we are aware of," since money is called the "unrighteous mammon" and cannot be trusted as true riches.

On the rich man and Lazarus, Henry takes the story as a warning about luxury and indifference to the poor: one enjoyed comfort and ended in torment, and the other was comforted. When the rich man asks for a messenger from the dead, Abraham sends him back to the Scriptures.

Gill says the master commended the steward not for dishonesty but for shrewdness: "the wit, and not the goodness of the man is commended." He calls riches the "mammon of unrighteousness" because they are so often gotten or used wrongly, and he denies that money can purchase God's favor.

Lewis does not comment on Luke 16, but his short novel The Great Divorce imagines the chasm of verse 26 as a bus ride from a gray town to the edge of heaven. The visitors are free to stay and change, but most choose to go back, because they will not give up some small attachment such as pride, grievance, or comfort.

t: Forgiveness, Faith, Ten Lepers, and the Coming Kingdom
set: Verse 11 puts Jesus "between Samaria and Galilee," on the border region where Jews and Samaritans lived uneasily side by side. A group of ten lepers could include both Jews and a Samaritan, since shared suffering broke down the usual barriers.

his.t: The border region mixed Jews and Samaritans, who normally kept their distance.
Many expected the kingdom with signs and force, so Jesus' answer surprised them.

cus.t: A priest had to declare a leper clean, so going to him meant trusting before healing.
Lepers had to stay away and call out "unclean," so these men stood far off.

cu: A person with leprosy had to be examined by a priest to be declared clean (Leviticus 13-14), so Jesus' command "Go, show yourselves to the priests" asks for obedience before any visible healing. Jews and Samaritans avoided each other, which gives weight to Jesus' words in verse 18 about "this foreigner." A mulberry tree had deep, tough roots, so telling it to be uprooted and planted in the sea was a picture of the…

ot.n: The laws for diagnosing and cleansing leprosy, including showing oneself to the priest.
Naaman, a foreign leper, healed by obedience and a washing in the Jordan.
The flood in the days of Noah.
The destruction of Sodom and the fate of Lot's wife.
The Son of Man coming with great glory, behind Jesus' use of the title in verses 22-30.

im.c: The Healing of Ten Lepers, by James Tissot (1886-1894), Luke 17:11-19
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry says giving offense is a great sin and forgiving a great duty, and that "Christians should be of a forgiving spirit, willing to make the best of every body." On the apostles' request for more faith, he says that growth in faith is something to press for in prayer, for "the increase of our faith is what we should earnestly desire." On the unprofitable servants he writes…

On the ten lepers, Henry observes that ingratitude is common and that thanks often come from the least expected person, here a Samaritan. On the kingdom, he says it is spiritual and does not come with outward display: "The kingdom of God will not change men's outward condition, but their hearts and lives." On the warnings of Noah and Lot, he reads them as calls to watchfulness…

Gill says the image of a tree uprooted and planted in the sea shows "what great things are done by faith," even when the faith is very small. He notes of the ten lepers that "instances of gratitude are few," and that Jews regarded Samaritans as strangers.

t: Persistent Prayer, Humility, and the Cost of Following
set: Jesus is nearly at the end of the road to Jerusalem. The temple (v.10) is the setting of the Pharisee and tax collector parable, and the story ends at Jericho (v.35), about fifteen miles northeast of Jerusalem and the usual last stop for pilgrims coming up from the Jordan Valley.

his.t: Tax collectors worked for Rome and were hated, as the one in the temple shows.
It lay about 15 miles from Jerusalem, the last stop before the long climb.

cus.t: Widows had few legal protections, so a widow pleading with a judge was truly powerless.
Pharisees fasted Mondays and Thursdays and tithed carefully, so his claims were real.

cu: Pharisees fasted twice a week, on Mondays and Thursdays, and tithed carefully, so the Pharisee's claims in verse 12 are not exaggerations by the standards of his day. Beating the breast was a sign of deep grief and shame. Widows had little legal standing and relied on judges for justice, so a judge's indifference to one was a serious wrong.

ot.n: God hears the cry of the widow and the fatherless and promises to act.
David's cry, "Have mercy on me, O God," the pattern for the tax collector's prayer.
The commandments Jesus lists to the ruler, which he claims to have kept.
"Then the eyes of the blind will be opened." A mark of the Messiah's coming.
"Is anything too hard for the Lord?" The background to "What is impossible with man is possible with God."

im.c: The Pharisee and the Publican, by James Tissot (1886-1894), Luke 18:9-14
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry takes the key to the widow parable from its opening verse, that "men ought always to pray, and not to faint." If an unjust judge yields to persistence, the righteous Father will much more hear His elect who cry day and night.

On the rich ruler, Henry says riches are a great hindrance: "How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!" He calls the camel and the needle a proverbial image of the extremely hard, and says salvation is impossible by human strength, but "the things which are impossible with men are possible with God." Of the blind man, he says: "Those who would speed…

Gill says the widow parable is meant to encourage prayer so that believers do not faint under trials, and he argues from lesser to greater: if an unjust judge gives way, God will surely avenge His elect.

t: Zacchaeus, the Ten Minas, and the Entry into Jerusalem
set: The chapter begins in Jericho, a major tax and trade center on the road between the Jordan and Jerusalem, and ends in Jerusalem itself. The final climb (about 17 miles, rising nearly 3,500 feet) leads past Bethphage and Bethany to the Mount of Olives, from which the temple and the whole city are visible.

his.t: It was a rich tax and trade center, so its chief tax collector was wealthy.
Herod's son traveled to Rome to claim a kingdom, much like the nobleman in the story.

cus.t: Chief tax collectors bought the right to collect for Rome and kept the extra.
Spreading cloaks on the road honored a king, as when Jehu was crowned.

cu: A chief tax collector bought the right to collect taxes for Rome and kept what he collected above the quota, so Zacchaeus was both rich and despised. Wealthy men did not run or climb trees, so his sprint shows how badly he wanted to see Jesus. Fourfold restitution was the penalty the Law required for stolen sheep (Exodus 22:1), and Zacchaeus applies it voluntarily to himself.

ot.n: The fourfold penalty for stealing a sheep, which Zacchaeus applies to himself.
"I will seek the lost," God's promise to seek and save His flock.
The king coming to Jerusalem on a colt, fulfilled in the entry.
"Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord," quoted by the crowd.
"The stones will cry out from the wall," behind Jesus' answer to the Pharisees.
The two prophetic texts joined in Jesus' words at the temple.

im.c: Zacchaeus in the Sycamore Awaiting the Passage of Jesus, by James Tissot (1886-1894), Luke 19:1-10
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry sees in Zacchaeus the proof of true repentance: a rich chief tax collector climbs a tree, receives Christ gladly, gives half his goods to the poor, and repays fourfold. Christ "came to save even the chief of publicans." On the parable of the pounds, he says it corrects the expectation of an immediate kingdom, so that the faithful are rewarded in proportion to their work…

On the entry into Jerusalem, Henry notes the disciples' joy for the miracles they had seen, including the raising of Lazarus, and says the humble procession shows that "Christ is entitled to a dominion over all the creatures." On the weeping, he says Jesus wept because Jerusalem "has not improved the day of her opportunities." On the temple, he writes, "The temple is a house…

Gill reads Zacchaeus's offer as genuine repentance and ties verse 10 to God's purpose "to seek and save that which was lost." In the parable, the nobleman is Christ, who goes away to receive his kingdom and returns; the servants are ministers entrusted with gifts, since "the ministry is a trade and merchandise." On the stones, he says the praise of Christ cannot be suppressed.

set: Jesus is teaching in the temple courts in Jerusalem during the week before His crucifixion. The courts were the busiest public space in the city and the natural place for rabbis to teach and debate.

his.t: Chief priests and elders ran the temple under Rome, and Jesus threatened their authority.
Many Jews hated the tax to Caesar, so the question was a trap.

cus.t: The silver denarius, a day's wage, carried the emperor's image and a claim to divinity.
A childless widow married her husband's brother to continue the family line.

cu: A denarius was a Roman silver coin worth a day's labor, stamped with the emperor's head and an inscription calling him son of a god, so many Jews found it offensive to carry. Asking "by what authority" was a formal challenge, as a teacher without recognized ordination was suspect.

ot.n: The song of the vineyard, in which Israel is the vineyard and God looks for justice but finds bloodshed.
"The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone," quoted in verse 17.
The law of levirate marriage, the basis of the Sadducees' puzzle.
"I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob," the text Jesus uses to prove the resurrection.
"The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at My right hand," the verse behind Jesus' question about David's Lord.

im.c: The Tribute Money, by James Tissot (1886-1894), Luke 20:20-26
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry says the leaders' refusal to answer honestly about John means they lose the right to a direct answer: "Those that bury the knowledge they have are justly denied further knowledge." He reads the vineyard as the church's privileges, with God as landlord and the prophets as His messengers, and notes that "those who reject Christ's ministers would reject Christ himself." On…

On taxes, Henry says Jesus separates civil duty from religious duty: we owe Caesar civil obedience, but only God can claim the heart. On the resurrection, he warns that without this doctrine "all religion falls to the ground." On David's Lord, he says Christ is David's Lord as God and David's Son as man. Of the scribes, he writes that "dissembled piety is double iniquity."

Gill identifies the vineyard with the Jewish people and the servants with the prophets, and ties the vineyard being given "to others" to the Romans' judgment on Judea and the Gentiles' reception of the gospel.

t: The Widow's Gift and the Coming Destruction
set: Jesus is still in the temple courts and sits near the treasury, where thirteen trumpet-shaped chests received offerings. The temple, rebuilt by Herod the Great, was one of the great buildings of the ancient world, with stones some of which measured over thirty feet.

his.t: Herod's rebuilt temple was a wonder of the world, which makes the prediction shocking.
Rome destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in AD 70, about forty years later.

cus.t: Thirteen trumpet-shaped chests held offerings, so large gifts were heard dropping in.
Two lepta were the smallest coins, worth a tiny fraction of a day's wage.

cu: Two small copper coins, the lepta, were the smallest coin in circulation and worth a small fraction of a day's wage. The wealthy often dropped large coins noisily into the trumpet-shaped receptacles, so the giving was public. Many in Jesus' time expected a Messiah to rescue Jerusalem and punish Rome, so His statement that the temple would be thrown down was shocking to the listeners.

ot.n: One like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, the source of verse 27.
Signs in the heavens and on earth before the day of the Lord.
The fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, an earlier case of the city's destruction.
God's special care for widows, behind Jesus' praise of the widow.
"The heavens will vanish like smoke," with God's salvation lasting forever, behind verse 33.

im.c: The Widow's Mite, by James Tissot (1886-1894), Luke 21:1-4
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons
