cm.n: Henry sees the widow's gift as proof that "charity to the poor is a main matter in religion." Christ notices both how much we give and how willingly we give, and He values her small gift above the rich men's larger ones.

Henry says Jesus uses the imagery of sun, moon, and stars as figures for the fall of Jerusalem, and that the same language points ahead to the last day and the terror it brings to people without faith. On the fig tree, he says we read the signs of the times as we read the budding of trees: when the causes appear, so does the advance of God's judgments and kingdom.

Gill says the widow gave "all the living she had" and values her gift by her ability to give, not its amount, so she gave more than the rich. He reads the armies of verse 20 as the Roman forces under Titus, and says that once the city was besieged its destruction was near and no deliverance was to be expected.

Lewis does not comment on Luke 21 by verse, but his essay "The World's Last Night" takes up the saying in verse 32 that "this generation will not pass away." He treats it candidly as a hard saying that Christians cannot ignore.

t: The Last Supper, Gethsemane, and Peter's Denial
set: The chapter moves from an upper room in Jerusalem, to the Mount of Olives across the Kidron Valley, to the house of the high priest. Jerusalem was packed with pilgrims for Passover, and a large furnished upper room (v.12) was typical of a house rented out to pilgrims for the feast.

his.t: Pilgrims packed Jerusalem for Passover, which is why the leaders wanted a quiet arrest.
The temple had its own guard, which the chief priests used to arrest Jesus at night.

cus.t: The meal recalled Israel's rescue from Egypt, with unleavened bread, bitter herbs and wine.
Gethsemane means "olive press," from the oil pressed on that hillside.

cu: The Passover meal recalled God's deliverance of Israel from Egypt, with unleavened bread, bitter herbs, and cups of wine through the evening. Jesus gives new meaning to the bread and the cup (the "new covenant," v.20). Reclining at table was the normal posture for a formal meal, and the greatest place was at the host's side.

ot.n: The first Passover, the meal Jesus celebrates and reinterprets.
The promise of a new covenant, which Jesus says is fulfilled in His blood.
Moses sprinkles the people with covenant blood, the pattern behind "the new covenant in My blood."
"He was numbered with the transgressors," quoted in verse 37.
The Son of Man seated at God's right hand, behind Jesus' answer in verse 69.
The Son of Man receiving authority, the source of the title.

im.c: Jesus Praying in the Garden, by Gustave Doré (1866), Luke 22:39-46
im.k: Public domain — Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry says Satan entering Judas shows that whoever betrays Christ or His truth is moved by him, and observes that when you see Judas "communing with the chief priests," mischief is being planned. On the Lord's Supper, he calls it "a commemorative sign or memorial of a Christ already come" that recalls His body broken and blood shed.

On Peter's denial predicted, Henry notes that "Christ knows us better than we know ourselves," and on Gethsemane, he describes the sleeping disciples as "sleeping for sorrow." On the look, he writes: "one look from Christ melted him into tears of godly sorrow for sin." The look is the center of the scene, because the same Lord whom Peter denied is the one who turns to him.

Gill says Satan entered Judas not "corporeally, as he did into those that were possessed by him," but into his heart, stirring his corruptions. He calls the Lord's Supper "a commemoration of the sacrifice of Christ," not a repetition of it.

t: The Trial, the Crucifixion, and the Burial
set: The council takes Jesus to Pilate, the Roman governor, who normally lived in Caesarea but came to Jerusalem for Passover to keep order. Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, was also in the city for the feast (v.7).

his.t: Pilate governed Judea for about ten years and was known for harshness toward Jews.
Antipas was in Jerusalem for Passover and had long wanted to see Jesus.

cus.t: Rome used it for slaves and rebels, a slow, public death meant to terrify.
Burial had to happen before the Sabbath began, so the women prepared spices later.

cu: Crucifixion was a Roman punishment for slaves, rebels, and the lowest criminals, designed to be public and slow. Jews who were hung on a tree were considered cursed (Deuteronomy 21:23), which made the cross an offense to many Jews. Burial before sundown was required by the Law, and with the Sabbath beginning at sunset (v.54), the women had to wait until Sunday to bring spices.

ot.n: The silent, innocent sufferer who bears sin and intercedes for transgressors.
The righteous sufferer mocked by onlookers, whose garments are divided by lots.
"Into Your hands I commit my spirit," the verse Jesus prays in verse 46.
"They will say to the mountains, Cover us," which Jesus quotes in verse 30.
The sun going down at noon and the earth darkened in broad daylight.
The temple veil separating the holy place from the Most Holy Place.

im.c: The Crucifixion, by Gustave Doré (1866), Luke 23:33-46
im.k: Public domain — Project Gutenberg

cm.n: Henry says Herod, who hoped to see a miracle, was "more abusive to Christ than Pilate was," since his greater knowledge made his contempt more deliberate. Of Simon of Cyrene being forced to carry the cross, he writes, "It was pity, but a cruel pity," meant to keep Jesus alive for more suffering.

On "Father, forgive them," Henry says the prayer shows that Christ's death was meant to secure forgiveness for sinners, and that their ignorance partly excuses them and makes them objects of prayer. Of the penitent criminal, he says it proves "even great sinners, if they be true penitents" can find mercy.

Gill says Herod and Pilate, who had been at odds (possibly over the Galileans of Luke 13:1), were reconciled by the trial and united against Christ, which he connects with Psalm 2:1. He reads "today you will be with Me in Paradise" as heaven, not an earthly garden, and argues that the word "today" shows Christ's soul went straight to heaven at death.

Lewis does not comment on Luke 23, but "The Perfect Penitent" in Mere Christianity reflects on why the cross happened. He says the fact that Christ's death put us right with God matters more than any one theory of how it works. His own best attempt is that only a perfectly good person could repent perfectly, so God became man to offer that repentance for us.

t: The Empty Tomb and the Road to Emmaus
set: The chapter begins at the garden tomb outside Jerusalem, follows two travelers on a seven-mile road to Emmaus (about 11 km), and ends on the Mount of Olives near Bethany, where Jesus is carried up. The exact site of Emmaus is uncertain, and scholars have proposed several villages west and northwest of Jerusalem.

his.t: The women came at dawn on the first day, after resting on the Sabbath.
Emmaus lay a few miles from Jerusalem, and its exact site is still debated.

cus.t: Spices honored the body, so the women did not expect a resurrection.
The host broke and blessed bread to start a meal, when they recognized Him.

cu: Jewish tradition set the first day of the week as the day after the Sabbath, the day when the women could finally bring spices. Burial spices were to honor the body, so the women do not expect a resurrection. Sharing a meal made a guest a friend, and the way Jesus takes, blesses, breaks, and gives the bread (v.30) echoes the feeding of the five thousand and the Last Supper.

ot.n: "You will not abandon me to the grave," the psalm Peter later cites for the resurrection (Acts 2:25-31).
The suffering servant who is raised and sees the fruit of his suffering.
"On the third day He will raise us up," a background for the third-day language.
Three days in the fish, a sign Jesus linked to His own burial and rising (Luke 11:30).
The seed of the woman who crushes the serpent, the first hint of a suffering victor.
The promise to pour out God's Spirit, the "promise of My Father" of verse 49.

im.c: The Pilgrims of Emmaus on the Road, by James Tissot (1886-1894), Luke 24:13-35
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry praises the women for coming to the tomb on the morning after the Sabbath, saying that "the zeal of some provokes others." He reads the angels' question as a rebuke to anyone who seeks Christ among dead idols, human traditions, or created things: "a reproof is given to those that look for him among the dead." On Emmaus, he notes that "their eyes were held, that they…

On the burning hearts, Henry says the disciples knew Jesus afterward because His teaching had moved them, and he links it to preaching that explains Scripture plainly and centers on Christ. He calls Christ "the best expositor of scripture," and says: "Christ's way of working faith in the soul, and gaining the throne there, is by opening the understanding." On the ascension, he…

Gill reads the angels' question as meaning that Christ, though dead, was now alive and not to be found in a tomb, and that He is found among living saints, not "dead sinners, or lifeless professors." Of the burning hearts, he says His words carried such power that "their hearts were warmed and glowed within them." He says Jesus ate the fish not from need but to prove He had…

set: John deliberately opens before Genesis-style time itself, then narrows in on a very specific place: Bethany beyond the Jordan, a different location from the Bethany near Jerusalem, where John the Baptist carried out his baptizing ministry.

his.t: Greek thinkers used logos for the order behind the world, and John fills it with a person.
Priests asked John if he was the Christ, Elijah, or the Prophet.

cus.t: Washing was common in Judaism, but John's baptism called for repentance.
Lambs were offered daily and at Passover, a picture of sacrifice.

cu: Rabbis of the era were typically addressed as "Rabbi" by genuine students seeking to learn from them — Nathanael and Andrew's disciples both use the title within their very first exchange with Jesus, signaling they already recognize Him as a teacher worth following.

ot.n: "In the beginning" — the deliberate opening echo that frames John's whole prologue as a second creation account.
"A voice of one calling in the wilderness" — quoted directly by John the Baptist to describe his own role.
Jacob's ladder, with angels ascending and descending — directly echoed in Jesus' closing promise to Nathanael.

im.c: Saint John the Baptist Sees Jesus from Afar, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry stresses why this opening matters practically, not just doctrinally: 'let none say that when we invite them to Christ we would draw them from God, for Christ is with God and is God.' He reads the light shining in darkness as reaching back before the incarnation itself — the eternal Word already at work in human reason and conscience, long before He took on flesh.

Gill traces 'the Word' back to a real linguistic precedent: the Aramaic Targums (Jewish paraphrases of the Old Testament) frequently used the phrase 'the Memra of the Lord' — 'the Word of the Lord' — as a way of referring to God's own active presence.

On Nathanael's confession, the early church father Chrysostom reads it as full recognition, not partial: 'Thou art He who was expected, thou art He who was sought for.' He credits Jesus' unexpected knowledge of Nathanael's private moment under the fig tree as proof enough — evidence Nathanael 'could not doubt for an instant.'

Lewis does not comment on John 1 by verse, but his Miracles chapter "The Grand Miracle" is about verse 14, "The Word became flesh." He calls the Incarnation the central miracle of Christianity and says that every other miracle either prepares for it or flows from it.

set: Cana was a small, unremarkable Galilean village — even Nathanael's own hometown per John 21:2 — a fitting, humble setting for the very first public sign Jesus performs. The chapter then shifts abruptly to Jerusalem's temple courts at Passover, when the city's population swelled dramatically with pilgrims.

his.t: Herod's temple had been under construction for forty-six years.
Jesus goes up for Passover, when crowds and money-changers filled the temple courts.

cus.t: Weddings lasted days, and running out of wine shamed the host.
Large stone jars held water for ritual washing, since stone stayed pure.

cu: The six stone water jars were specifically for Jewish ceremonial washing — stone was preferred because, unlike clay, it couldn't contract ritual impurity. Money changers exchanged ordinary coinage for the Tyrian silver required for the temple tax, and animal sellers supplied pilgrims with sacrifices vetted on-site — legitimate services that had crowded out the Court of the Gentiles' actual purpose.

ot.n: "Zeal for Your house will consume me" — quoted directly by the disciples as they recall this scene.
"A house of prayer for all nations" — the standard Jesus' action restores against the temple's commercialized Court of the Gentiles.
The Lord suddenly coming to His temple to purify it — background for Jesus' unannounced, forceful arrival.

im.c: The Marriage at Cana, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry notes Mary's approach carefully: she doesn't tell Jesus what to do, only states the need — 'they have no wine' — leaving the how entirely to Him. He reads her instruction to the servants, 'whatsoever he saith unto you, do it,' as good counsel for anyone who wants Christ present at their own affairs: don't prescribe the method, just obey whatever He actually says.

Gill works out the real scale of the miracle: six jars holding twenty to thirty gallons each comes to somewhere around one hundred twenty to one hundred eighty gallons of wine — enough, by some contemporary estimates, for over a hundred guests.

Clarke reads Jesus' address to Mary, 'Woman,' as carrying no coldness in the original — a perfectly respectful and even affectionate title in that culture, the same word He later uses to Mary from the cross itself (19:26). He treats her confidence in instructing the servants as a sign of quiet, settled faith, not presumption.

set: The chapter opens somewhere in Jerusalem, likely just after the temple cleansing of chapter 2, then shifts to the Judean countryside where Jesus' disciples baptize, and to Aenon near Salim in the Jordan Valley, where John continued his own ministry.

his.t: A member of the Sanhedrin and a respected teacher of Israel.
Jesus' disciples and John both baptized at once, which stirred rivalry.

cus.t: Teachers often studied by night, away from crowds and scrutiny.
Hebrew and Greek use one word for wind, breath and spirit.

cu: Approaching a rabbi privately at night wasn't unusual for a serious student wanting uninterrupted time, though Nicodemus's caution as a prominent Sanhedrin member also likely reflects real risk to his public standing.

ot.n: The bronze serpent lifted up by Moses in the wilderness — directly applied by Jesus to His own coming crucifixion.
God's promise of cleansing water and a new heart given by His Spirit — background for Jesus' language of being born "of water and the Spirit."
Abraham's willingness to give up his only son Isaac — echoed in God's own giving of His "one and only Son" in v.16.

im.c: Interview between Jesus and Nicodemus, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry reads Nicodemus's nighttime visit sympathetically but honestly: 'Nicodemus was afraid, or ashamed to be seen with Christ, therefore came in the night... though he came by night, yet afterward he owned Christ publicly.' On God's love in v.16, he writes simply, 'behold, and wonder, that the great God should love such a worthless world.'

Poole reads John the Baptist's 'he must increase' through the image John himself had already used of the morning star giving way to sunrise: 'he is the rising sun... he must shine every day more and more. But I must decrease... I must every day decay, and grow less and less, as Christ increaseth.' A willing, joyful fading rather than a bitter one.

Gill notes the real historical shape of John's decrease: not just in public esteem, but quite literally in circumstance — 'quickly after this he was put into prison, and there put to death.' His willing decrease wasn't abstract humility; it led directly and soon to his own execution.

Lewis does not comment on John 3 verse by verse, but "Making and Begetting" in Mere Christianity explains why Jesus is called the only begotten Son (v.16). He says that to beget is to bring forth something of the same kind as yourself, while to make is to produce something different, like a man who begets a child but builds a statue.

set: Jesus deliberately travels through Samaria rather than around it, a route many Jews avoided given centuries of hostility between the two groups. Jacob's well near Sychar still exists today, deep enough (over 100 feet) that the woman's comment about Jesus having "nothing to draw with" makes immediate practical sense.

his.t: Centuries of hostility split Jews from Samaritans over worship and descent.
Samaritans worshiped on Gerizim, while Jews insisted on Jerusalem.

cus.t: Women drew water in cool morning or evening, so noon hints she avoided others.
Jews often avoided Samaritan cups and bowls as unclean.

cu: Jewish-Samaritan hostility traced back to the Assyrian conquest of the northern kingdom, when Samaritans intermarried with foreign settlers and built a rival temple on Mount Gerizim rather than worshiping in Jerusalem.

ot.n: Jacob's purchase of land near Shechem, the same plot associated with the well where this conversation takes place.
The Assyrian resettlement of the northern kingdom that produced the Samaritans' distinct, mixed religious identity, and centuries of tension with Jews.
God as "the spring of living water," contrasted with broken cisterns that can't hold water — background for Jesus' whole living-water image.

im.c: Jesus and the Woman of Samaria, by Gustave Doré (1866)
im.k: Public domain — Project Gutenberg

cm.n: Henry notes Jesus waives the entire Jewish-Samaritan feud rather than engaging it: 'some differences are best healed by being slighted.' He reads Jesus' surprising willingness to speak openly with her as itself part of the lesson — 'moderate men of all sides are men wondered at' — crossing a boundary His own disciples wouldn't have dared cross.

On 'worship in spirit and truth,' Henry reasons directly from God's own nature: 'the divine nature is a very good reason for the spirituality of divine worship — if we do not worship God, who is a spirit, in the spirit, we neither give him the glory due to his name.' True worship, in his reading, was never really about which mountain or which city.

Guzik reads Jesus' exposure of the woman's past as an act of mercy rather than shame: 'Jesus confronted the woman's sinful life not to shame her, but as the first step of the Spirit's work — convicting of sin so she could receive the living water He offered.' The hard truth comes first, but only in service of the gift that follows it.

set: Archaeologists have located twin pools with five surrounding colonnades just north of the Jerusalem temple mount, matching John's description closely. "Bethesda" likely means "house of mercy" — a fitting name for the site of Jesus' compassion here.

his.t: An unnamed feast brought crowds to Jerusalem.
The pool lay near the Sheep Gate, a busy entry where temple animals were brought.

cus.t: Carrying a mat on the Sabbath was counted as work.
Some believed an angel stirred the water to heal.

cu: Rabbinic tradition had extended Sabbath restrictions well beyond anything commanded in the Law itself, and carrying even a small mat counted as forbidden "work" under those added rules — which is exactly what the religious leaders confront the healed man about, not the healing itself.

ot.n: The Son of Man given everlasting dominion and authority — directly behind Jesus' claim to judge "because He is the Son of Man."
An early, explicit prophecy of two resurrections — to life and to judgment — directly echoed in v.29.
God's promise of a coming Prophet like Moses — background for Jesus' claim that Moses himself "wrote about Me."

im.c: The Pool of Bethesda, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: On Jesus' claim to equality with the Father, Henry writes a memorable line in Latin: 'Ecce intelligunt Judaei, quod non intelligunt Ariani' — 'Behold, the Jews understand what the Arians do not.' His point: Jesus' own opponents, who wanted Him dead, correctly grasped that He was claiming full deity — a claim later heretics tried to soften or deny outright.

Henry translates 'Bethesda' directly as 'the house of mercy,' noting that whatever the pool's uncertain history, 'therein appeared much of the mercy of God to the sick and diseased.' He reads the invalid man's honest, unembellished answer to Jesus — no excuse-making, just a plain statement of his situation — as itself a kind of quiet readiness for grace.

Gill reads Jesus' later warning, 'stop sinning, or something worse may happen to you,' as a real clue to the man's original condition — speculating his thirty-eight-year infirmity may have arisen 'from some sin of his, from a vicious course of living, perhaps intemperance,' rather than being unrelated to his own choices.

set: The crowd gathers on the eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee near Bethsaida, with grassy, sloping terrain matching John's description. The following discourse takes place back across the water in Capernaum's synagogue — archaeology has uncovered a black basalt first-century foundation beneath the later limestone synagogue still…

his.t: The feast recalled the exodus, when God fed Israel with manna.
The crowd wanted to make Him king by force, a real risk under Rome.

cus.t: Barley was the poor man's bread, a boy's small lunch.
Jesus' words sounded shocking, since the Law forbade drinking blood.

cu: Two hundred denarii represented roughly two-thirds of a year's wages for a laborer, giving real weight to Philip's despair at feeding the crowd. Rabbis commonly taught seated, which is why Jesus "sat down" with His disciples before the crowd even arrived — a detail signaling formal teaching was about to happen.

ot.n: God's provision of manna in the wilderness — the direct background against which Jesus presents Himself as the true bread from heaven.
"He gave them bread from heaven to eat" — quoted directly by the crowd concerning the manna.
Elisha feeding a hundred men with twenty loaves of bread — an earlier, smaller-scale miracle Jesus' feeding of five thousand far exceeds.

im.c: Christ Feeding the Multitude, by Gustave Doré
im.k: Public domain — Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: On 'eat My flesh and drink My blood,' Henry is careful to call it figurative language, not literal instruction: 'this is certainly a parable or figurative expression.' He notes Jesus had already compared Himself to bread, necessary food, and now to flesh, which is delicious — 'a feast of fat things,' language borrowed directly from Isaiah 25:6.

Henry names three real motives behind the crowd's attempt to crown Jesus by force: love of ease (a king who could feed them without labor), a hope of shaking off Roman rule, and simple political ambition. None of these, he notes, had anything to do with actually believing who Jesus was.

A widely used modern Catholic study note observes a real shift partway through this discourse: up through verse 50, 'bread of life' functions as a figure for God's revelation in Jesus generally, while from verse 51 onward the language becomes markedly more concrete and sacrificial — 'my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world' — pointing toward His coming death.

t: Jesus at the Feast of Tabernacles
set: The Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot) fell in autumn, roughly five months after Passover, commemorating Israel's wilderness wandering. Each day of the feast included a water-drawing ceremony from the Pool of Siloam, carried in procession to the temple — the vivid, immediate backdrop for Jesus' "living water" declaration on the…

his.t: Leaders there were seeking to kill Him, so His brothers' push to go public was risky.
Many thought the Christ must come from Bethlehem, not Galilee.

cus.t: Pilgrims lived in leafy shelters for a week to remember the wilderness.
Priests poured water at the altar each morning of the feast.

cu: Every male Israelite dwelt in temporary branch-covered booths throughout the seven-day feast, a lived reenactment of the wilderness years. The debate over Sabbath-day circumcision was a real point of rabbinic discussion — Mosaic law required circumcision on the eighth day even if it fell on a Sabbath, a precedent Jesus uses directly against His accusers' own logic.

ot.n: The original institution of the Feast of Tabernacles, commemorating Israel's wilderness dwelling in temporary booths.
"Come, all you who are thirsty" — the open invitation directly echoed in Jesus' cry on the feast's last day.
The prophecy that the Messiah would come from Bethlehem — the exact objection some in the crowd raise against Jesus, whom they knew only as coming from Galilee.

im.c: Jesus Teaches in the Synagogues, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry notes the real historical custom behind Jesus' 'living water' cry: on the feast's last day, priests carried water from the Pool of Siloam to the temple in procession, 'with sound of trumpet and other ceremonies,' pouring it out before the Lord at the altar.

On Jesus' calm response to His skeptical brothers, Henry draws a broader lesson: 'when we cannot do what and where we would, we must do what and where we can.' He reads Jesus' refusal to be pressured into a premature public show as itself a model of patient, well-timed obedience rather than passivity.

Guzik cites two older scholars on why Jesus' brothers pushed Him toward public display: Tasker observed they 'imagined His glory to be limited to demonstrations of His miraculous powers, whereas in reality it could only be supremely displayed by His crucifixion'; Trench put it more bluntly — 'they believed in the world rather than in Him.'

set: Still the Feast of Tabernacles, when giant lampstands lit the temple's Court of the Women each night — the vivid, literal backdrop for Jesus' declaration "I am the light of the world," spoken, John notes, right near the temple treasury where those very lamps stood.

his.t: Under Rome the Jewish courts could not carry out executions, which sharpens the trap.
Descent from Abraham gave Jews a deep sense of security.

cus.t: Jesus wrote on the ground, and John never says what.
Giant lamps in the Court of Women lit the temple during Tabernacles.

cu: Roman authorities alone held the legal right of execution in occupied Judea, making the leaders' question about stoning the woman a deliberate trap — any answer risked either contradicting Mosaic law or Roman law. The Law itself required at least two witnesses to establish a capital charge, a detail Jesus later invokes directly regarding His own testimony.

ot.n: The Law's actual penalty for adultery, invoked (and weaponized) by the woman's accusers.
God's own self-naming, "I AM WHO I AM" — directly echoed in Jesus' climactic declaration, "before Abraham was born, I am."
Abraham's faith and his willingness to offer Isaac — background for Jesus' claim that "Abraham rejoiced that he would see My day."

im.c: Jesus and the Woman Taken in Adultery, by Gustave Doré (1866)
im.k: Public domain — Project Gutenberg

cm.n: Henry reflects on the woman being caught in the act itself: 'those that promise themselves secrecy in sin deceive themselves... sometimes it proves a mercy to sinners to have their sin brought to light, that they may do no more presumptuously.' Public exposure, however painful, becomes in his reading the occasion for the mercy that follows.

On the accusers' trap, Henry lays out exactly how it was designed to fail either way: if Jesus said release her, He'd appear to override Moses' law; if He said stone her, He'd be reported to Rome for claiming an execution authority only Roman governors held. Jesus' answer, Henry notes, sidesteps the false choice entirely by turning the question back on the accusers themselves.

Guzik points out a detail easy to miss: 'there was also a man involved in this very act of adultery — yet the guilty man was not brought before Jesus for judgment.' The accusers' selective enforcement, he suggests, exposes their real motive as trapping Jesus rather than genuinely upholding the Law.

Lewis does not comment on John 8, but his chapter "The Shocking Alternative" in Mere Christianity is about claims like verse 58, "Before Abraham was born, I am!" He says that a man who claimed to be before Abraham and to be the great I AM would be either a lunatic or a liar, and that nobody should patronize Him as a wise moralist.

t: Jesus Heals the Man Born Blind
set: Archaeologists uncovered the actual first-century Pool of Siloam in 2004, at the southern end of Hezekiah's ancient water tunnel — pilgrims used its water in temple festival ceremonies, giving Jesus' instruction real, immediate significance beyond just a place to wash.

his.t: Many assumed illness was punishment for sin, and Jesus rejected that.
People who confessed Jesus as Christ could be put out of the synagogue.

cus.t: Saliva was a folk remedy, though Jesus needed no medicine.
Water from Siloam was drawn each morning for the Tabernacles ceremony.

cu: Rabbinic tradition had expanded the Sabbath's prohibited categories of "work" to thirty-nine specific activities, including kneading — which is exactly what mixing spit and dirt into mud amounted to, giving the Pharisees their technical objection.

ot.n: Job's own suffering, wrongly assumed by his friends to trace back to personal sin — the same faulty assumption behind the disciples' opening question here.
The Servant of the Lord given "as a light... to open the eyes that are blind" — directly fulfilled in this sign.
Seeing without perceiving, hearing without understanding — the exact pattern Jesus names in the Pharisees at the chapter's close.

im.c: The Healed Blind Man Tells His Story to the Jews, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry calls out the disciples' question as 'uncharitably censorious' — assuming without evidence that this man must have committed some extraordinary sin to deserve such a fate. Jesus' answer, he notes, overturns two common assumptions at once: that such calamities are always direct punishment, and that they serve no larger purpose — here, the man's blindness becomes the very…

Henry frames the healed beggar as an unlikely but effective witness: 'it is an encouragement to those who are concerned for the cause of Christ to hope that it shall never be lost for want of witnesses,' when even a poor blind beggar can be found standing firm against the very people most determined to discredit him.

Poole is precise about what Jesus' answer actually denies: not that suffering and sin are unrelated in general, but that this particular suffering was not brought about 'so as to bring this suffering upon him' by any specific wrongdoing of the man or his parents. The purpose instead lay in what God's power and goodness would go on to display through him.

set: This chapter spans two distinct settings months apart: the immediate aftermath of chapter 9's controversy, and later the Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) in winter, when Jesus walks in Solomon's Colonnade — a covered walkway on the temple's east side that would have offered real shelter from the cold.

his.t: Hanukkah remembered the temple's rededication after the Maccabean revolt.
Prophets often called Israel's leaders shepherds, good or bad.

cus.t: At night several flocks shared a pen, and each sheep knew its own shepherd's voice.
A shepherd could lie across the pen's opening to guard it.

cu: First-century Judean sheepfolds were often simple stone enclosures with a single narrow opening; at night the shepherd himself would frequently lie across that gap, literally becoming the door his sheep couldn't pass except through him.

ot.n: God's condemnation of Israel's failed shepherds and His promise to personally search for and gather His flock — directly behind Jesus' entire shepherd discourse.
"The LORD is my shepherd" — the most familiar Old Testament backdrop to Jesus' claim, "I am the good shepherd."
"I said, you are gods" — quoted directly by Jesus in His defense against the charge of blasphemy.

im.c: The Good Shepherd, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry notes the leaders demand a direct answer, 'not by parables... but totidem verbis — in so many words' — no more of the light-of-the-world or good-shepherd imagery, just a plain yes or no.

Henry observes that even without further theological debate, the reaction alone settles what Jesus meant: 'if we should altogether hold our peace concerning this sense of the words, even the stones which the Jews took up to cast at him would speak it out' — they clearly understood Him to be claiming full deity, and He never once denied that was His meaning.

Guzik draws on two older scholars for a precise grammatical point: 'one is neuter in gender, not masculine: the Father and the Son are not personally one, but essentially' (Alford); Trench put it even more directly — 'the word 'One' is neuter, and means one Essence: it is not masculine, which would have been one Person.' A small grammatical detail carrying real theological…

set: Bethany sat less than two miles east of Jerusalem, an easy walk even on a Sabbath — close enough that many mourners from the city had already come to comfort Mary and Martha by the time Jesus arrives.

his.t: It lay about two miles from Jerusalem, so mourners from the city came.
The Sanhedrin feared Rome would destroy the temple if the crowds rallied to Jesus.

cus.t: Jews believed the spirit lingered three days, so four days proved real death.
Professional mourners and visitors comforted the family for a week.

cu: Public mourning in this culture was loud and communal — professional wailers, flute players, and friends sitting an extended period of shared grief, which explains why so many people from Jerusalem are already gathered at the sisters' house. Burial involved wrapping the body in strips of linen with spices, then sealing it in a rock-cut tomb with a stone across the entrance — exactly the scene Jesus confronts.

ot.n: Elijah and Elisha's earlier resurrections of individual children — real precedents, though on a smaller scale than raising a man four days in the tomb.
The suffering servant dying for the transgressions of others — echoed, likely unknowingly, in Caiaphas's own prophecy that one man should die for the nation.
An early explicit prophecy of resurrection — background for Martha's own stated belief in a resurrection "at the last day."

im.c: The Resurrection of Lazarus, by Gustave Doré (1866)
im.k: Public domain — Project Gutenberg

cm.n: On the shortest verse in Scripture, Henry draws out real theological weight: 'that Jesus Christ was really and truly man... he gave this proof of his humanity, in both senses of the word — that, as a man, he could weep, and, as a merciful man, he would weep, before he gave this proof of his divinity' in raising Lazarus moments later.

Henry notes something genuinely touching about the sisters' grief: their brother's estate would likely pass to them, yet 'whatever they got by their brother's death, heartily wished him alive again' — their sorrow, in other words, was real love, not calculation.

On why Jesus wept despite knowing He was about to raise Lazarus, Guzik writes: 'Jesus shared in the grief of those who mourn. Yet unlike any other, God the Son was able to do something about their grief.' He notes John deliberately uses two different Greek words — one for Jesus' own quiet weeping, another for the loud, public mourning of the crowd around Him.

set: This chapter opens at a dinner in Bethany six days before Passover, then moves to Jesus' entry into Jerusalem the next day — the same route Lazarus's tomb sat along, meaning many in the crowd greeting Jesus had likely just witnessed or heard firsthand about his resurrection.

his.t: The leaders also planned to kill Lazarus because many believed through him.
Gentile God-fearers came to worship at Passover.

cus.t: Nard was an imported perfume worth about a year's wages.
Palms were a national symbol, welcoming a hoped-for king.

cu: Pure nard was imported from India and represented roughly a year's wages, making Mary's gift genuinely extravagant rather than merely sentimental. Anointing was a gesture reserved for honoring kings or preparing the dead for burial — Mary's act carries both meanings at once, whether or not she fully understood that herself.

ot.n: The King coming "gentle and riding on a donkey" — directly fulfilled and quoted in v.15.
The exact pilgrim psalm the crowd is quoting when they shout "Hosanna" and "blessed is he who comes."
Both quoted directly by John to explain the crowd's unbelief despite witnessing so many signs.

im.c: The Ointment of the Magdalene, by James Tissot (1886-1894) — Tissot's title for the anointing at Bethany
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry reads the Greeks' request as the actual trigger for Jesus' declaration that His hour had come: 'do the Gentiles begin to enquire after me? Does the morning-star appear to them?... Then the hour is come for the glorifying of the Son of man.' The wider world beginning to seek Him out, not a Jewish crowd, is what Jesus treats as the real sign His time had arrived.

Ellicott notes that John alone names Mary — Matthew and Mark say only "a woman" — and that she is true here to the character Luke gives her. The "pound" is the Greek litra, the Roman pound of twelve ounces, and the ointment came from the East in sealed flasks that were broken when used, so the perfume filled the house.

Gill does the arithmetic on Judas's objection: three hundred Roman pence, each worth about seven and a half pence in his own day's money, comes to nine pounds, seven shillings, and sixpence — a real sum in the 1700s. He also reads the fragrance filling the whole house as an emblem of Christ's "sweet savour" spreading through the world in the preaching of the gospel.

set: Early Christian tradition locates this upper room on Mount Zion in Jerusalem. Archaeological excavations nearby have uncovered first-century ritual purification baths, underscoring just how seriously purity customs were taken at Passover — making Jesus' choice to personally wash dusty feet, rather than insist on formal ritual…

his.t: The meal took place just before the feast.
The chief priests were looking for someone to hand Jesus over quietly.

cus.t: Washing feet was the work of the lowest slave, not a teacher.
Giving a morsel to a guest honored him, which made the betrayal sharper.

cu: Washing a guest's feet was standard hospitality in a world of sandals and dusty roads, but it was specifically the lowest household task, normally assigned to the least-senior servant present — often a Gentile or female slave, never expected of a guest's own social equals, let alone their acknowledged teacher.

ot.n: "He who shares my bread has lifted up his heel against me" — quoted directly by Jesus to describe His own betrayal by Judas.
The suffering servant's exaltation despite disfigurement and rejection — background for Jesus' repeated language of being "glorified" even as His betrayal unfolds.
"Love your neighbor as yourself" — the older commandment Jesus' "new commandment" deliberately raises to a new, self-sacrificial standard.

im.c: The Washing of the Feet, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry notes the Greek phrase behind 'loved them to the end' is eis telos — literally 'to perfection' — reading Jesus' love as constant and complete rather than merely lasting until a deadline: 'nothing can separate a believer from the love of Christ; he loves his own... unto perfection.'

On why loving one another counts as a 'new' commandment when Leviticus already required it, Henry explains that rabbinic tradition had buried the original command under layers of permitted revenge and self-interest — 'as it came from Christ new, it was new to the people,' restored rather than invented, but genuinely new in the form they'd actually receive it.

A modern commentary observes something easy to miss: Jesus washes the feet of every disciple at that table without exception — including 'the feet of the one who will betray him before the meal is even over, Judas... and the one who will deny being one of his disciples, Peter.' The act of love comes before either failure, not after repentance.

t: I Am the Way, the Truth, and the Life
set: Still the same evening as the foot washing, in the upper room — a moment of quiet instruction sandwiched between Judas's departure into the night and Jesus' prayer and arrest still to come.

his.t: Jesus speaks hours before His arrest, with the leaders already plotting.
Rome's "peace" was kept by force, which sharpens "not as the world gives."

cus.t: A groom prepared a room at his father's house before the wedding.
Peace was the usual Jewish greeting, meaning wholeness, not only calm.

cu: A first-century household's father commonly added rooms onto the family home as sons married and stayed within it — a familiar, homely picture behind Jesus' promise of "many rooms" prepared for His disciples in His Father's house, rather than a picture of a distant hotel.

ot.n: Moses' request to see God's glory, met with the reply that no one can see God's face and live — background for the weight of Philip's request and Jesus' remarkable answer.
The priestly blessing of peace — background for the richer, more personal peace Jesus promises to leave with His disciples.
God's Spirit guiding and comforting His people in the wilderness — an early picture of the Helper's promised comforting role.

im.c: Address to Saint Philip, by James Tissot (1886-1894) — “He who has seen Me has seen the Father”
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry traces the Greek word behind 'mansions' (monai) to a root meaning 'abiding places' — not temporary lodging but durable dwelling: 'here we are as in an inn; in heaven we shall gain a settlement.' He notes the disciples had given up their own houses to follow Christ, 'who had not where to lay his head, but the mansions in heaven will make them amends.'

Wesley sees Jesus answering three separate questions in one sentence. Thomas had asked about the way, so Jesus says "I am the way"; the question of knowing, so "I am the truth"; the question of where He was going, so "I am the life." He adds that verse 4's "way" is "of faith, holiness, sufferings," and that verse 26 is a clear promise to the apostles that the Spirit would…

This Victorian collection of sermon outlines stresses that the Greek behind "mansions" (monai) means abiding dwelling-places, and that Jesus is describing a Father's house, not a hotel: "no wayside inn, no temporary abode." It adds that heaven is therefore "no unknown land, no land of strangers" for believers, but a home prepared for a family that will always live there.

set: Spoken the night before the crucifixion, most likely after the meal and on the way toward Gethsemane (14:31; 18:1). The disciples had just walked past the temple, whose entrance was famously decorated with a massive golden vine symbolizing Israel — a striking backdrop for Jesus calling Himself the "true" vine.

his.t: Followers of Jesus would soon face expulsion and hostility from rulers.
A golden vine decorated the temple entrance, a well-known symbol of Israel.

cus.t: Vinedressers cut back branches in winter so the vine bears more.
Dead branches were gathered and burned as fuel.

cu: Vineyards covered the Judean hillsides, and pruning was a familiar annual task — cutting away dead wood and also trimming healthy shoots so the vine's strength went into fruit rather than leaves. The golden vine on Herod's temple, described by the historian Josephus, had clusters of grapes as large as a person, donated in gold leaf by wealthy Jews as a symbol of national identity.

ot.n: Israel as God's vineyard that produced only wild grapes — the failure Jesus' claim to be the "true" vine answers.
Israel pictured as a vine brought out of Egypt and planted by God.
"They hated me without reason" — the verses Jesus says are fulfilled in the world's hatred of Him.

im.c: Our Lord Jesus Christ, by James Tissot (1886-1894), from his upper-room sequence
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry reads "true" as the opposite of counterfeit: Christ is not like the wild vine in 2 Kings 4:39 that poisoned those who gathered from it, but a real, fruitful plant — the one that Judah's vine in Genesis 49:11 and Joseph's vine in Genesis 49:22 only pointed toward. He also notes it reflects Christ's humility that He chose such a low, ordinary comparison for Himself.

On "apart from Me you can do nothing," Henry makes a practical point: being fruitful matters so much to our happiness that it becomes the strongest reason to stay connected to Christ — "the best argument to engage us to abide in Christ is, that otherwise we cannot be fruitful." On friends versus servants, he adds that those who do a servant's duty are advanced to a friend's…

Guzik reads the branches that are "taken away" as ones that were never truly abiding, shown by the fact that they bore no fruit — and presses the emphasis plainly: "there are no true disciples who do not abide." A branch only has life as long as it stays connected to the vine, the same way disciples only live spiritually when connected to the Master.

set: Still the night before the crucifixion, with the group most likely having left the upper room and heading toward the Garden of Gethsemane. Jerusalem was swollen with Passover pilgrims, and the religious leaders were already plotting against Jesus.

his.t: Being put out of the synagogue meant losing community and livelihood.
Some who killed believers would think they served God.

cus.t: The prophets often used labor pains as a picture of pain turning to joy.
To ask in someone's name meant coming with their authority.

cu: The synagogue was far more than a place of worship — it was the social and economic center of Jewish community life. Being put out of it meant losing community, livelihood, and reputation together. Excavations at Capernaum and Magdala have uncovered stone benches and reading platforms that show how central these buildings were.

ot.n: Childbirth used as a picture of sudden joy following pain — the same image Jesus uses in verse 21.
God's promise to write His law on His people's hearts — background for the Spirit teaching and guiding believers from within.
The shepherd struck and the sheep scattered — echoed in Jesus' prediction that the disciples will scatter, each to his own home.

im.c: The Last Supper, by Gustave Doré (1866) — the night of the farewell discourse
im.k: Public domain — Project Gutenberg

cm.n: Henry notices something about what Jesus leaves out: He explains the weeping and the joy but says nothing more about the "little while," "because he saw that this perplexed them more than any thing; and it is of no consequence to us to know the times and the seasons." He also stresses that the sorrow doesn't just get replaced — it is turned into joy, since "the most precious…

On the Spirit's work of conviction, Henry observes the order He follows: "first to convince, and then to comfort." He lists six angles on sin the Spirit presses — its fact, its fault, its folly, its filth, its fountain in a corrupt nature, and its fruit, since "the end thereof is death."

The Anglican scholar Alford singles out the three key words of verses 8-11 — sin, righteousness, and judgment — and reads them as marking "the three great steps of advance in spiritual truth among men," a progression rather than three unrelated topics.

set: Prayed late on the night Jesus was betrayed, very likely in or just outside the upper room, after the Passover meal had ended, Judas had left, and the long farewell teaching of chapters 13-16 was finished.

his.t: Jesus prays knowing the cross is hours away.
Jerusalem was packed with pilgrims, and the arrest came within hours.

cus.t: Jews often prayed with eyes lifted toward heaven.
God's name stood for His character and presence.

cu: Passover was observed reclining at table with four cups of wine shared during the meal. Jesus' prayer here is often placed after the meal's close, in a setting already full of themes of deliverance and praise. The prayer is called "high priestly" because it resembles the priest who carried the names of Israel's tribes on his breastplate before God (Exodus 28:29).

ot.n: The high priest carrying the names of Israel's tribes over his heart into God's presence — the picture behind calling this the High Priestly Prayer.
God revealing His name to Moses — background for Jesus' repeated statement that He has made the Father's name known.
The priestly blessing, a pattern of a priest speaking God's care over His people.

im.c: Prayer of Jesus in the Garden of Olives, by Gustave Doré (1866) — the same night as the prayer of John 17
im.k: Public domain — Project Gutenberg

cm.n: Henry reads "this is eternal life, that they may know You" as describing both a present reality and a future one: now it is a "believing knowledge" of God and Christ, later it will be direct knowledge. Those who already live in communion with God, he says, are "in the suburbs of life eternal" and know by experience what it is — "if this be heaven, heaven is sweet."

On "sanctify them by the truth," Henry clarifies that the word does not sanctify on its own — otherwise it would always work — but is the instrument the Spirit commonly uses, being "the seed of the new birth" and "the food of the new life." He also reads the request as setting the disciples apart for their office, the way the Levitical priests were consecrated, but "really…

Spurgeon turns verse 3 into a pointed personal question: "Do you know God? Do you know Jesus Christ? Are you on speaking terms, on loving terms, with them? Are they your friends? Then you have eternal life." For him the definition is less a doctrine to debate than a relationship to check.

t: The Arrest and Trial of Jesus
set: The Kidron Valley runs between Jerusalem's eastern wall and the Mount of Olives. The garden on the far side, traditionally Gethsemane ("oil press"), sat among olive groves — a secluded spot Judas knew because Jesus had often met His disciples there.

his.t: Annas was the former high priest and the power behind Caiaphas.
Only Rome could execute, so the leaders brought Jesus to Pilate.

cus.t: People warmed themselves at night around fires of charcoal.
The leaders avoided Pilate's headquarters so they would stay ritually clean.

cu: Annas had served as high priest from AD 6 to 15 until Rome removed him, but his family kept the office afterward, including his son-in-law Caiaphas, so he still carried real influence — which is why the questioning begins with him. John's word for the arresting force suggests a sizeable group of soldiers working alongside the temple officers.

ot.n: The servant who does not open His mouth and is taken away through unjust judgment — echoed in Jesus' calm answers throughout the hearings.
Betrayal by a close friend, already applied to Judas in chapter 13.
David crossing the Kidron Valley as a rejected king — a parallel often drawn with Jesus crossing it here.

im.c: The Betrayal, by Gustave Doré (1866)
im.k: Public domain — Project Gutenberg

cm.n: Henry notices the direction of the fall: the arresting party "went backward, and, like men thunder-struck, fell to the ground" — not forward, as if humbling themselves and yielding, but backward, "as standing it out to the utmost." On the leaders refusing to enter Pilate's hall "lest they should be defiled," he calls it superstition and "vile hypocrisy": careful to avoid a…

Clarke points out that none of the other Gospel writers mention the arresting party falling to the ground, and reads it as Jesus choosing to prove that their power could not prevail against Him "if he chose to exert his might." On "that they might eat the passover," he notes some read the phrase as covering the other sacrifices of the Passover festival rather than the lamb…

Wesley is struck by what happens next: "How amazing is it, that they should renew the assault, after so sensible an experience both of his power and mercy!" His explanation is that the priests in the group probably talked themselves and their attendants into believing even this had been done by "Beelzebub," and that they escaped further harm only through God's providence, not…

set: The chapter moves from the Praetorium and the judgment seat at the Stone Pavement (Gabbatha) to Golgotha, "The Place of the Skull," outside the city walls but near enough that many people read the sign above the cross. It ends in a nearby garden with a new, unused tomb belonging to Joseph of Arimathea.

his.t: The cry "no friend of Caesar" threatened Pilate's career under Tiberius.
Pilate's sign read Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews, in three languages.

cus.t: Soldiers claimed the executed man's clothing, and cast lots for the seamless one.
About seventy-five pounds of spices were wrapped with the linen.

cu: Roman flogging used leather straps embedded with bone or metal and often killed its victims. A victim usually carried the crossbeam to the execution site, and a notice stating the crime was posted above him — Pilate's was written in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek so every group in Jerusalem could read it.

ot.n: "They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing" — quoted directly in verse 24.
No bone of the Passover lamb may be broken — applied in verse 36 to the soldiers not breaking Jesus' legs.
"They will look on the One they have pierced" — quoted in verse 37.

im.c: The Crucifixion, by Gustave Doré (1866)
im.k: Public domain — Project Gutenberg

cm.n: On Pilate's "What I have written, I have written," Henry sees more than stubbornness: "what he had written was what God had first written, and therefore he could not alter it," pointing to Daniel's prophecy that Messiah the prince would be cut off.

Henry's shorter commentary notes that Jesus died in less time than crucified people commonly did, which "showed that he had laid down his life of himself." On "It is finished," he reads it as the Father's counsels concerning His sufferings now fulfilled — "an end is made of transgression by bringing in an everlasting righteousness."

Guzik draws attention to the two men who buried Jesus: Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, both previously secret disciples, who stepped forward at the moment it was riskiest. He adds that the burial itself served as proof — "no one could tell Joseph of Arimathea or Nicodemus that Jesus did not really die."

t: The Empty Tomb and the Risen Jesus
set: The chapter begins at the new rock-cut tomb in the garden near Golgotha, where Jesus was buried at the end of chapter 19, and moves to a locked room in Jerusalem, probably the same city quarter where the disciples had been staying.

his.t: The disciples hid, since the Jewish leaders had just had Jesus executed.
Mary Magdalene, whose word was not valued in court, is the first to see Him.

cus.t: Burial cloths and a separate face cloth lay neatly in the tomb.
Rock-cut tombs were sealed with a heavy stone, so rolling it away took strength.

cu: A body was wrapped in strips of linen with spices, and the face covered with a separate cloth. John's note that the head cloth was rolled up and lying apart is often read as showing an orderly scene rather than hurried theft. In this culture a woman's testimony carried little weight in legal settings, yet all four Gospels report women as the first witnesses.

ot.n: God's Holy One will not see decay — quoted in the apostles' later preaching as pointing to the resurrection.
God breathing life into Adam — echoed when Jesus breathes on His disciples.
Revival and raising up "on the third day" — often connected by readers to the timing of the resurrection.

im.c: Mary Magdalene Questions the Angels in the Tomb, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry makes a point about why the resurrection matters to the whole transaction: "if Christ gave his life a ransom, and had not taken it again, it would not have appeared that his giving it was accepted as satisfaction." On John's closing verses, he says the other signs were left unwritten so that all might believe Jesus is the promised Messiah and, by that faith, obtain…

Ellicott draws attention to the eyewitness detail in verses 6-7: Peter "beholds" the linen cloths with a different, more careful Greek verb than John uses when he only sees them from outside. Of the head cloth folded in a separate place, he says it reaches the climax of "the minute knowledge and remembrance of an eye-witness" — the fact that it was folded "did not escape the…

Wesley reads "do not cling to me" as a gentle "detain me not now" to Mary, who was holding His feet, with more opportunities to come. He sees the message "go to my brothers" as an unspoken forgiveness, since Jesus never mentions the disciples' failure.

t: Breakfast by the Sea and Peter Restored
set: The scene moves from Jerusalem back to Galilee, to the shore of the Sea of Tiberias (another name for the Sea of Galilee), where several of the disciples had been fishermen. The shoreline is only about a hundred yards from the boat when the miraculous catch is dragged in.

his.t: Herod Antipas named his capital for the emperor Tiberius, so the lake took the Roman name.
Jesus hints at Peter's death, and early tradition says he was martyred under Rome.

cus.t: Galilean fishermen worked at night, using nets let down from boats.
Bread and fish were the staple meal of the lakeshore.

cu: Night was the usual time for net-fishing on the lake, which explains why the disciples worked through the dark and came ashore at dawn with nothing. A well-preserved first-century fishing boat found near Kibbutz Ginosar in 1986 shows the size and construction of vessels like theirs. Shared meals were a central sign of fellowship, so Jesus serving bread and fish is both practical hospitality and a deliberate gesture.

ot.n: God promising to seek out His scattered sheep and tend them Himself — the background to Jesus handing the care of His flock to Peter.
"The LORD is my shepherd" — the most familiar Old Testament picture behind the shepherd language of this chapter.
The wider Scriptural pattern of God commissioning one person for the sake of many, often cited when readers reflect on Peter's commission.

im.c: The Second Miraculous Draught of Fishes, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry lays out three ways to read Jesus' "do you love Me more than these?": more than you love these people (James, John, Andrew), more than these boats and nets, or more than these other disciples love Me.

The church father Jerome, writing on Ezekiel 47, reports that ancient writers on natural history counted 153 kinds of fish — and read John's number as meaning the apostles' catch took in every kind, a picture of the gospel reaching all types of people. Modern scholar D. A. Carson takes a more cautious line: if John intended symbolism with 153, he has hidden it well.

Ellicott reads the exact figure as a mark of firsthand memory rather than a code: the fish were all "great," so their size and number led to an exact tally being taken, which "would be talked of among the Apostles and their friends and fellow-craftsmen" and is recorded with "the picturesque exactness which is characteristic of St. John."

set: Luke picks up where his Gospel ended. For forty days the risen Jesus appears to the apostles, then rises from the Mount of Olives, about a Sabbath day's walk from Jerusalem. The eleven return to an upper room in the city, where about 120 believers pray together until the Spirit comes.

his.t: Luke says Jesus showed himself alive over forty days.
Acts 1 gives a second account of his death, alongside Matthew 27.

cus.t: About 1,100 yards, the farthest a person could walk on the Sabbath.
A way of leaving a choice in God's hands, used often in Israel.

cu: Casting lots to choose Matthias (v.26) was an ordinary way to seek God's choice in Israel: priestly duties were assigned that way (Luke 1:9), and Proverbs 16:33 says the lot is cast but the decision is the Lord's. This is the last time the New Testament records it.

ot.n: Judas's empty place, read as a pattern of Scripture.
"Let another take his office."
The Son of Man comes with the clouds, as the angels promise.

im.c: The Ascension and the choosing of Matthias (Acts 1), from a 16th-century print series on Acts.
im.k: Print series on Acts (16th c.), Rijksmuseum, CC0 / Wikimedia Commons

set: It is Pentecost, the harvest festival fifty days after Passover, and Jerusalem is full of Jews from across the Mediterranean world. The believers are together in a house or hall in the city, and the crowd gathers when they hear the noise.

his.t: Jews from the whole empire came to Jerusalem for the feast.
Greek was shared, but many people still prayed in home languages.

cus.t: The feast of weeks, fifty days after the Passover offering.
About nine in the morning, when the pilgrims were awake but sober.

cu: Pentecost (Shavuot) was one of three pilgrim festivals when Jewish men were expected to come to Jerusalem. That is why the crowd is so international, with visitors from Parthia to Rome. Later Jewish tradition also tied the feast to the giving of the law at Sinai.

ot.n: The Spirit poured out on all people, quoted by Peter.
David, who died, speaks of one whose body will not decay.
Babel scattered the languages; Pentecost gathers hearers.

im.c: Pentecost, by El Greco (c. 1600).
im.k: El Greco (c. 1600), Prado Museum / Wikimedia Commons

t: A Lame Man Healed at the Temple
set: Peter and John go up to the Temple for the afternoon prayer at three o'clock. At the gate called Beautiful, a man lame from birth is carried there daily to beg. After he is healed, the crowd rushes together in Solomon's Colonnade, along the eastern edge of the Temple courts, and Peter preaches again.

his.t: Prayer was offered morning and afternoon with the daily sacrifice.
Solomon's Colonnade was a covered walk where teachers gathered.

cus.t: The sick and disabled sat by busy gates where worshipers gave alms.
About three in the afternoon, the time of the afternoon sacrifice.

cu: The apostles still keep Jewish hours of prayer, so the earliest church was not separate from the Temple. Begging at a busy gate was the only option for a man who could not work, and religious teaching urged giving to the poor at exactly such places.

ot.n: The prophet like Moses, whom Peter says is Jesus.
The servant who is glorified, echoed in "his servant Jesus."
All peoples blessed through Abraham's seed.

im.c: The Healing of the Lame Man, Raphael's 1515 cartoon for a tapestry.
im.k: Raphael (1515), Victoria and Albert Museum / Wikimedia Commons

t: Peter and John Before the Council
set: Priests, the captain of the Temple guard, and Sadducees arrest Peter and John, who spend the night in custody. The next day they stand before the Sanhedrin, the same council that condemned Jesus, with Annas, Caiaphas, John, and Alexander among the family of the high priest present.

his.t: The aristocratic priests denied the resurrection and controlled the Temple.
Annas and his family held the high priesthood for decades.

cus.t: The arrest came at evening, so the hearing waited until morning.
Land was a family inheritance, so giving it up was costly.

cu: The Sadducees were the priestly party and rejected the resurrection, so a message about the risen Jesus hit them directly. The believers also share what they own so no one lacks, which is a free act of love rather than a rule, as the example of Barnabas shows.

ot.n: The rejected stone becomes the cornerstone.
Kings and rulers gather against the Lord's anointed.
The Creator God who made heaven and earth, addressed in prayer.

im.c: Peter heals the lame man at the Temple (Acts 3), from a 16th-century print series on Acts.
im.k: Print series on Acts (16th c.), Rijksmuseum, CC0 / Wikimedia Commons

t: Ananias, Sapphira, and the Apostles' Courage
set: The church is growing fast in Jerusalem, meeting in Solomon's Colonnade. A couple, Ananias and Sapphira, lie about the price of land they sold. The apostles are arrested and jailed, an angel opens the doors at night, and they are back teaching in the Temple by morning.

his.t: A leading Pharisee, the grandson of Hillel and a teacher of Paul.
Theudas and Judas the Galilean led failed uprisings that Gamaliel recalls.

cus.t: Verse 30 says Jesus was hanged on a tree, a phrase for crucifixion.
Thirty-nine lashes were the usual Jewish punishment for public offenses.

cu: Selling property and giving some of the money was voluntary, as Peter says in verse 4. The sin was pretending to give everything. Gamaliel, a teacher of the law and Paul's own teacher, urges patience by citing two earlier rebel movements.

ot.n: Achan's hidden theft, another sin inside the community that was judged.
Hanging on a tree, the curse Jesus bore.
Three men who would not bow, who say God must be obeyed.

im.c: The Death of Ananias, Raphael's 1515 cartoon for a tapestry.
im.k: Raphael (1515), Victoria and Albert Museum / Wikimedia Commons

set: The church in Jerusalem now includes two groups: Hebrew-speaking Jews and Greek-speaking Jews from the Diaspora. The Greek speakers' widows are being overlooked in the daily food distribution. The Twelve call everyone together and ask them to choose seven men to oversee it, and the seven all have Greek names.

his.t: Two language groups lived in the church, as in the city.
Jews from across the empire had their own synagogues in Jerusalem.

cus.t: Widows received daily food, a duty Israel owed to the poor.
A sign of blessing and commissioning for a task.

cu: Widows had no income and depended on community help. Synagogues in Jerusalem often served particular groups, which is why Stephen debates with the "Synagogue of the Freedmen," made up of Jews from Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia, and Asia.

ot.n: Moses lays hands on Joshua, a pattern for commissioning.
Moses' face shone; Stephen's looks like an angel's.
The widow, the orphan and the foreigner were to be cared for.

im.c: Stephen before the high priest (Acts 6-7), from a 16th-century print series on Acts.
im.k: Print series on Acts (16th c.), Rijksmuseum, CC0 / Wikimedia Commons

set: Stephen stands before the Sanhedrin and answers the charge that he speaks against the Temple and the law. He retells Israel's history from Abraham to Solomon. The council erupts when he says he sees the Son of Man standing at God's right hand, and they drag him out of the city and stone him as a young man named Saul watches.

his.t: Israel's leaders prized the Temple, the law, and Moses above all.
Rome kept the power of capital punishment, so this stoning was irregular.

cus.t: A sign of rage, as in Psalm 35:16 and Job 16:9.
Witnesses removed outer robes to throw stones freely.

cu: Stoning was the penalty for blasphemy under the law, and the witnesses were to throw first (Deuteronomy 17:7), which is why they lay their cloaks at Saul's feet. Rome reserved the right of execution, so this killing was probably a mob act, not a legal sentence.

ot.n: God calls Abraham while he is still outside the land.
Moses is rejected the first time, as Jesus was.
Heaven is God's throne; no house can contain him.

im.c: The Stoning of Saint Stephen, by Rembrandt (1625).
im.k: Rembrandt (1625), Musée des Beaux-Arts de Lyon / Wikimedia Commons

t: The Gospel Goes to Samaria and Ethiopia
set: After Stephen's death the believers scatter across Judea and Samaria. Philip, one of the seven, preaches in a Samaritan city, and Peter and John come from Jerusalem to pray for the new believers. An angel then sends Philip south on the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza, where he meets an Ethiopian official reading Isaiah.

his.t: They shared the first five books of Moses but worshiped on Mount Gerizim.
The kingdom south of Egypt was ruled by queen mothers called Candace.

cus.t: The word comes from Simon, who tried to buy the Spirit's power with money.
People read aloud, which is how Philip could hear the Ethiopian.

cu: "Candace" (v.27) was not a name but the title of the queen mother of Kush, the kingdom south of Egypt that Greeks called Ethiopia. A eunuch could serve the court but, under Deuteronomy 23:1, could not enter the assembly of Israel. Samaritans and Jews also avoided one another, so Philip crossed two lines in one chapter.

ot.n: The Servant is led like a sheep to slaughter, the passage Philip explains.
Eunuchs are promised a place and a lasting name.
The law that barred the eunuch from the assembly.

im.c: Philip baptizes the Ethiopian official, by Rembrandt (1626).
im.k: Rembrandt (1626), Museum Catharijneconvent, Utrecht / Wikimedia Commons

t: Saul Meets Jesus on the Damascus Road
set: Saul sets out for Damascus, about 135 miles north of Jerusalem, with letters from the high priest to arrest followers of the Way. A light from heaven stops him on the road, and Jesus speaks. He is led blind into Damascus, where Ananias finds him on Straight Street and restores his sight.

his.t: Damascus was a major caravan city, then under Nabataean King Aretas IV.
A Pharisee trained under Gamaliel and a Roman citizen from birth.

cus.t: Saul neither ate nor drank for three days, a sign of shock and repentance.
Their work was unclean, so Simon's trade put him at the edge of society.

cu: The high priest's letters show the Sanhedrin's authority over synagogues far outside Judea. Followers of Jesus were first called "the Way" (v.2), a name for a whole way of life. Saul is lowered through a window in a basket (v.25), and Paul recalls this in 2 Corinthians 11:32-33.

ot.n: The servant as a light for the Gentiles, echoed in Saul's call.
God appoints a prophet before birth and tells him not to be afraid.
Elijah raises a widow's son, a pattern for Tabitha.

im.c: The Conversion of Saint Paul, by Caravaggio (c. 1600).
im.k: Caravaggio (c. 1600), Santa Maria del Popolo, Rome / Wikimedia Commons

set: In Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea, a centurion named Cornelius has a vision. In Joppa, Peter prays on a rooftop at noon and has a vision of a sheet full of animals. Men from Cornelius arrive, and Peter goes with them to Caesarea, where the Holy Spirit falls on a Gentile household as he preaches.

his.t: Herod built it as a Roman port and Pilate governed from here.
A Roman unit of about 600 soldiers stationed in Judea.

cus.t: Jewish food laws kept Jews from sharing meals with Gentiles.
The sixth hour was a common prayer time, and roofs were quiet places.

cu: Cornelius was a "God-fearer," a Gentile who worshiped Israel's God and prayed and gave alms but had not become a Jew. Jews avoided eating with Gentiles and entering their homes, which is why Peter says in verse 28 that God has shown him not to call anyone unclean. The vision used food laws to make that point.

ot.n: The list of clean and unclean animals, now reframed.
God shows no partiality and takes no bribe.
The Spirit poured out on all, now on Gentiles too.

im.c: Peter's vision of the sheet with animals, by Domenico Fetti (early 17th century).
im.k: Domenico Fetti (early 17th c.), Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna / Wikimedia Commons

set: Peter returns to Jerusalem and defends his visit to a Gentile home. Meanwhile believers who fled after Stephen's death reach Antioch in Syria and speak to Greeks as well as Jews. Barnabas goes there from Jerusalem, fetches Saul from Tarsus, and teaches the new church for a year.

his.t: A great city on the Orontes river, home to a large Jewish community.
A food shortage under Emperor Claudius hit Judea hard.

cus.t: Jewish believers were wary of eating with uncircumcised Gentiles.
Each disciple gave according to his ability, a model for later churches.

cu: "Christians" (v.26) is probably a name given by outsiders, a Greek word with a Latin-style ending meaning "followers of Christ." Antioch was the third largest city of the Roman world, a major crossroads with a mixed population. A famine during the reign of Claudius, around AD 46-48, is also mentioned by ancient historians.

ot.n: The Spirit is poured out on everyone, as Peter recalls.
The light to the nations reaches Antioch.
Foreigners who join the Lord are welcomed to his house.

im.c: Peter's vision of the unclean animals (Acts 10:9-16), from a 16th-century print series on Acts.
im.k: Print series on Acts (16th c.), Rijksmuseum, CC0 / Wikimedia Commons

set: King Herod Agrippa I, who rules Judea under Rome, has James, John's brother, killed with the sword. He arrests Peter during the days of Unleavened Bread and chains him between two soldiers. An angel leads Peter out at night, and he goes to the house of Mary, mother of John Mark, where the church is praying.

his.t: Grandson of Herod the Great, ruled Judea AD 41-44 and courted Jewish favor.
The first apostle to die, killed around AD 44.

cus.t: Four groups of four soldiers took turns, each guarding for three hours.
Early believers met in homes, and Mary's house was large enough for many.

cu: Four squads of four soldiers took turns guarding Peter, who is chained to two of them. Herod waits for Passover to end before bringing him out for trial. When Rhoda says Peter is at the door, the believers say "It must be his angel," which shows a popular belief that a person has a guardian angel.

ot.n: Eat ready to leave: the Passover pattern of deliverance.
The angel of the Lord camps around those who fear him.
"I will not die but live" is a fitting echo of Peter's release.

im.c: The Deliverance of Saint Peter, by Raphael (c. 1514).
im.k: Raphael (c. 1514), Vatican Museums / Wikimedia Commons

set: The church at Antioch fasts and prays, and the Spirit says to set apart Barnabas and Saul. With John Mark they sail from Seleucia to Cyprus, preach at Salamis, and cross the island to Paphos, where the proconsul Sergius Paulus believes.

his.t: A senatorial province governed by a proconsul from the capital at Paphos.
A Roman colony in the highlands, placed there to guard the road.

cus.t: The church commissions its missionaries with fasting and prayer.
A gesture of rejection that Jesus taught his disciples (Luke 9:5).

cu: In a synagogue the Law and the Prophets were read, and visitors with something to say might be invited to speak (v.15). From verse 9, Luke calls Saul "Paul," his Roman name, and the focus of the story shifts to him. A proconsul governed a senatorial province like Cyprus.

ot.n: "You are my Son," quoted as fulfilled in the resurrection.
The light for the Gentiles, the basis for Paul's turn.
"A work in your days" is quoted as a warning.

im.c: Paul confronts the sorcerer Elymas on Cyprus (Acts 13:6-12), from a 16th-century print series on Acts.
im.k: Print series on Acts (16th c.), Rijksmuseum, CC0 / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul and Barnabas preach in Iconium until a plot to stone them forces them out. In Lystra, a city in Lycaonia, Paul heals a man lame from birth and the crowd cries out that the gods have come down. Jews arrive from Antioch and Iconium, win the crowd over, and stone Paul.

his.t: A rural region of central Anatolia with its own language and gods.
Lystra was a Roman colony, but many locals kept older customs.

cus.t: Priests offered sacrifices with garlands at the city gates.
A sign of grief and horror at blasphemy, as in verse 14.

cu: The crowd speaks Lycaonian (v.11), so Paul and Barnabas do not understand what is happening until the priest of Zeus brings garlands and oxen. The people call Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes because Paul does the talking. A local legend told of Zeus and Hermes once visiting the region in disguise and being turned away, which may explain the eager welcome.

ot.n: The Creator who made heaven, earth, sea and all that is in them.
The Lord who made heaven and earth and keeps faith forever.

im.c: The Sacrifice at Lystra, Raphael's 1515 cartoon for a tapestry.
im.k: Raphael (1515), Victoria and Albert Museum / Wikimedia Commons

set: Teachers from Judea come to Antioch insisting that Gentile believers be circumcised to be saved. Paul and Barnabas travel to Jerusalem with others to settle the matter with the apostles and elders. After debate, Peter and James speak and the council sends a letter to the Gentile churches.

his.t: Some Jewish believers held that Gentiles must become Jews first.
The brother of Jesus led the Jerusalem church and speaks last.

cus.t: The covenant sign for Abraham's household, required of any male convert.
Official letters opened with "greetings" and named their senders.

cu: Circumcision was the sign of the covenant given to Abraham, so asking Gentiles to skip it was a major break. The four requests in the letter (food offered to idols, blood, strangled animals, and sexual immorality) match the rules for foreigners living among Israel in Leviticus 17-18, and James says Moses is read in the synagogues every Sabbath (v.21).

ot.n: The fallen tent of David rebuilt, so the Gentiles seek the Lord.
Rules on blood for the foreigner living among Israel.
Circumcision as the sign of the covenant with Abraham.

im.c: Peter preaching in Jerusalem, from a 16th-century print series on Acts.
im.k: Print series on Acts (16th c.), Rijksmuseum, CC0 / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul and Silas revisit Derbe and Lystra, where Timothy joins them. Forbidden by the Spirit to go to Asia or Bithynia, they reach Troas and Paul sees a man of Macedonia in a vision. They cross the Aegean to Philippi, a Roman colony. By the river outside the city they meet Lydia.

his.t: Philippi was settled by veterans and ruled under Roman law.
Citizens could not be beaten or imprisoned without a proper trial.

cus.t: Without a synagogue, Jews gathered near water for prayer.
A slave girl was thought to speak for the Pythian oracle.

cu: Philippi seems to have had no synagogue (tradition required ten Jewish men), so a small group meets for prayer by the river. Lydia was a dealer in purple cloth, a luxury trade, from Thyatira. The "we" in verse 10 suggests the author, Luke, has joined the group. Roman citizens could not be beaten without a trial, which is why Paul later insists on an apology (v.37).

ot.n: Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.
God shatters gates of bronze and cuts iron bars.

im.c: Paul speaks to the women at Philippi (Acts 16:13-15), from a 16th-century print series on Acts.
im.k: Print series on Acts (16th c.), Rijksmuseum, CC0 / Wikimedia Commons

t: Paul in Thessalonica, Berea, and Athens
