set: Paul and Silas travel along the Egnatian Way through Amphipolis and Apollonia to Thessalonica, where Paul reasons from the Scriptures in the synagogue for three Sabbaths. A mob forces them to leave, and they go to Berea, where the Jews examine the Scriptures daily.

his.t: Thessalonica's city rulers carried this rare title, as Luke says.
The city was proud of its schools, though its glory days were past.

cus.t: The Bereans checked every claim against Scripture.
Ancient writers mention altars to unnamed gods in Athens.

cu: In Athens, Epicureans (who held that the gods were distant) and Stoics (who believed in an impersonal divine reason) argued in the marketplace. The Areopagus was the city's ancient council. Paul quotes the poets Epimenides and Aratus: "In him we live and move and have our being" and "We are his offspring" (v.28).

ot.n: All humans are made in God's image from one origin.
The Creator gives breath to all people.
God set the boundaries of the nations.

im.c: St Paul Preaching in Athens, Raphael's 1515 cartoon for a tapestry.
im.k: Raphael (1515), Victoria and Albert Museum / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul reaches Corinth, a busy port and Roman colony, and meets Aquila and Priscilla, Jews who left Rome after Claudius expelled them. They share a trade as tentmakers. Paul preaches in the synagogue until opposition leads him to the house of Titius Justus next door.

his.t: Around AD 49 Claudius expelled Jews from Rome after disputes over "Chrestus."
Proconsul of Achaia about AD 51-52, brother of the philosopher Seneca.

cus.t: Leatherwork and tent cloth were a common trade for Tarsus natives.
A vow ended with cutting the hair, as in Numbers 6.

cu: Claudius expelled Jews from Rome (often dated about AD 49; Suetonius reports it but gives no year), which explains why Aquila and Priscilla are in Corinth. Paul works as a tentmaker so as not to burden the church. The Nazirite-like vow that ends with cutting his hair at Cenchreae (v.18) was a sign of thanks or devotion.

ot.n: "I am with you; do not fear," like the Lord's promise to Paul.
The Nazirite vow ends with the cutting of the hair.

im.c: A letter of the emperor Claudius naming Gallio as proconsul of Achaia, found at Delphi. It helps date Paul's stay in Corinth to about AD 51-52.
im.k: Gérard, CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul returns to Ephesus, the capital of the province of Asia. He finds some disciples who know only John's baptism, and he baptizes them in Jesus' name. He argues in the lecture hall of Tyrannus daily for two years so that all of Asia hears the word.

his.t: Her temple drew pilgrims and made the city a center of trade.
Officials of the province who sponsored games, some of them Paul's friends.

cus.t: Spells were written on scrolls and sold for high prices.
Craftsmen sold small silver models of the goddess's temple.

cu: Ephesus was home to the great temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world, and a thriving trade in silver shrines. The "Ephesian letters" mentioned in magic were charms written on scrolls. The burned scrolls were worth 50,000 silver coins (v.19), and one coin was a day's wage.

ot.n: Sorcery and divination are forbidden to Israel.
The folly of those who make idols of wood and metal.

im.c: The Preaching of Saint Paul at Ephesus, by Eustache Le Sueur (17th century).
im.k: Eustache Le Sueur (17th c.), Louvre / Wikimedia Commons

t: Eutychus and the Farewell at Miletus
set: After the riot, Paul sails to Macedonia and Greece, spends three months in Greece, and heads back through Macedonia. On the first day of the week at Troas, Paul speaks late into the night, and a young man named Eutychus falls from a third-floor window and is raised.

his.t: Paul carried gifts from Gentile churches to Jerusalem.
A port city whose harbor was silting up, near Ephesus.

cus.t: The Lord's Supper was part of a shared meal on Sunday.
Prayer on the shore was a physical sign of deep farewell.

cu: The church meets on "the first day of the week" (v.7) to break bread, a very early record of Sunday worship. Eutychus fell asleep in an upper room full of lamps, and Paul spoke until midnight and then until dawn. Verse 35 preserves a saying of Jesus, "It is more blessed to give than to receive," that none of the Gospels records.

ot.n: Samuel asks whether he has taken anything from anyone.
God judges bad shepherds and promises to shepherd his sheep.

im.c: Paul raises Eutychus at Troas (Acts 20:7-12), from a 16th-century print series on Acts.
im.k: Print series on Acts (16th c.), Rijksmuseum, CC0 / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul sails from Miletus to Tyre, Ptolemais, and Caesarea, where Philip's four daughters live and the prophet Agabus warns that the Jews in Jerusalem will bind Paul. In Jerusalem James and the elders ask Paul to join four men completing a vow and pay their costs.

his.t: A Roman garrison overlooked the Temple courts from the northwest.
Josephus describes an Egyptian prophet who led a failed uprising around AD 54.

cus.t: Men finishing the vow shaved their heads and offered sacrifices.
Many Jewish believers were strict about the law, as James says.

cu: Paul's purification and payment for the Nazirite vow showed that he still honored the law as a Jew. The accusation that he had taken Trophimus, an Ephesian Gentile, into the inner courts was serious, because that was punishable by death. The Roman commander thought Paul was an Egyptian rebel who had led 4,000 "assassins" into the wilderness (v.38).

ot.n: The ritual that ends a Nazirite vow, which Paul funds.
Foreigners may not enter the sanctuary, the reason for the mob's outrage.

im.c: Paul is seized in Jerusalem (Acts 21:27-36), from a 16th-century print series on Acts.
im.k: Print series on Acts (16th c.), Rijksmuseum, CC0 / Wikimedia Commons

t: Paul's Defense on the Temple Steps
set: Standing on the steps of the Antonia fortress, Paul asks the Roman commander for permission to speak and addresses the crowd in Aramaic. He tells how he persecuted the church, met Jesus on the road to Damascus, was healed by Ananias, and was sent to the Gentiles.

his.t: Citizens were exempt from scourging and had the right to a hearing.
Paul was trained at Gamaliel's feet in the strict Pharisee tradition.

cus.t: The common language of Judea, a close relative of Hebrew.
A sign of anger or of readiness to throw stones.

cu: Speaking in "the Hebrew dialect" (v.2) means Aramaic, the language most Jews of Judea spoke, and it quieted the crowd. Throwing off cloaks and tossing dust into the air (v.23) were signs of rage. Under Roman law it was a serious crime to flog a Roman citizen without a trial, and the commander himself says he paid a large sum for his citizenship.

ot.n: The servant sent as a light to the nations.
The God of our fathers, the title Ananias uses.

im.c: Paul before the Sanhedrin (Acts 22:30-23:11), from a 16th-century print series on Acts.
im.k: Print series on Acts (16th c.), Rijksmuseum, CC0 / Wikimedia Commons

set: The commander brings Paul before the Sanhedrin. Paul says he has lived with a clear conscience and is rebuked by the high priest. He then divides the council by saying he is on trial for the resurrection. That night the Lord tells him to take courage.

his.t: The two parties disagreed on resurrection, angels and spirits.
The high priest from AD 47 to 59 was known for greed and violence.

cus.t: They bound themselves by a curse to fast until Paul was dead.
The escort left at the third hour of the night, about nine.

cu: The Sadducees denied the resurrection, angels, and spirits, and the Pharisees affirmed them, so Paul's remark started a fight in the council. The oath of the forty men called a curse on themselves if they ate before Paul was dead. The escort of 470 soldiers (200 soldiers, 70 horsemen, 200 spearmen) left at nine at night and traveled about 35 miles to Antipatris before turning back.

ot.n: Do not speak evil of a ruler of your people.
Prophets who coat a flimsy wall with whitewash.

im.c: Paul before the Sanhedrin (Acts 23), from a 16th-century print series on Acts.
im.k: Print series on Acts (16th c.), Rijksmuseum, CC0 / Wikimedia Commons

set: Five days later the high priest Ananias arrives in Caesarea with elders and a lawyer named Tertullus to accuse Paul before Felix. Paul answers the charges point by point. Felix, who knows something about the Way, puts off a decision.

his.t: A freed slave who ruled Judea AD 52-59 with a heavy hand.
A name Jews used for the new movement, which Paul accepts.

cus.t: Orators praised the judge before making their case.
Paul could receive visits from friends while being held.

cu: Tertullus opens with flattery, as was usual in Roman courts. Felix was a freed slave who rose to be governor of Judea (AD 52-59), and Tacitus describes him as cruel and greedy. Drusilla, his wife, was Jewish, the daughter of Herod Agrippa I. Paul calls the Way what they call a "sect" and says he worships the God of his ancestors.

ot.n: A resurrection of the righteous and the wicked.
God will bring every deed into judgment.

im.c: Paul Before Felix, by William Hogarth (1747-51).
im.k: William Hogarth (1747-51) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Festus arrives as the new governor and goes up to Jerusalem, where the leaders ask for Paul to be brought there, planning an ambush. Festus returns to Caesarea and hears the case. When he asks Paul if he will go to Jerusalem for trial, Paul exercises his right as a Roman citizen and appeals to Caesar.

his.t: Governor of Judea from about AD 59 and a more able ruler than Felix.
Great-grandson of Herod the Great and the last Herodian king.

cus.t: A citizen could appeal to the emperor to stop a local trial.
Local rulers paid formal visits to new Roman governors.

cu: A Roman citizen who appealed to the emperor stopped the local trial and went to Rome (v.12). At the time the emperor was Nero. Festus did not know what to write to the emperor, since he found no charge worthy of death, so he welcomed Agrippa's Jewish expertise.

ot.n: A charge needs witnesses, and false witnesses are judged.
The first to state a case seems right until the other comes.

im.c: Paul before Festus and Agrippa (Acts 25-26), from a 16th-century print series on Acts.
im.k: Print series on Acts (16th c.), Rijksmuseum, CC0 / Wikimedia Commons

set: In a grand audience hall in Caesarea, with Festus, Agrippa II, Bernice, and the city leaders present, Paul is invited to speak for himself. He tells of his life as a Pharisee, his persecution of the church, and the vision on the Damascus road.

his.t: He controlled the Temple's appointments and the high priests' garments.
Paul calls it the strictest sect of his religion.

cus.t: Farmers prodded oxen with a sharp stick, and kicking back only hurt the ox.
Prisoners spoke in chains before the court.

cu: Agrippa II was raised in Rome and was recognized as an authority on Jewish customs (v.3). The Lord's phrase "it is hard for you to kick against the goads" (v.14) was a common Greek proverb: an ox that kicked against the sharp stick only hurt itself. Paul also stands in chains throughout (v.29).

ot.n: The servant opens blind eyes and brings prisoners from darkness.
God promises to rescue a prophet sent to the nations.

im.c: Paul and King Agrippa, by Hendrick Bloemaert.
im.k: Hendrick Bloemaert, Centraal Museum Utrecht / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul and other prisoners are put in the care of a centurion named Julius and sail from Caesarea in the autumn. After stops at Sidon and Myra they board an Alexandrian grain ship, struggle past Cnidus, and anchor at Fair Havens on Crete.

his.t: Large ships from Alexandria carried grain to feed Rome.
A centurion of the Augustan Cohort who treated Paul with kindness.

cus.t: The Day of Atonement fell in early autumn and marked the end of safe sailing.
Sailors dropped a weighted line to measure the depth near shore.

cu: Sailing was dangerous after mid-September and nearly impossible from November to March. "The Fast" (v.9) is the Day of Atonement, around late September or early October. The crew passed ropes under the hull to hold it together (v.17), threw cargo and tackle overboard, and finally took soundings and dropped anchors off the stern.

ot.n: Sailors in a storm cry to the Lord, who calms the waves.
A prophet on a ship in a storm, with cargo thrown overboard.

im.c: Saint Paul Shipwrecked on Malta, by Laurent de La Hyre (17th century).
im.k: Laurent de La Hyre (17th c.) / Wikimedia Commons

set: The survivors land on Malta, where a viper bites Paul and he suffers no harm. Paul heals the father of Publius, the chief official of the island, and many others. After three months they sail on a ship from Alexandria, landing at Syracuse, Rhegium, and Puteoli, and travel by road to Rome.

his.t: The city had a large Jewish community and a growing church.
Prisoners awaiting trial could live in private housing under guard.

cus.t: The twin gods were patrons of sailors and carved on ship prows.
A soldier was chained to the prisoner day and night.

cu: The ship's figurehead of Castor and Pollux (v.11), the twin gods of sailors, shows that Alexandrian grain ships sailed under pagan protection. From Puteoli travelers joined the Appian Way to Rome, and the Forum of Appius lay 43 miles and Three Taverns 33 miles from the city. Paul is chained to a soldier but lives in his own rented quarters and receives all visitors.

ot.n: Hearts grown dull and ears that barely hear, quoted by Paul.
God's way and saving power made known among all nations.

im.c: Paul bitten by a viper on Malta, by Maerten de Vos (c. 1568-70).
im.k: Maerten de Vos (c. 1568-70) / Wikimedia Commons

t: Paul’s Greeting and the Wrath Revealed
set: Paul writes to Christians in Rome, the capital of the empire, a city of perhaps a million people. He has never been there but has long wanted to go (vv.10-13). The church meets in homes and includes Jews and Gentiles. After the greeting he states his theme and begins to explain why the whole world needs the gospel.

his.t: Probably begun by visitors from Jerusalem and by Jews and Gentiles who moved to the capital. Nobody knows who founded it.
Roads and sea lanes led to Rome, so news and people from every province arrived there.

cus.t: “Slave” could be a humble word in Rome, but in Scripture it was used of God’s chosen leaders such as Moses.
Greeks divided the world into Greeks and “barbarians,” people who didn’t speak Greek. Paul says the gospel is for both (v.14).

cu: Paul opens in the style of a Greek letter (sender, recipient, greeting), but expands every part with a summary of the gospel. He calls himself a “servant” (Greek doulos, slave), a title that was a mark of honor in the Old Testament, when it was used of Moses and David.

ot.n: “The righteous shall live by faith.” Paul’s summary of the gospel.
Israel exchanged God’s glory for an image of an ox, a pattern Paul says repeats.
Humans were made in God’s image, the image people then trade for idols.

im.c: Saint Paul Writing His Epistles, by Valentin de Boulogne (about 1618-20). Romans was probably dictated to a scribe, Tertius (Romans 16:22).
im.k: Valentin de Boulogne (c. 1618-20), Museum of Fine Arts, Boston / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul turns to someone who condemns the people described in chapter 1. He is probably speaking to a moral, religious person, and soon addresses a Jew by name (v.17). He argues that God judges everyone by the same standard, with no exceptions for those who have the law or the right heritage.

his.t: Several synagogues existed in Rome, and Jews held a respected place, but they were often resented for their customs.
Roman Stoics also taught that people should do what they judge in others. Paul uses that common ground.

cus.t: The sign of the covenant for Jewish males. Some thought it guaranteed God’s favor, and Paul says it means nothing without obedience.
Jews were to bind the law to their hands and foreheads. Paul says the real place for it is the heart.

cu: Jews were proud of having the law, circumcision, and being “a guide to the blind” (vv.17-20). Paul answers by saying that what counts is a changed heart. He ends with a play on words: a true Jew is one “inwardly,” and his praise is from God, not people (vv.28-29).

ot.n: God repays everyone for what they have done.
God’s law written on hearts under the new covenant.
God’s name is dishonored among the nations because of his people.

im.c: Papyrus 113, a small fragment from Oxyrhynchus usually dated to about the 3rd century. This side has Romans 2:12-13, on hearers and doers of the law.
im.k: Sackler Library, Oxford, public domain / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul answers the objections that came to mind in chapter 2, gives the verdict that all are under sin, and then, in verse 21, turns to the good news. This short passage (vv.21-26) is often called the center of the letter.

his.t: Once a year the high priest sprinkled blood on the mercy seat. Paul says Jesus is that place of mercy.
Redemption was a familiar idea in a world where slaves were bought and freed.

cus.t: People in Roman society boasted in family, rank, and achievements. Paul says faith leaves no room for it (v.27).
The Shema, “the Lord is one,” was the Jewish creed. Paul uses it to say that God must be the God of Gentiles too (v.29-30).

cu: The “mercy seat” behind the word “propitiation” (v.25) was the gold cover of the ark of the covenant, sprinkled with blood on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). Redemption (v.24) was the price paid to free a slave or prisoner.

ot.n: “There is no one who does good,” part of Paul’s chain of quotations.
The blood on the mercy seat on the Day of Atonement.
The just live by faith, Paul’s lifelong text.

im.c: Papyrus 40, a Greek papyrus usually dated to about the 3rd century. This page has Romans 3:21-26, Paul's central statement on being made right by faith.
im.k: Heidelberg Institute for Papyrology, public domain / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul now proves from Scripture that being right with God by faith is not a new idea. He turns to Abraham, the founding father of the Jews, and shows that Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised, so he is the father of all who believe, Jew or Gentile.

his.t: Abraham was about a hundred and Sarah about ninety when Isaac was born (Genesis 17:17; 21:5).
Genesis 15 comes years before Genesis 17, a timing Paul uses to make his point.

cus.t: An accounting word. A sum is put to someone’s account. Paul says righteousness is put to the believer’s account.
Abraham’s name means “father of many,” given in Genesis 17:5.

cu: Jews of Paul’s day often described Abraham as being justified because he kept the law before it was given or because of his faithful testing. Paul argues the opposite, from Genesis 15:6, that Abraham simply believed. The idea of being “credited” (v.3) comes from accounting.

ot.n: “Abraham believed the Lord, and he credited it to him as righteousness.”
“Blessed is the one whose sin the Lord will not count against him.”
Abraham is made “a father of many nations.”

im.c: Sarah leads Hagar to Abraham, by Matthias Stom (17th century). Paul says Abraham believed God though his own body and Sarah's womb were as good as dead (Romans 4:19).
im.k: Matthias Stom (c. 1632-39) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul now spells out what follows from being made right by faith: peace with God, a hope that does not disappoint, and the certainty of God’s love shown at the cross. In the second half he compares Adam and Christ: one man brought sin and death into the world, and one man brings righteousness and life.

his.t: Paul says death reached everyone because Adam’s sin opened the door and then all sinned (v.12).
Between Adam and Moses people died even without the law, showing sin was already at work (v.13-14).

cus.t: The word in v.2 was used of being introduced to a king. Believers are brought into God’s presence.
Heroic friends sometimes died for each other, but Paul says Christ died for people who had nothing to offer (v.7-8).

cu: Paul says we were “enemies” (v.10), a word that could describe actual warring parties. “Peace” in the Roman world was supposed to come from the emperor’s victories (Pax Romana). Paul says true peace comes from the cross.

ot.n: The fall of Adam, whose act Paul says reached everyone.
The servant makes many righteous, behind Paul’s “one man’s obedience.”
The law at Sinai that made sin more visible.

im.c: Adam and Eve, an engraving by Albrecht Dürer (1504). In Romans 5 Paul sets the first Adam beside Christ, the last.
im.k: Albrecht Dürer (1504), National Gallery of Art, Washington / Wikimedia Commons

t: Dead to Sin, Alive to God
set: Paul faces a likely objection: if grace is greater where sin is greater, why not sin more? He answers that those who belong to Christ have died to sin, as pictured in baptism, and are now alive to God. He compares two masters, sin and God, and says everyone serves one or the other.

his.t: Perhaps a third of Rome’s population were slaves or former slaves. Many in the church were.
Christians were baptized at once after confessing Christ, as Acts shows.

cus.t: Soldiers received a wage. Paul says sin pays its servants with death, but God gives life freely.
The word describes offering something as a sacrifice or reporting for duty.

cu: Baptism in the early church was by immersion, so going under water pictured burial and coming up pictured resurrection. Slavery was common in Rome, so the picture of “presenting yourselves” as slaves (v.16) was clear to all.

ot.n: The penalty for disobedience was death, the “wages” of sin.
Israel passed through the sea and left slavery. Paul pictures baptism similarly.
God promises a new heart and a new Spirit.

im.c: The Baptism of Christ, by Piero della Francesca (after 1451). Paul reads baptism as a burial and a rising with Christ (Romans 6:3-4).
im.k: Piero della Francesca (after 1451), National Gallery, London / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul explains how believers are released from the law, using an example from marriage. Then he asks if the law is sin, and answers no: it shows sin up. The last half describes a person who wants to do what is right but can’t, and cries out for rescue.

his.t: Readers have long disagreed whether Paul describes his life before Christ, his life as a believer, or Israel under the law.
Paul insists the law is holy, righteous, and good (v.12). The problem is sin.

cus.t: The tenth commandment deals with desire, not action, which is where Paul says he saw his sin.
A woman was bound to her husband while he lived, and free to remarry after his death.

cu: In Roman and Jewish law, a married woman was bound to her husband until his death. Paul uses it as a picture: believers died with Christ, so the old tie to the law is ended and they belong to someone new.

ot.n: “You shall not covet,” the commandment that exposed Paul’s sin.
The serpent deceived Eve, and Paul says sin deceived him.
The word is near, a text Paul will use in chapter 10.

im.c: Paul in Prison, by Rembrandt (1627). It is an imagined scene: Romans was not written from prison, but the painting suits Paul's cry in Romans 7:24.
im.k: Rembrandt (1627), Staatsgalerie Stuttgart / Wikimedia Commons

set: This chapter is often called the high point of the letter. After the struggle of chapter 7, Paul declares no condemnation, describes life under the Spirit, calls believers children of God, and closes with a hymn to God’s love that nothing can break.

his.t: This chapter mentions the Spirit nearly twenty times, more than the rest of the letter combined.
Paul lists dangers (v.35) that many of his readers faced or would face under Nero.

cus.t: A Roman might adopt an adult to carry his name and inheritance. Paul says God does this for believers.
The first of the harvest, given to God as a promise of the rest (v.23).

cu: Adoption in Roman law gave a person full rights as an heir. “Abba” (v.15) was the Aramaic word for father, used by Jesus (Mark 14:36), and a child’s word of intimacy.

ot.n: Creation was cursed because of Adam, the reason it “groans.”
“For your sake we face death all day long,” quoted of suffering.
The servant is vindicated, behind “Who will bring a charge?”

im.c: Papyrus 27, a leaf from Oxyrhynchus usually dated to the 3rd century. This side holds Romans 8:12-27, on life in the Spirit.
im.k: Cambridge University Library, public domain / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul begins with deep grief for his own people, the Israelites, who have so many privileges but have mostly not believed. He then explains that God’s promise has not failed, because it was never based on physical descent. He walks through God’s choice of Isaac, Jacob, and Pharaoh, and the calling of Gentiles.

his.t: The adoption, the covenants and the law are listed as real privileges (vv.4-5).
Isaiah’s “remnant” is a small group that stays faithful, a pattern Paul says holds now.

cus.t: The firstborn son normally got the larger inheritance. God reversed that for Jacob and Esau.
Potters were common in towns, and Jeremiah 18 uses the image of clay shaped by the potter.

cu: Paul’s list of Israel’s privileges (vv.4-5) comes from what Jews took pride in: adoption, glory, covenants, the law, worship, promises, and the patriarchs. The image of a potter and clay (vv.20-21) was a common picture of God’s power.

ot.n: “It is through Isaac that your offspring will be reckoned.”
“I will have mercy on whom I have mercy.”
The stone laid in Zion, which is a stumbling block or a foundation.

im.c: Esau Selling His Birthright, by Hendrick ter Brugghen (about 1625). Romans 9:10-13 recalls Jacob and Esau to show that God's choice rests on his call.
im.k: Hendrick ter Brugghen (c. 1625) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul keeps praying for Israel and explains why they have not yet received the gospel: they pursued righteousness by the law and did not submit to God’s way. He says salvation is near, in the mouth and the heart, and open to everyone who calls on the Lord.

his.t: Many Jews were deeply devoted to God, as Paul himself had been (Acts 22:3).
Letters and news traveled with couriers. Paul sees every preacher as one who carries news.

cus.t: Early Christians publicly said “Jesus is Lord,” which could cost them in a world of emperor worship.
A runner arriving with news of victory was welcomed with joy.

cu: Verse 9 is one of the earliest creeds: “Jesus is Lord.” In a world where “Caesar is lord” was a political slogan, saying it of Jesus was a bold claim. Paul’s “beautiful feet” (v.15) comes from messengers who ran across hills with news of victory.

ot.n: “The word is very near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart.”
“Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”
“How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news.”

im.c: The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (about 125–100 BC), the kind of scroll Jesus unrolls in the Nazareth synagogue (Luke 4).
im.k: Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul asks, “Did God reject his people?” and answers no. There is a remnant, as in Elijah’s day, and Israel’s stumbling has opened the door for Gentiles. He warns Gentile believers not to boast, using the picture of a wild olive branch grafted into a cultivated tree, and he ends with a hymn of praise.

his.t: In a dark time, God kept seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal, the pattern for the remnant.
The Roman church had tension between Jews and Gentiles after Claudius’s edict.

cus.t: Olive trees took years to bear fruit and could live for centuries. They were a symbol of Israel (Jeremiah 11:16).
A first batch of dough offered to God made the whole lump holy (v.16).

cu: Grafting wild branches into a cultivated olive tree was backwards, since farmers usually grafted good branches into wild stock. Paul says it is “contrary to nature” (v.24) on purpose, to show that God’s kindness is unexpected.

ot.n: God kept seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal.
The deliverer will come from Zion and turn Jacob from ungodliness.
“Who has known the mind of the Lord?”

im.c: Olive Trees, painted by Vincent van Gogh at Saint-Rémy in November 1889. Paul pictures Israel and the Gentiles as an olive tree (Romans 11:17-24).
im.k: Vincent van Gogh (1889) / Wikimedia Commons

set: After eleven chapters of doctrine, Paul turns to practice with “Therefore.” He urges believers to offer their whole selves to God, to be transformed by renewed minds, and to serve one another with the gifts God gives. The chapter then lists marks of genuine love, including blessing enemies.

his.t: Early house churches needed teachers, givers, and helpers. Paul shows the variety.
Christians in Rome would soon face real hostility under Nero.

cus.t: Travelers relied on private homes. Hospitality was a main way the church spread.
The meaning is debated. It may refer to the shame that makes an enemy repent.

cu: Roman and Jewish worship involved bringing animals to be killed. Paul says the sacrifice God now wants is a living person. The “body” of Christ (vv.4-5) was a picture in Greek writers too, but Paul uses it for the church.

ot.n: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him,” quoted in v.20.
“It is mine to avenge; I will repay.”
Love your neighbor, the heart of the command that follows.

im.c: Papyrus 31, a fragment in the John Rylands Library, usually dated to about the 7th century, so much later than Paul. It has Romans 12:3-8, on the gifts the members of one body hold.
im.k: John Rylands Library, Manchester, public domain / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul writes to Christians living in the capital, under an emperor, probably Nero in the early part of his reign. He tells them to be subject to governing authorities, to pay taxes, and to owe nothing but love. He ends with a call to wake up because salvation is nearer than when they first believed.

his.t: The first years of Nero’s rule (AD 54-59) were relatively stable. Later he persecuted Christians.
Jews were expelled from Rome around AD 49 for unrest, so Paul’s readers knew what official anger felt like.

cus.t: Rome collected direct taxes (tribute) and indirect ones such as customs duties. Both are named in v.7.
The right to carry the sword meant the government’s power to punish with death.

cu: Taxes in Rome were often unfair, and in AD 58 there was an uproar over the tax collectors. Paul tells believers to pay what they owe (v.7). The “armor of light” (v.12) is a soldier’s image used elsewhere by Paul (Ephesians 6).

ot.n: “Love your neighbor as yourself,” the sum of the law.
God removes kings and sets up kings.
The commandments Paul lists, summed up by love.

im.c: A portrait of the emperor Nero, who ruled when Paul wrote Romans 13:1-7.
im.k: cjh1452000, CC BY-SA 3.0 / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul addresses a practical divide in the Roman church: some believers ate anything and treated all days alike, while others avoided meat and kept special days. Jews and Gentiles likely stood on both sides. Paul tells each side to welcome the other and to answer to the Lord, not to each other.

his.t: The “weak” are those with scruples, not weak in character. The “strong” are those who feel free.
Much of Rome’s meat came from temple sacrifices, so a conscience could be pricked.

cus.t: Jews kept Sabbath and festivals. Some Gentile believers may have had other days or none.
Daniel and his friends ate only vegetables in Babylon (Daniel 1:12), a model for staying clean.

cu: Jews kept food laws and the Sabbath. Meat in Roman markets might have been offered to idols first, so some believers ate only vegetables. Wine could also be tied to pagan offerings. Eating together was the church’s center, so these issues were serious.

ot.n: “Every knee will bow before me.”
Daniel asked for vegetables and water in Babylon.
The food laws behind the scruples of the weak.

im.c: A painted scene of food from Pompeii, made before AD 79. Romans 14 is about what Christians eat and drink at the table.
im.k: Unknown Roman artist (before AD 79), public domain / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul continues his plea for unity with Christ as the example, then describes his mission. He has preached from Jerusalem around to Illyricum and now plans to go to Spain, stopping in Rome on the way. First he must take a collection for the poor in Jerusalem, and he asks the Romans to pray.

his.t: Paul organized this offering during his third journey (1 Corinthians 16; 2 Corinthians 8-9).
Rome had ruled Spain for two centuries. There were already Jewish communities, though no record of Paul reaching it.

cus.t: “To be helped on my journey” (v.24) means to supply food, money, and companions for the next stage.
Paul calls the first converts of an area “firstfruits,” echoing the offering of the harvest.

cu: The collection (vv.25-27) was money from Gentile churches in Macedonia and Achaia for poor believers in Jerusalem. It was a gift but also a sign of unity between Jewish and Gentile believers. Spain was the far west of the Roman world and had Latin-speaking cities.

ot.n: “I will praise you among the Gentiles.”
“Rejoice, you Gentiles, with his people.”
The root of Jesse will rise to rule the nations, and the nations will hope in him.

im.c: The roads around Rome on the Peutinger Table, a medieval copy of a Roman road map. Paul hoped to pass through Rome on his way to Spain (Romans 15:24, 28).
im.k: Konrad Miller (1888 copy of the Peutinger Table), CC BY-SA 3.0 / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul commends Phoebe, who carries the letter, and sends greetings to over two dozen people in Rome by name, including Priscilla and Aquila. He warns against people who cause divisions, sends greetings from his coworkers in Corinth, and ends with a doxology.

his.t: Jews expelled from Rome by Claudius, they met Paul in Corinth (Acts 18) and later returned. A church met in their home.
Paul’s companion in Corinth, called the city’s “director of public works” (v.23).

cus.t: A normal greeting between family members that Paul asks believers to share.
Greetings mention groups meeting in homes: those with Aristobulus, Narcissus, and others.

cu: Letters were carried by trusted friends, who also read them aloud and explained them. Phoebe is called a “servant” or deacon of the church at Cenchreae and a “benefactor” (v.1-2), someone who helped many, Paul included.

ot.n: God will crush Satan under their feet (v.20), echoing the first promise.
Those who were not told will see, behind “obedience of faith” to the nations.
Wisdom and power belong to God, echoed in the doxology.

im.c: Saint Paul with Aquila and Priscilla, by Jan van de Venne (17th century). Paul greets the couple first in Romans 16:3-5.
im.k: Jan van de Venne (17th century), CC0 / Wikimedia Commons

t: Division and the Wisdom of the Cross
set: Corinth was a wealthy Roman colony, rebuilt by Julius Caesar, set on the narrow land bridge between two seas. It had a mixed population, a lively trade, and a reputation for loose morals. Paul greets the church, then tackles the first problem: members are lining up behind favorite teachers.

his.t: Paul stayed eighteen months in Corinth (Acts 18), and worked with Priscilla and Aquila.
Members of Chloe’s household brought Paul word of the quarrels. Little else is known about her.

cus.t: Greek teachers had loyal students who defended them against rivals, a pattern Paul says has crept into the church.
Romans reserved it for slaves and rebels. Citizens were almost never crucified.

cu: Greek cities valued polished speakers, and followers often attached themselves to a favorite teacher. That fits Paul’s opening complaint, “I follow Paul,” “I follow Apollos.” A cross was the most shameful punishment Rome had, so preaching a crucified Savior sounded absurd.

ot.n: “The wisdom of the wise will perish.”
“Let the one who boasts boast in this: that they know me.”
Isaiah mocks the wise men of Egypt, the pattern Paul recalls.

im.c: Saint Peter and Saint Paul, by El Greco (about 1590-1600). In 1 Corinthians 1:12 some in Corinth said "I follow Paul" and others "I follow Cephas", which is Peter.
im.k: El Greco (about 1590-1600) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul recalls how he first came to Corinth “in weakness and fear and much trembling,” preaching only Jesus Christ crucified. He says true wisdom comes from the Spirit, who reveals what no human eye has seen, and he contrasts the natural person with the one who has the Spirit.

his.t: He came to Corinth after a poor reception in Athens (Acts 17) and was discouraged (Acts 18:9).
Pilate and Herod did not understand who they were crucifying.

cus.t: Public speaking was an art form. Teachers like the Sophists traveled and charged fees for show.
Mystery cults offered hidden knowledge to initiates. Paul says God’s mystery is for all believers.

cu: Greek orators prided themselves on style. Paul refused to put on a show, preaching plainly so that faith would rest on God’s power, not human skill. The phrase “mature” (v.6) may recall the initiated in mystery religions, a term Paul reuses.

ot.n: “No eye has seen any God besides you.”
“Who has known the mind of the Lord?”
Wisdom, might, and wealth are not to be boasted in.

im.c: Saint Paul Preaching in Athens, Raphael's design for a tapestry (1515). Paul came to Corinth from Athens (Acts 17:22 to 18:1) and tells the Corinthians he did not come with lofty words of wisdom (1 Corinthians 2:1-5).
im.k: Raphael (1515), Victoria and Albert Museum / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul tells the Corinthians that their jealousy and quarreling show they are still spiritual infants. Teachers such as himself and Apollos are only servants, so the church belongs to God. He pictures the church as a field and a building, and warns every builder to be careful how he builds.

his.t: A Jewish teacher from Alexandria, skilled with Scripture, who taught in Corinth after Paul (Acts 18:24-28).
They worked in the same field. Paul says their roles were different but unified.

cus.t: Gold and silver survive fire, while wood and straw do not.
In pagan cities, a temple was the god’s home. Paul says God’s home is his people.

cu: Builders in Corinth worked with expensive marble and gold or with cheap wood and straw, and fire tested the result. Paul uses that image for church work: what lasts will stand and what doesn’t will burn, though the builder is saved.

ot.n: “He catches the wise in their craftiness.”
“The Lord knows the thoughts of man.”
God asked for a sanctuary so that he could dwell among his people.

im.c: Wheatfield with a Reaper, by Vincent van Gogh (September 1889). Paul calls the church "God's field": one plants, another waters, and God gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6-9).
im.k: Vincent van Gogh (September 1889) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul finishes his case about divisions. He asks the Corinthians to think of the apostles as servants and stewards, not stars. He contrasts their pride with the apostles’ hardships and calls them to imitate him, and he sends Timothy to remind them. He closes with a warning that he may come with a rod.

his.t: A general’s parade ended with captives, some of whom were executed. Paul says the apostles are at the end of the line.
Paul’s young co-worker, who joined him in Acts 16, was sent ahead to Corinth.

cus.t: Often a trusted slave who ran the household. His job was faithfulness.
A disciplinary tool. A father might use it on a child.

cu: A steward managed a household for the master and had to be trustworthy. The “spectacle” (v.9) pictures the end of a Roman triumph, when condemned prisoners were paraded and sent to die in the arena.

ot.n: Do not boast in wisdom, but in knowing the Lord.
The “remnant” image behind Paul’s sense of the faithful.

im.c: A carved relief of a gladiator found at Ephesus (Ephesus Museum, Turkey). Fights in the arena were a common public show in Roman cities. Paul says God has put the apostles on display "as men sentenced to death" (1 Corinthians 4:9) and speaks of fighting "beasts at Ephesus" (15:32).
im.k: Carole Raddato, CC BY-SA 2.0 / Wikimedia Commons

t: Dealing With Sin in the Church
set: Paul turns to a case of sexual immorality that even pagans condemned: a man living with his father’s wife (probably his stepmother). The church was proud rather than grieving. Paul tells them to remove him, using the picture of the Passover yeast that spreads through the whole batch of dough.

his.t: Paul wrote earlier, telling them not to associate with immoral people (v.9), and they misunderstood.
Cicero called this kind of union unheard of, and Roman law prohibited it.

cus.t: Before Passover, families searched the house with a lamp and removed all leaven.
The Jewish community could exclude a person. Paul asks the church to do the same.

cu: At Passover, Jewish families removed all yeast from the house. Paul says, “Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed,” so the church should clean out the old yeast of malice. Handing someone over to Satan (v.5) means putting him outside the church.

ot.n: “Purge the evil from among you.”
Forbids relations with a father’s wife.
Remove all yeast from the house at Passover.

im.c: The Ghent Altarpiece, by Jan van Eyck (finished 1432), with the Adoration of the Lamb in the center. Paul writes "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" (1 Corinthians 5:7).
im.k: Jan van Eyck (finished 1432) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul rebukes believers who sued each other in pagan courts and reminds them that saints will one day judge the world. Then he moves to sexual immorality: the Corinthians seem to have argued that the body does not matter. Paul says the body belongs to the Lord and is a temple of the Holy Spirit.

his.t: Judges were often corrupt, and the process favored the wealthy.
Slaves were “bought with a price” in the market. Paul says Christ bought believers.

cus.t: Corinthians seem to have said “All things are lawful.” Paul quotes and qualifies it.
Another slogan: “Food is for the stomach.” Paul answers that the body is for the Lord.

cu: Roman courts favored the rich, and civil cases were often a way to shame a rival. Paul says believers should settle disputes within the church. “All things are lawful for me” was probably a Corinthian slogan he quotes, which he corrects.

ot.n: “The two will become one flesh,” quoted of union with a prostitute.
The saints will judge, behind “the saints will judge the world.”
God promises to live among his people.

im.c: The Last Judgment, by Michelangelo (1536-41), in the Sistine Chapel. Paul asks, "Do you not know that the saints will judge the world?" (1 Corinthians 6:2).
im.k: Michelangelo (1536-41) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul begins to answer the Corinthians’ written questions. Some seem to have said it is good to avoid sex altogether, and others were wondering about divorce, mixed marriages, and whether the unmarried should marry.

his.t: A husband or wife could divorce simply by declaring it. Many Corinthians were remarried.
Claudius’s reign had food shortages, a possible “present distress.”

cus.t: Vv.36-38 may be about engaged couples or fathers giving daughters in marriage, and commentators disagree.
Paul says slaves should accept freedom if it comes, but not worry if it doesn’t.

cu: In the Roman world, marriage often joined families and property, and divorce was easy. Paul gives wives and husbands equal rights over each other’s bodies (vv.3-4), which was unusual. “The present distress” (v.26) may refer to a famine or the wider hardships of the time.

ot.n: The marriage union Paul assumes.
God hates divorce, behind Jesus’ teaching.
The Mosaic divorce provision Jesus said was a concession.

im.c: The Arnolfini Portrait, by Jan van Eyck (1434), a married couple in their home. It comes from a different time and place, but it is a picture of the marriage Paul writes about in 1 Corinthians 7.
im.k: Jan van Eyck (1434) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Corinth had many temples, and much of the meat sold in its markets had first been offered to idols. Some believers thought this meat was harmless because idols are nothing. Others, still troubled, thought eating it was worship. Paul says knowledge puffs up but love builds up.

his.t: Trade guilds held banquets at temples in honor of patron gods, and members were expected to attend.
Meat came mostly from sacrifices, so even a normal meal could raise the question.

cus.t: Temples had dining rooms. Paul mentions someone “reclining at table in an idol’s temple” (v.10).
To the Greeks, conscience was a witness within, a sense of moral self-awareness.

cu: Public meals often took place in temple dining rooms for guilds, weddings, and festivals. Declining an invitation could mean social isolation. Leftover meat from sacrifices was sold in the markets.

ot.n: “The Lord our God, the Lord is one.” The foundation for Paul’s answer.
The foolishness of idols made by hand.
The earth is the Lord’s, behind 10:26.

im.c: A Greek red-figure drinking cup with a symposium scene, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston. Such cups were made centuries before Paul, but dinner parties with wine and couches were part of social life in Corinth, the setting of 1 Corinthians 8 and 10.
im.k: Mark Landon, CC BY 4.0 (Museum of Fine Arts, Boston) / Wikimedia Commons

set: To show how love limits freedom, Paul describes his own conduct. As an apostle he had the right to be supported by the churches, to marry, and to travel with a wife, but he chose to give them up so no one could say he preached for gain. He closes with the picture of an athlete in training.

his.t: Paul worked with leather or goat-hair cloth, probably alongside Priscilla and Aquila.
Held in spring near Corinth, the games drew visitors from around the Greek world.

cus.t: Isthmian winners got a wreath of pine (earlier celery), which wilted quickly.
Athletes swore to ten months of training. Paul uses it as a picture of self-discipline.

cu: Traveling teachers and philosophers expected pay. Paul instead worked as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3). The Isthmian Games, one of the major Greek athletic festivals, were held near Corinth every two years, so the runner and boxer images were familiar.

ot.n: “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.”
Priests received a share of what was offered.
Provisions for the Levites.

im.c: A Greek prize vase with a foot race, made about 530-520 BC (British Museum). Paul uses runners and boxers in the games as a picture of discipline (1 Corinthians 9:24-27).
im.k: Attributed to the Euphiletos Painter (about 530-520 BC), British Museum / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul recalls the wilderness generation: all were baptized into Moses, ate the same spiritual food, and drank from the rock, yet most died in the desert because of idolatry and immorality. Those events are “examples for us.” He warns against idol feasts but explains how to handle meat of uncertain origin.

his.t: Israel wandered forty years after refusing to enter the land.
The Moabites led Israel into feasting and sexual sin (Numbers 25), and 24,000 died.

cus.t: To eat at a god’s table was to share in his worship.

cus.h: Head Coverings in the Lord’s Supper
cus.t: See chapter 11 for the next set of worship matters.

cu: Idol feasts involved eating at a temple table, which Paul says is sharing in the worship of demons. The Lord’s Supper is a sharing in Christ’s body and blood, so the two cannot be mixed. In a private home, meat could be eaten without asking where it came from.

ot.n: Israel sat down to eat and drink and rose to play, the golden calf.
Israel’s immorality at Peor.
Water from the rock, which Paul reads as Christ.

im.c: The Adoration of the Golden Calf, by Nicolas Poussin (about 1634). Paul recalls Israel's idolatry at Sinai as a warning for the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 10:6-7).
im.k: Nicolas Poussin (about 1634) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul turns to worship. He first deals with head coverings, a hard passage about differences between men and women in prayer and prophecy. Then he rebukes the Corinthians for their celebration of the Lord’s Supper, where the rich ate first and the poor went hungry, and recalls what Jesus did on the night he was betrayed.

his.t: Verses 23-26 are the oldest written account of the Lord’s Supper, from around AD 54.
About forty people could fit in a wealthy home, and fewer in the dining room.

cus.t: Respectable women usually covered their hair in public. Men prayed uncovered. The passage addresses local custom and creation.
The Roman dining room held about nine on couches. Others stood in the atrium.

cu: The Lord’s Supper began as a real meal in a house. In Roman homes, the wealthy ate in the dining room and the rest in the courtyard. The rich therefore arrived early and ate well, while poorer members and slaves came later. Paul says that is not the Lord’s Supper.

ot.n: The creation of Eve from Adam, which Paul cites on men and women.
Blood of the covenant at Sinai.
The promise of a new covenant.

im.c: The Last Supper, by Leonardo da Vinci (1495-98). Paul passes on what he "received from the Lord" about that night (1 Corinthians 11:23-26).
im.k: Leonardo da Vinci (1495-98) / Wikimedia Commons

set: The Corinthians had asked about spiritual gifts. Paul says that all gifts come from the same Spirit and are given for the good of all. He uses the human body to show that every member is needed and none can say to another, “I don’t need you.”

his.t: Pagan worship in Corinth included ecstatic experiences, so the church needed guidance about what came from the Spirit.
The lists in 12:8-10, 28-30 and Romans 12:6-8 do not match, so they are samples.

cus.t: The story of Menenius Agrippa, who calmed a revolt with a tale about the belly and limbs, was a Roman classic.
Terra-cotta body parts were offered at healing shrines in Corinth.

cu: Greek writers used a body as a picture of the city, with the belly representing the people and the head the rulers, to urge unity. Paul adapts it: Christ is the head, and every member, including the weak, matters.

ot.n: Idols are mute. Paul reminds the Corinthians that they were led astray to mute idols.
The Spirit rested on the elders and they prophesied.

im.c: Pentecost, by El Greco (about 1600). Paul says the gifts differ but come from one Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:4-11).
im.k: El Greco (about 1600), Museo del Prado / Wikimedia Commons

set: In the middle of Paul’s teaching on spiritual gifts stands this poem on love. It is not a wedding reading but a rebuke: the Corinthians who prized flashy gifts lacked the love that makes them worth anything. Paul shows that love outlasts every gift.

his.t: Corinthian bronze was a luxury product, and the city produced mirrors.
It sits in a letter about quarrels and pride. Every line corrects something in Corinth.

cus.t: Ancient mirrors were polished metal, so the image was blurred.
Paul compares himself to a child who has put away childish things.

cu: Corinth was famous for its bronze work, so “a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal” would have been a familiar sound, often used in pagan worship. Mirrors were polished metal, giving a dim reflection (v.12).

ot.n: God speaks to Moses face to face, not in riddles.
God desires mercy rather than sacrifice.

im.c: Charity, by Andrea del Sarto (1518). The Greek word for love in 1 Corinthians 13 is agape, which older English Bibles translated "charity".
im.k: Andrea del Sarto (1518), Louvre / Wikimedia Commons

set: The Corinthians treasured speaking in tongues. Paul tells them that prophecy, which builds up the whole church in a language all understand, is better in public. He gives rules for tongues, interpretation, and prophecy, and ends with a call for order, including guidance about women’s speaking.

his.t: The oracle at Delphi, not far from Corinth, was famous for ecstatic utterances.
Women prayed and prophesied (11:5), so 14:34-35 likely addresses a specific disruption.

cus.t: A person who spoke in a tongue, or another, was to interpret it so all could say “Amen.”
Unbelievers might attend a house church, which Paul wants to be convincing and not confusing.

cu: Pagan worship often involved ecstatic and chaotic cults. Paul says the Corinthians’ meetings must instead build up outsiders who come in. Verses 34-35 are debated: Paul may be addressing disruptive questions in worship, and interpreters disagree on how far the instruction extends.

ot.n: God will speak to this people through foreign lips, a sign for unbelievers.
Two or three witnesses to establish a matter.
Paul’s “as the Law also says” may point back to creation order.

im.c: The Tower of Babel, by Pieter Bruegel the Elder (1563). The scattering of languages in Genesis 11 is the background to Paul's talk of tongues that no one understands (1 Corinthians 14:10-11).
im.k: Pieter Bruegel the Elder (1563), Vienna / Wikimedia Commons

t: The Resurrection of Christ and Believers
set: Some Corinthians said there is no resurrection of the dead. Paul answers with the longest argument in the letter. He starts with the gospel he preached, listing the witnesses of Christ’s resurrection, then shows that denying the resurrection undoes everything. He ends with the nature of the resurrection body and a victory shout.

his.t: Verses 3-5 are probably a formula Paul received soon after his conversion, within a few years of the cross.
Many of them were still alive when Paul wrote, he says (v.6).

cus.t: The practice in v.29 is obscure and debated. Paul mentions it without endorsing it.
A bare seed is buried and rises as something new.

cu: Greeks generally hoped for an immortal soul but found a bodily resurrection absurd, as Acts 17:32 shows. Paul uses farming as an image: a seed is sown and a different body comes up. The “last trumpet” (v.52) recalls trumpets at Israel’s feasts and the day of the Lord.

ot.n: Adam became a living being.
“You put everything under his feet.”
“Where, O death, is your sting?”

im.c: The Resurrection, a panel of the Isenheim Altarpiece by Matthias Grünewald (1512-16). Paul gives the creed he received: Christ died, was buried and was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).
im.k: Matthias Grünewald (1512-16), Isenheim Altarpiece / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul ends with the collection for the poor Christians in Jerusalem, his travel plans, and greetings. He expects to stay in Ephesus until Pentecost and then to come to Corinth through Macedonia. He ends with a handwritten greeting and the word “Maranatha.”

his.t: Paul gathered money from the Gentile churches for Jerusalem’s poor and wanted to deliver it himself (Romans 15:25-27).
The first convert in Achaia (v.15), a household leader who served the church.

cus.t: Giving on “the first day of the week” (v.2) suggests that early Christians met on that day.
A normal greeting for close family.

cu: Paul tells the Corinthians to set aside money on the first day of the week, probably the day of worship. The word “Maranatha” is Aramaic for “Our Lord, come!” or “Our Lord has come,” and it was preserved untranslated among Greek-speaking Christians.

ot.n: “Be strong and take heart, all you who hope in the Lord.”
“Be strong and courageous.”

im.c: Saint Paul at his Writing Desk, by Rembrandt (about 1629-30). At the end of the letter Paul adds a greeting "in my own hand" (1 Corinthians 16:21).
im.k: Rembrandt (about 1629-30) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul begins with praise to God for comfort. He tells of a crisis in Asia so severe that he “despaired even of life,” and then explains why he changed his travel plans: he did not want to come in grief again. He insists that his word to them has not been yes and no, because God’s promises in Christ are always yes.

his.t: Paul was nearly killed, perhaps in Ephesus (Acts 19:23-41; 1 Cor 15:32).
Paul had planned two visits, but changed his plan after his painful second visit.

cus.t: A stamped mark of ownership on documents and goods.
The Greek word arrabōn was a first installment guaranteeing the full purchase.

cu: “Seal” and “down payment” (vv.21-22) are business terms. A seal marked ownership, and a down payment was the first installment guaranteeing the rest. Paul uses both to describe the Spirit.

ot.n: “I, even I, am he who comforts you.”
“I believed, therefore I spoke.”
Two or three witnesses, behind Paul’s call to God as witness.

im.c: The Good Samaritan, painted by Vincent van Gogh in 1890 after Delacroix. Paul calls God "the God of all comfort" who comforts us so that we can comfort others (2 Corinthians 1:3-4). The painting shows one man caring for a wounded stranger; Paul does not mention the Samaritan.
im.k: Vincent van Gogh (1890), after Eugène Delacroix / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul tells why he wrote the “severe letter” rather than visit again: he wanted to spare them. The one who caused pain has been disciplined enough, and Paul asks the church to forgive and restore him. Paul left Troas restless because Titus was not there, and moved on to Macedonia.

his.t: Paul wrote a tearful letter between 1 and 2 Corinthians. It is lost, unless part of it is in chapters 10-13.
Paul’s trusted co-worker, sent to Corinth to see how the church responded.

cus.t: Rome’s greatest victory ceremony, with captives, trophies, incense, and a parade to the Capitol.
Paul says rivals traded in God’s word, like merchants watering down wine.

cu: A triumphal procession had captives, burning incense, and the victorious general. To the victors the smell meant life, and to the captives it meant death. Paul pictures himself as one led in Christ’s victory march, spreading the fragrance of knowing him.

ot.n: Satan’s deception, behind “we are not unaware of his schemes.”
The offering as a sweet aroma to the Lord.
The incense in the sanctuary.

im.c: The Return of the Prodigal Son, by Rembrandt (about 1668). Paul asks the church to forgive the man who caused pain, to comfort him, and to reaffirm their love for him (2 Corinthians 2:7-8). The painting shows Jesus' parable in Luke 15, not Paul's story, but it pictures a welcome back.
im.k: Rembrandt (about 1668) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Rival teachers had arrived in Corinth with letters of recommendation. Paul says the Corinthians themselves are his letter, written by the Spirit on hearts. He contrasts the ministry of the old covenant, written on stone, with the new covenant of the Spirit, and compares Moses’ veiled face with the unveiled face of believers.

his.t: They arrived with letters and credentials and questioned Paul.
Moses covered his face after speaking with God, and Paul says the glory was fading.

cus.t: A letter of introduction was a basic form of trust in the Roman world.
Jews read Moses in the synagogue, and Paul says a veil lies over their reading.

cu: Letters of recommendation were a common way for traveling teachers to win trust. The veil on Moses’ face (Exodus 34:29-35) is read by Paul as a picture of how many Jews still read the old covenant without understanding that Christ fulfills it.

ot.n: Moses’ face shone, and he veiled it.
The law written on hearts.
A new heart and a new spirit.

im.c: Moses with the Ten Commandments, by Rembrandt (1659). Paul speaks of the glory on the face of Moses, of the veil he wore, and of a veil that lies over the minds of those who read the old covenant (2 Corinthians 3:7-16).
im.k: Rembrandt (1659) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul explains why he does not lose heart. The gospel is a treasure, and he and his team are cheap clay jars that hold it, so that the power is seen to come from God. He describes his troubles in a series of contrasts and says that suffering now prepares an eternal weight of glory.

his.t: They were stored in clay jars in caves near Qumran, hidden for nearly two thousand years.
He lists beatings, shipwrecks, and prison in chapter 11.

cus.t: Cheap, breakable, and disposable. They show how plain the vessel is compared to what it holds.
Paul’s picture of being “struck down but not destroyed” sounds like a gladiator.

cu: Clay jars were the cheap, common containers of the ancient world, used for oil, grain, and money. Valuables were sometimes hidden in them, like the Dead Sea Scrolls. “Light from darkness” recalls the first day of creation.

ot.n: “Let there be light,” the picture of God’s work in a heart.
“I believed, therefore I spoke.”
People in darkness have seen a great light, a picture close to Paul’s.

im.c: Adoration of the Shepherds, by Gerard van Honthorst (1622), lit by the light that comes from the child. Paul says God, who first said "Let light shine out of darkness," has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of God's glory in the face of Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).
im.k: Gerard van Honthorst (1622) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul describes our earthly body as a tent and our resurrection body as a house from God, and so he lives with confidence. Then he turns to the heart of his message: the love of Christ compels him, believers are a new creation, and God reconciled the world to himself in Christ and has given the message of reconciliation to his…

his.t: Acts 18:3 says Paul and Aquila made tents. Ancient tents were often of leather or goat-hair cloth, but the material of Paul’s tents is not stated.
Emperors sent legates to govern provinces and envoys to kings, speaking on the emperor’s behalf.

cus.t: The Greek word is bēma, the raised platform on which a magistrate sat.
The Spirit is the pledge of the full inheritance.

cu: Acts 18:3 says Paul made tents, so a “tent” may have come easily to him as a picture of the temporary body. An “ambassador” (v.20) spoke for a ruler who was not present, and his authority came entirely from the one who sent him.

ot.n: “Behold, I am doing a new thing.”
The Lord laid on him the iniquity of us all.
The Day of Atonement sin offering.

im.c: The Crucifixion, from the Isenheim Altarpiece by Matthias Grünewald (1512-16). Paul says the love of Christ compels him, because one died for all (2 Corinthians 5:14-15).
im.k: Matthias Grünewald (1512-16), Isenheim Altarpiece / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul appeals for the Corinthians to respond to God’s grace, listing his own hardships as an example of faithful service. He asks them to open their hearts as he has opened his, and warns them not to be “unequally yoked” with unbelievers, a phrase about partnership in pagan worship.

his.t: The nine hardships in vv.4-5 are among several such lists Paul gave (11:23-29; Romans 8:35).
Pagan temples hosted banquets that business associates attended.

cus.t: Two animals pulled a plow together, so mismatched pairs made the work harder.
The hearts and affections were thought to be in the chest and “cramped” or “wide.”

cu: Many scholars hear an echo of Deuteronomy 22:10, which forbids yoking an ox with a donkey, in Paul’s warning against partnerships that mix pagan worship with the worship of Christ. First Corinthians 8 and 10 show that some Corinthian Christians were invited to temple dinners, and some felt free to go.

ot.n: “In the day of salvation I helped you.”
Do not plow with an ox and a donkey together.
“I will walk among you.”

im.c: Ploughing in the Nivernais, by Rosa Bonheur (1849), with teams of yoked oxen. Paul writes "Do not be yoked together with unbelievers" (2 Corinthians 6:14). Many scholars hear an echo of Deuteronomy 22:10, which forbids ploughing with an ox and a donkey together.
im.k: Rosa Bonheur (1849) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul continues with a plea for them to make room in their hearts. Then he tells what happened after he reached Macedonia: he was worn down by fights and fears, but God comforted him by the coming of Titus, who brought good news of the Corinthians’ repentance and love.

his.t: A Gentile coworker, Titus was sent to Corinth and brought back the report.
Paul faced opposition in Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea, and had no rest.

cus.t: A word for a strong ardor to do right.
Paul speaks of the church clearing itself of blame.

cu: Paul distinguishes two kinds of sorrow. Godly grief leads to repentance and life, while worldly sorrow leads to death. He lists seven effects of godly sorrow in v.11, the language of a church cleared of guilt.

ot.n: David confesses, “I have sinned against the Lord.”
A broken and contrite heart God will not despise.
Nineveh’s repentance saved them.

im.c: Saint Peter Repentant, by Georges de La Tour (about 1645). Paul writes that godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation (2 Corinthians 7:10). The painting shows Peter after he denied Jesus (Luke 22:62), not a scene from Paul's letter.
im.k: Georges de La Tour (about 1645), Cleveland Museum of Art / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul begins the appeal for the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He points to the churches of Macedonia, who gave generously despite deep poverty, and urges the Corinthians to finish what they started a year earlier. He announces Titus’s return with two other brothers.

his.t: Macedonia was a Roman province, and Paul says the churches there faced a severe trial and deep poverty (v.2).
Famine struck Judea (Acts 11:28), and believers there were poor.

cus.t: Paul says the abundance of one meets the need of another (v.14), so that there is equality.
Paul has others handle the money so no one can blame him.

cu: Giving across churches shows unity between Jews and Gentiles. Paul does not command it, and he stresses that gifts should match a person’s means. The Macedonian churches begged for the privilege of giving.

ot.n: The manna gathered by each family met their need.
The generous will be blessed.

im.c: The Gathering of the Manna, by Nicolas Poussin (1637-39). Paul quotes the manna story of Exodus 16 to teach fair sharing between the churches: the one who gathered much had nothing left over, and the one who gathered little had no lack (2 Corinthians 8:15).
im.k: Nicolas Poussin (1637-39), Louvre / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul continues the appeal. He had boasted of Corinth’s readiness to the Macedonians, and sends the brothers ahead so that the gift is ready when he arrives with some Macedonians. He teaches that giving is like sowing, and that God loves a cheerful giver.

his.t: Paul worries that if Macedonian delegates arrive and find nothing ready, it would shame them.
Jews gave to the poor as an act of righteousness, which Paul builds on.

cus.t: Seed was scattered by hand across the field.
The Greek word is hilaros, from which we get “hilarious.” It means glad, not grudging.

cu: Farmers broadcast seed by hand. Sowing generously meant a larger harvest, a proverb Paul applies to giving. Paul speaks of giving as thanksgiving overflowing to God, because those helped will pray for the givers.

ot.n: “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor.”
In the Greek version, God blesses a cheerful giver.
God supplies seed for the sower and bread for food.

im.c: The Sower with Setting Sun, by Vincent van Gogh (1888). Paul writes that whoever sows generously will reap generously, and that God supplies seed to the sower (2 Corinthians 9:6-10).
im.k: Vincent van Gogh (1888) / Wikimedia Commons

set: The tone changes. Paul now answers critics who say he is bold in letters but weak in person, and who compare themselves to him. He says his weapons are spiritual, that he will use his authority to build up, and that he will boast only within the field God assigned to him.

his.t: Some said Paul’s letters were weighty but his presence and speech were contemptible.
Paul insists his field of work includes Corinth, because he came there first.

cus.t: Fortresses on hills in the ancient world, which siege engines battered.
Visitors came with credentials, and Paul says that’s not the same as being commended by God.

cu: Greek rhetoric prized a commanding presence, and Paul’s critics said his “bodily presence is weak.” Paul’s mention of “strongholds” (v.4) draws on siege warfare. His boasting only “in the Lord” (v.17) quotes Jeremiah.

ot.n: “Let the one who boasts boast in this: that they know me.”
God puts on righteousness as a breastplate.
A wise man scales the city of the mighty.

im.c: The fall of the walls of Jericho, a manuscript painting by Jean Fouquet (15th century). Paul says his weapons "have divine power to demolish strongholds" (2 Corinthians 10:4). Paul does not mention Jericho; the picture shows the best-known story of God bringing down a stronghold.
im.k: Jean Fouquet (15th century) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul reluctantly boasts, calling it foolishness, because rival “super-apostles” have charmed the Corinthians with a different Jesus and a different gospel. He compares himself with them, and rather than boast of strengths he lists his sufferings: beatings, shipwrecks, dangers, and sleepless nights, and the escape from Damascus.

his.t: Acts records some: Philippi (16:22-23), Lystra stoning (14:19), but not three shipwrecks, which came before Acts 27.
Aretas’s governor guarded the gates, and Paul was lowered through a window (Acts 9:25).

cus.t: Jews stopped at 39 so as not to exceed the limit by miscounting.
Roman lictors beat with rods. Paul was a citizen, but not always spared.

cu: Beating with rods was a Roman punishment, and the “forty lashes minus one” was the Jewish synagogue punishment, designed to stay under the limit of Deuteronomy 25:3. Paul had gone through both. Bridging the gap between the wall and the ground in a basket (v.33) was a humiliating escape.

ot.n: The serpent deceived Eve, the image of v.3.
The beating limit of forty lashes.
Boast only in the Lord.

im.c: The Fall and Expulsion from the Garden of Eden, by Michelangelo (1509-10), in the Sistine Chapel. Paul fears that, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, the minds of the Corinthians may be led astray from devotion to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:3).
im.k: Michelangelo (1509-10), Sistine Chapel / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul tells of a vision fourteen years before in which he was caught up into the third heaven, then describes a thorn in the flesh given to keep him humble. He asked the Lord three times to remove it. The Lord answered, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.”

his.t: About AD 42, possibly during his years in Syria and Cilicia before the first journey.
At Galatia he mentions a bodily illness (Galatians 4:13-14), though no one knows if this is the thorn.

cus.t: A Persian word for a garden. Jews used it for the place of the righteous after death.
Miracles and endurance, which Paul says he did among them.

cu: Paul speaks of himself in the third person, out of humility. Some Jewish writers counted three or seven heavens, and the “third heaven” is usually taken as the place of God’s presence. The thorn (skolops) is a stake or splinter. Its nature is unknown: an illness, an opponent, or a temptation have all been suggested.

ot.n: Those not driven out will be “thorns in your sides.”
The Lord is near to the brokenhearted.
Every charge established by two or three witnesses.

im.c: The Ecstasy of Saint Paul, by Nicolas Poussin (about 1649-50). Paul writes of a man "in Christ" who was caught up to the third heaven and to Paradise (2 Corinthians 12:2-4). The painter shows Paul lifted by angels, but Paul himself describes no scene and says the man heard things that cannot be told.
im.k: Nicolas Poussin (about 1649-50), Louvre / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul warns the Corinthians that he is about to come a third time and will not spare them if they have not repented. He urges them to test themselves and to see whether Christ is in them. He ends with simple instructions: rejoice, aim for restoration, and live in peace, and gives a benediction naming the whole Trinity.

his.t: Paul spent three months in Greece (Acts 20:2-3), and Romans is usually thought to have been written during that stay.
The Greek word for “test” means to prove genuine, as a metal is tested.

cus.t: Paul compares Christ’s crucifixion in weakness with his living by God’s power.
A greeting kiss was common among family and close friends.

cu: “Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15) was a legal rule that Paul invokes. The holy kiss was a standard greeting in the early church.

ot.n: Every matter established by two or three witnesses.
The priestly blessing, which Paul’s closing blessing may recall.
Seek peace and pursue it.

im.c: The Trinity, an icon by Andrei Rublev (early 15th century). Paul ends the letter with the blessing of "the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit" (2 Corinthians 13:14). Rublev painted the icon around the three visitors who came to Abraham (Genesis 18).
im.k: Andrei Rublev (early 15th century) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul skips his usual thanksgiving and goes right to the point: he is amazed the Galatians are turning to a different gospel. He tells how he received his message not from people but by revelation from Jesus Christ, and describes his life before conversion and his first years afterward in Arabia, Damascus, and Syria.

his.t: He was a zealous Pharisee who persecuted the church (Acts 8-9).
He spent time in Arabia and Damascus before visiting Jerusalem about AD 36.

cus.t: A solemn curse, devoting something to God’s judgment.
Pharisees took pride in observing ancestral traditions.

cu: Letters in the Greek world began with a thanksgiving to the gods. Paul leaves it out. “Accursed” (v.8-9) translates anathema, a word for being devoted to destruction. “Zealous for the traditions” describes his strict life as a Pharisee.

ot.n: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you.”
The servant called from the womb.
A prophet who leads astray must be rejected.

im.c: The Conversion of Saul, an engraving by Nicolas Beatrizet (about 1545) after Michelangelo's fresco in the Pauline Chapel at the Vatican. Paul says that God was pleased to reveal his Son to him, and that he had once tried to destroy the church (Galatians 1:13-16). Acts 9 tells the story of the road to Damascus; Galatians does not.
im.k: Nicolas Beatrizet after Michelangelo (about 1545), Metropolitan Museum of Art / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul tells how, fourteen years later, he went to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus and laid out his gospel to the leaders. They added nothing to it and agreed that he would go to the Gentiles. Then he tells of a later confrontation with Peter at Antioch, where Peter withdrew from eating with Gentiles.

his.t: Probably the famine visit (Acts 11:30) or the council visit (Acts 15), and scholars disagree.
The first city where Jews and Gentiles shared one church (Acts 11:19-26).

cus.t: A gesture of agreement and partnership.
Sharing a meal signaled acceptance and equality.

cu: Jews did not normally eat with Gentiles because of food laws and purity rules. Peter had eaten freely with Gentiles until emissaries came from James. Paul saw this as a statement that Gentile believers were second class.

ot.n: “No one living is righteous before you.”
The promise to Abraham that Paul takes up in chapter 3.

im.c: The Embrace of the Apostles Peter and Paul, an icon by Angelos Akotantos (active 1436-1450), in the Ashmolean Museum. Paul says James, Cephas and John agreed to a partnership with him and Barnabas by a handshake (Galatians 2:9). Later in the same chapter he opposes Peter to his face at Antioch (2:11-14).
im.k: Angelos Akotantos (active 1436-1450), Ashmolean Museum / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul turns sharply to the Galatians, calling them foolish. They began with the Spirit and now think the flesh will complete it. He reasons from Scripture that Abraham was justified by faith and that the law, which came 430 years later, cannot cancel the promise. The law was a guardian until Christ came.

his.t: From Abraham’s promise to the law at Sinai. Paul uses the time gap as an argument.
Wealthy Greek and Roman families used slaves to supervise their sons.

cus.t: Deuteronomy 21:23 said a hanged man was cursed. Paul reads that as Christ taking the curse.
A child was legally like a slave until the date set by the father.

cu: A pedagogue (v.24) was a household slave who escorted a child to school and kept him in line. Paul says the law was like that: a custodian for a time, not the teacher. The coming of Christ ended that stage.

ot.n: “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.”
“The righteous will live by faith.”
“Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree.”

im.c: Christ on the Cross, by Diego Velázquez (about 1632), in the Prado. Paul tells the Galatians that Jesus Christ was set before their eyes as the crucified one (Galatians 3:1), and that on the cross he took the law's curse on himself (3:13).
im.k: Diego Velázquez (about 1632), Prado Museum / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul explains that those who were children under the law were like slaves until God sent his Son to redeem them and adopt them. He pleads with the Galatians, recalls their warm welcome of him, and ends with an allegory of Hagar and Sarah.

his.t: He first preached to them because of a bodily illness (v.13-14).
Abraham had Ishmael by Hagar the slave and Isaac by Sarah, the free woman.

cus.t: A father decided when a son became an heir, in the Roman and Greek world.
Jewish feast days, months, and years were things Gentile believers were taking up.

cu: “The fullness of time” (v.4) points to a time set by the Father, as in the Roman custom of a father setting an age when an heir came into his inheritance. Paul’s allegory follows a Jewish teaching method that used Old Testament stories as pictures.

ot.n: “Cast out the slave woman and her son.”
“Sing, barren woman, you who never bore a child.”
Hagar and Ishmael.

im.c: Abraham Casting Out Hagar and Ishmael, by Guercino (1657), in the Brera Gallery in Milan. In Galatians 4:21-31 Paul reads the story of Hagar and Sarah as a picture of two covenants, and he ends with the command to drive out the slave woman and her son (4:30, quoting Genesis 21:10).
im.k: Guercino (1657), Brera Gallery, Milan / Wikimedia Commons

t: Freedom and the Fruit of the Spirit
set: Paul tells the Galatians to stand firm in freedom and not accept circumcision as a way of being right with God. Freedom is not a license for the flesh, but a call to serve in love. He contrasts the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit.

his.t: It was the main question in Acts 15.
Greek moral writers also listed vices. Paul’s list shows what the flesh looks like.

cus.t: The law as a way to earn favor was a heavy yoke.
The fruit was thought of as the natural result of a tree’s life.

cu: “Bite and devour one another” (v.15) is the language of wild animals fighting. “Fruit” is singular in v.22, as one unified harvest rather than separate gifts. “Against such things there is no law” plays on the legal theme.

ot.n: “Love your neighbor as yourself.”
The command of circumcision.

im.c: Basket of Fruit, by Caravaggio (about 1599), in the Ambrosiana in Milan. Paul sets the works of the flesh against the fruit of the Spirit, which he lists as love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:19-23).
im.k: Caravaggio (about 1599), Pinacoteca Ambrosiana, Milan / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul gives practical advice for the church. He tells the strong to restore those who fall gently, to carry one another’s burdens, and to give generously. Then he takes the pen himself and writes the last lines in large letters, warning that the agitators want to boast in the Galatians’ circumcision, while he boasts only in the…

his.t: He wrote the end of many letters (1 Cor 16:21; Col 4:18; 2 Thess 3:17).
Paul had been beaten and stoned in Lystra (Acts 14:19).

cus.t: Slaves and temple servants were sometimes marked. Paul says his scars show whom he serves.
Teachers could count converts as a proof of success.
