cu: Letters were dictated to a scribe and the author often added a few lines in his own hand as a signature. Paul’s “large letters” (v.11) may reflect poor eyesight or emphasis. “The marks of Jesus” (v.17) were scars from beatings.

ot.n: Whoever sows injustice reaps calamity.
Those who plow evil reap the same.
Peace on Israel, behind the “Israel of God.”

im.c: The Gleaners, by Jean-François Millet (1857), in the Musée d'Orsay. Paul tells the Galatians not to grow weary in doing good, because in due time they will reap if they do not give up, and to do good to everyone, above all to the household of faith (Galatians 6:9-10). The law of Moses left the edges of the field for the poor to glean (Leviticus 19:9-10).
im.k: Jean-François Millet (1857), Musée d'Orsay / Wikimedia Commons

set: Ephesus was the leading city of Roman Asia, famous for the temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders. Paul writes to the believers there, probably with other churches in mind.

his.t: A port city of a quarter million, home to the temple of Artemis and a center of magic arts (Acts 19).
About three years in the city, two of them teaching daily in the hall of Tyrannus (Acts 19:9-10; 20:31).

cus.t: A seal marked ownership and protection.
Romans adopted adult heirs to carry on a family name.

cu: Verses 3-14 are one sentence in Greek, a flowing hymn. “Sealed” with the Spirit (v.13) refers to the mark of ownership on goods and letters. “Adoption” as sons gives believers a full share of the inheritance.

ot.n: God chose Israel because he loved them.
“Sit at my right hand.”
Everything under his feet.

im.c: Christ Pantocrator, a sixth-century icon at Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai, one of the oldest surviving icons of Christ. In Ephesians 1:20-23 Paul says God seated Christ at His right hand, far above every rule and authority, and made Him head over all things for the church.
im.k: Unknown artist (6th century), Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai / Wikimedia Commons

t: Saved by Grace, One in Christ
set: Paul reminds the readers that they were dead in sins, following the world and the prince of the power of the air. But God, rich in mercy, made them alive with Christ and saved them by grace. He then shows that Gentiles, once far off, have been brought near, and the wall dividing Jew from Gentile has been broken down.

his.t: Josephus describes the stone barrier with its warning inscription.
Gentiles were “without God” as far as Israel’s covenant went.

cus.t: Roman citizenship was a high privilege. Paul says Gentiles now share in Israel’s commonwealth.
A stone set at the corner or the top of a building that held the walls together. Scholars disagree whether Paul means a foundation stone or a capstone.

cu: In the Jerusalem Temple, a stone wall carried a warning in Greek that Gentiles could not go further under penalty of death. Paul alludes to that barrier when he speaks of “the dividing wall of hostility” (v.14).

ot.n: “Peace, peace to those far and near.”
A tested stone, a precious cornerstone.
The Prince of Peace.

im.c: The Anastasis fresco in the Chora Church in Istanbul, painted about 1320. Christ pulls Adam and Eve out of their tombs. In Ephesians 2:4-6 Paul says God made us alive together with Christ and raised us up with Him.
im.k: Unknown artist (about 1320), Chora Church, Istanbul / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul calls himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of the Gentiles, writing probably from Rome. He explains the mystery revealed to him: Gentiles are fellow heirs and members of one body.

his.t: He was held in Rome for two years (Acts 28:30).
Many in Ephesus believed in spirits and magic. Paul says Christ rules over them.

cus.t: Kneeling was an earnest posture for prayer.
“Every family” (v.14) plays on the Greek words for father and family.

cu: “Mystery” in Greek religions meant secrets known only to initiates. For Paul it is a secret now openly shared. “Bow my knees” (v.14) is a physical sign of earnest prayer. Jews usually stood to pray.

ot.n: The measure of God is higher than heaven and deeper than the grave.
All nations will be blessed through Abraham.

im.c: Paul in Prison, by Rembrandt (1627). It is an imagined scene: Romans was not written from prison, but the painting suits Paul's cry in Romans 7:24.
im.k: Rembrandt (1627), Staatsgalerie Stuttgart / Wikimedia Commons

set: The letter turns from belief to behavior. Paul urges the readers to live worthy of their calling, in humility and gentleness, keeping the unity of the Spirit. Christ gave leaders to equip the saints so the body grows up. Paul then tells them to put off the old self and put on the new.

his.t: Christ’s ascension is described in terms of a victor handing out gifts.
Converts left behind habits of pagan life.

cus.t: A victorious king gave gifts to his followers.
Greek ethics warned against unrestrained anger. Paul adds a time limit: do not let the sun go down on it.

cu: Paul quotes a psalm about a conqueror who gives gifts to his people, which was the practice of a victorious general sharing spoil. “Put off” and “put on” are clothing images. Baptism candidates may have changed clothes.

ot.n: “You ascended on high, leading captives.”
“Speak the truth to one another.”
“Be angry, and do not sin.”

im.c: The Ascension, by Rembrandt (1636), in the Alte Pinakothek in Munich, one of the paintings of his Passion cycle. In Ephesians 4:8-10 Paul says that Christ "ascended on high" and gave gifts to His people.
im.k: Rembrandt (1636), Alte Pinakothek, Munich / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul tells his readers to imitate God, walk in love, and avoid the impurity common in the surrounding culture. They are light in the Lord. He then gives instructions for the Christian household, beginning with a call for mutual submission and showing husbands and wives as a picture of Christ and the church.

his.t: Greek and Roman writers wrote on how to run a household. Paul changes the shape.
Pagan feasts and festivals often involved drunkenness. Paul tells them to be filled with the Spirit instead.

cus.t: The male head had legal authority over the family. Paul modifies it with love.
Believers sang psalms and hymns and spiritual songs to one another.

cu: Roman households were headed by the father, with authority over wife, children, and slaves. Paul’s instruction to husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church, giving himself up for her, was a radical change from Roman custom.

ot.n: “A man shall leave his father and mother and be united to his wife.”
“Arise, shine, for your light has come.”
The offering that pleases God.

im.c: The Arnolfini Portrait, by Jan van Eyck (1434), a married couple in their home. It comes from a different time and place, but it is a picture of the marriage Paul writes about in 1 Corinthians 7.
im.k: Jan van Eyck (1434) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul finishes the household instructions with children and parents, slaves and masters. Then he calls the readers to be strong in the Lord and to put on the full armor of God, describing the equipment of a Roman soldier. He asks for prayer and sends Tychicus.

his.t: Acts 28:16 says a soldier guarded Paul in Rome, and Acts 28:20 mentions his chain.
A trusted coworker from Asia, named as the bearer of both Ephesians and Colossians (Ephesians 6:21-22; Colossians 4:7-9).

cus.t: Paul calls it "the first commandment with a promise" (Exodus 20:12).
Perhaps a third of urban people were slaves. Paul tells masters to stop threatening them.

cu: Paul was chained to a Roman guard, so the soldier’s armor was before his eyes. The belt, breastplate, shoes, shield, helmet, and sword each stand for an element of faith. The large shield (thureos) could be soaked and held against flaming arrows.

ot.n: God puts on righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet.
The gospel of peace brought by beautiful feet.
Honor your father and mother.

im.c: Knight, Death and the Devil, an engraving by Albrecht Dürer (1513). Many art historians read the armored rider as a Christian soldier who keeps going in spite of fear. Paul's call to put on the full armor of God (Ephesians 6:10-18) is one of the texts behind that picture.
im.k: Albrecht Dürer (1513), National Gallery of Art, Washington / Wikimedia Commons

set: Philippi was a Roman colony, a mini-Rome in Macedonia, where Paul had been jailed for casting a spirit out of a slave girl (Acts 16). Years later he writes from prison to thank the church. He rejoices that his chains have spread the gospel, and he says that for him to live is Christ and to die is gain.

his.t: A city named for Philip II of Macedon, who took it in 356 BC. After the battle of 42 BC, where Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius, it became a Roman colony, and more settlers came after Actium in 31 BC.
Paul says his imprisonment became known to the whole palace guard (1:13). The Greek word can mean the emperor’s guard or a governor’s residence. Acts 28:16 says a soldier guarded Paul in Rome.

cus.t: Philippi was a Roman colony settled by veterans and governed by Roman law. Paul’s words for conduct (1:27) and citizenship (3:20) come from this civic setting.
A word meaning shared work and common cause.

cu: Colonists were Roman citizens who kept Roman law. Paul’s language of “citizenship” (v.27) would have rung true for them. “Imprisonment” in the empire meant being chained to a guard, which gave Paul a captive audience.

ot.n: “This will turn out for my deliverance.”
The nations will bow, echoed in chapter 2.

im.c: Paul in Prison, by Rembrandt (1627), in the Staatsgalerie Stuttgart. It is an imagined scene. In Philippians 1:7 and 1:13 Paul says he is in chains, and in 1:12-14 he says his imprisonment has helped spread the gospel.
im.k: Rembrandt (1627), Staatsgalerie Stuttgart / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul asks the Philippians to be of one mind, putting others first. As an example, he quotes or composes a hymn: Christ, who was equal with God, made himself nothing, took a servant’s form, and died on a cross, and God exalted him above every name. Paul then sends news about Timothy and Epaphroditus.

his.t: Many scholars think 2:6-11 is an early hymn or poem that Paul quotes or shapes. Others think he wrote it for this letter. The text does not say.
The Philippians’ messenger, who almost died in Paul’s service.

cus.t: The most shameful death. Roman citizens were normally exempt.
A libation was wine or oil poured out for a god. Paul pictures his own life being poured out over the sacrifice of their faith (2:17).

cu: Roman society prized honor and rank. In a colony that valued status, the picture of Christ giving up rank was a challenge. The hymn moves from humbling to exalting, like the descent and rise of a story.

ot.n: “Every knee will bow, every tongue will swear.”
The servant poured out his life unto death.
A crooked and twisted generation.

im.c: Christ on the Cross, by Diego Velázquez (about 1632), in the Prado. In Philippians 2:8 Paul says that Christ became obedient to death, even death on a cross.
im.k: Diego Velázquez (about 1632), Prado Museum / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul warns against those who insist on circumcision and then lists his impressive credentials: circumcised on the eighth day, of Benjamin, a Hebrew, a Pharisee, a zealous persecutor, blameless in law. He counts all of it as rubbish compared to knowing Christ, and presses on toward the goal.

his.t: He was a Pharisee, a student of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), and a zealous persecutor.
Teachers who insisted Gentile believers must be circumcised.

cus.t: A newborn Jewish boy was circumcised on the eighth day.
Paul pictures a runner straining toward the finish (3:13-14). Greek games gave a wreath to the winner, as at the nearby Isthmian Games.

cu: In Philippi, a Roman colony, citizenship was a prized possession. Paul says “our citizenship is in heaven.” The Greek athletic image of straining toward the finish line (v.13-14) also was familiar in Greek cities.

ot.n: The eighth-day circumcision.
Benjamin, Paul’s tribe.
“Whom have I in heaven but you?”

im.c: A Greek prize vase with a foot race, made about 530-520 BC (British Museum). In Philippians 3:13-14 Paul pictures himself as a runner who forgets what is behind and strains toward the prize.
im.k: Attributed to the Euphiletos Painter (about 530-520 BC), British Museum / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul asks two women, Euodia and Syntyche, to agree, and calls on the church to rejoice always, not worry, and think on whatever is true and honorable. He thanks the Philippians for their gift and shares that he has learned contentment in plenty and in want.

his.t: Two women who worked beside Paul in the gospel. Their quarrel was serious enough to name.
Paul says the Philippians sent help more than once while he was in Thessalonica (4:15-16). He also says Macedonian believers supplied his needs in Corinth (2 Corinthians 11:9).

cus.t: The language of the sacrifices at the Temple.
A register of those who belong to God (Exodus 32:32; Psalm 69:28). City rolls of citizens give a picture of what such a book meant.

cu: In the Roman world, a gift like this came with the expectation of repayment. Paul says he is not asking for more, and calls their gift a fragrant offering. “Caesar’s household” (v.22) means imperial slaves and freedmen.

ot.n: “You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you.”
“I sought the Lord, and he answered me.”
Moses and the book of life.

im.c: Saint Paul Writing His Epistles, by Valentin de Boulogne (about 1618-20). Philippians is a thank-you letter, and in chapter 4 Paul thanks the church for its gift and tells them to bring everything to God in prayer.
im.k: Valentin de Boulogne (c. 1618-20), Museum of Fine Arts, Boston / Wikimedia Commons

set: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus Valley, near the bigger cities of Laodicea and Hierapolis. Paul has not been there, but Epaphras brought news of their faith. He thanks God for them, prays for their growth, and gives one of the grandest descriptions of Christ in the New Testament.

his.t: Paul says the Colossians learned the gospel from Epaphras (1:7) and calls him one of their own (4:12). He is with Paul as the letter is written (Philemon 23).

Tacitus says Laodicea was destroyed by an earthquake in Nero’s reign, about AD 60, and rebuilt from its own funds (Annals 14.27). Some later writers add Hierapolis and Colossae. The letter does not mention it.

cus.t: In Israel the firstborn son held the place of honor and received a double share of the inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:17). Psalm 89:27 calls the king God’s firstborn. Paul uses the word for Christ’s rank over creation (1:15).
The geographer Strabo says the Laodicea area had sheep with fine dark wool and that a color of wool was named for Colossae (12.8.16).

cu: Colossae had been known for its wool and its dyes. Earthquakes struck the Lycus Valley, including one in AD 60-61 which destroyed Laodicea. Paul’s picture of Christ as the one in whom all things “hold together” spoke to a world that felt unstable.

ot.n: Wisdom was present at creation, behind “firstborn.”
“I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings.”
Humans were made in God’s image.

im.c: Christ Pantocrator, a sixth-century icon at Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai. Colossians 1:15-20 calls Christ the image of the invisible God, the one through whom and for whom all things were made.
im.k: Unknown artist (6th century), Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul tells how hard he is working for the Colossians and the Laodiceans, whom he has not met. He warns them not to be taken captive by philosophy or by rules about food, festivals, and angel worship. Believers have been circumcised, buried, and raised with Christ and need no further additions.

his.t: Paul says he struggles for those at Laodicea too (2:1), and asks that this letter be read there and that the Colossians read the letter from Laodicea (4:16).

The letter never names the teachers. It points to food, festivals and Sabbaths (2:16), visions and the worship of angels (2:18), and a “philosophy” of human tradition (2:8). Scholars still debate where it came from.

cus.t: The Greek word in 2:14 means a handwritten record of debt. Papyrus IOUs could be canceled by crossing them out, and Paul says God wiped out the record and nailed it to the cross.
After a great victory a Roman general led his captives through the streets in a procession. Paul pictures Christ leading the defeated powers this way (2:15).

cu: Special days, new moons, and Sabbaths were Jewish observances, and “worship of angels” (v.18) and “elemental spirits” suggest local religion. Paul says these are shadows, but the substance is Christ.

ot.n: Human commands taught as rules.
Circumcision of the flesh.
The victor leading captives.

im.c: Christ on the Cross, by Diego Velázquez (about 1632), in the Prado. Colossians 2:14 says God took the record of debt against us and nailed it to the cross.
im.k: Diego Velázquez (about 1632), Prado Museum / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul tells the Colossians to seek the things above, where Christ is, because they have died and their life is hidden with Christ. He lists vices to put to death and virtues to put on. He then gives household instructions for wives, husbands, children, parents, slaves, and masters.

his.t: Paul speaks to both slaves and masters (3:22-4:1). Onesimus, called one of you (4:9), is sent with Tychicus; most readers think he is the slave of Philemon.
Greeks used barbarian for people who did not speak Greek and often thought of Scythians, from north of the Black Sea, as especially wild. Paul names both to show that no one is outside Christ (3:11).

cus.t: Paul pictures taking off the old self and putting on the new, like a change of clothes (3:9-10). Later churches gave new white robes at baptism, which is later than Paul.
Believers taught each other with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs.

cu: Roman households included slaves. Paul’s “Whatever you do, work heartily” (v.23) reframes daily work as worship. In the new community, ethnic, religious, and social distinctions no longer divide (v.11).

ot.n: Humans made in God’s image, which the new self restores.
Christ seated at God’s right hand.
The Lord is compassionate and gracious, the pattern for believers.

im.c: The Resurrection, a panel of the Isenheim Altarpiece by Matthias Grünewald (1512-16). Colossians 3:1 says that since you have been raised with Christ, you are to strive for the things above, and the chapter goes on to say what that means for daily life.
im.k: Matthias Grünewald (1512-16), Isenheim Altarpiece / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul asks for prayer, tells them to be wise toward outsiders, and sends greetings from many co-workers, including Tychicus, Onesimus, Aristarchus, Mark, Luke, and Demas. He asks that this letter be shared with Laodicea and tells Archippus to complete his ministry.

his.t: Luke is called the beloved physician (4:14). Mark, the cousin of Barnabas (4:10), is usually identified with John Mark, who left Paul and Barnabas in Acts 13:13.

Paul does not say what this letter was. Suggestions are a lost letter, Ephesians as a circular letter, or Philemon. A Latin “Epistle to the Laodiceans” exists, but it is a much later patchwork of Paul’s phrases.

cus.t: Salt gave food flavor and kept it from spoiling, so speech “seasoned with salt” (4:6) can mean words that are both pleasant and sound.
Most people heard letters read in groups.

cu: Letters were passed among churches and read aloud. “Seasoned with salt” (v.6) means speech that is tasty and preserves. Tychicus would deliver the letter and also explain news.

ot.n: A gentle answer turns away wrath.
Set a guard over my mouth.
Salt of the covenant on every offering.

im.c: Saint Paul at his Writing Desk, by Rembrandt (about 1629-30). In Colossians 4:18 Paul adds a greeting in his own hand and asks the church to remember his chains.
im.k: Rembrandt (about 1629-30) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Thessalonica was a busy port on the Via Egnatia, the capital of Macedonia. Paul, Silas, and Timothy had preached there for a few weeks, then were forced to leave. Paul writes to thank God for the church’s faith, love, and hope, and for how they turned from idols and became an example to others.

his.t: Acts 17:1-4 says Paul reasoned from the Scriptures in the synagogue on three Sabbaths, and that some Jews, many God-fearing Greeks and several leading women believed. Paul says they “turned to God from idols” (1:9), so many converts were not Jews.

Thessalonica was a free Greek city that honored Rome and its rulers. Bronze coins of the city from the reign of Augustus show Julius Caesar with the legend THEOS, “god,” on one side and Augustus on the other.

cus.t: Inscriptions from Roman Thessalonica name cults of Dionysus, Sarapis, Zeus Hypsistos and others. Paul says the believers “turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God” (1:9), a break that probably cost them a place in the civic and family…
The Greek verb in 1:10 means to wait for or await someone. Paul describes the believers as people who serve God now while they wait for His Son from heaven.

cu: Thessalonica was a Greek city with many gods, including the emperor cult. “Turned to God from idols” (v.9) describes a break with civic worship that could cost them socially.

ot.n: The foolishness of idols.
Our God is in heaven; idols are silver and gold.
The Son of Man comes from heaven.

im.c: Saint Paul Writing His Epistles, by Valentin de Boulogne (about 1618-20). First Thessalonians opens with three names, "Paul, Silvanus and Timothy" (1:1), and is probably the earliest of Paul's letters that survive.
im.k: Valentin de Boulogne (c. 1618-20), Museum of Fine Arts, Boston / Wikimedia Commons

set: Critics may have accused Paul of being a fraud like wandering philosophers who preached for money. He reminds the Thessalonians of how he behaved: gentle like a nursing mother, working day and night to avoid being a burden, and exhorting them like a father. He expresses longing to see them again.

his.t: Acts 17:5-9 says some Jews, jealous of Paul’s success, gathered men from the marketplace and a mob, attacked Jason’s house, and dragged him and others before the politarchs.

Paul says he tried more than once to return, but “Satan hindered us” (2:18). Acts 17:9 says Jason and the others had to post bond. Some scholars think that bond kept Paul away, but he does not say what the hindrance was.

cus.t: Paul compares himself to a nursing mother caring for her own children (2:7) and, a few verses later, to a father who encourages and urges each child (2:11). Early manuscripts differ in 2:7 between “gentle” and “infants,” which changes the first picture.

Paul says he and his team worked “night and day” so as not to burden the church (2:9; 2 Thessalonians 3:8). Manual trades were often looked down on by the educated. Philippians 4:16 says the Philippians also sent help while he was in Thessalonica.

cu: Traveling teachers often asked for fees, and some were swindlers. Paul worked at his trade, probably tentmaking, so the gospel could be preached free of charge (v.9).

ot.n: The measure of sin is not yet full.
Prophets killed, behind “killed the prophets.”

im.c: Paul speaks to the women at Philippi (Acts 16:13-15), from a 16th-century print series on Acts. In 1 Thessalonians 2:2 Paul recalls that he had "suffered and been mistreated in Philippi" before he came to Thessalonica.
im.k: Print series on Acts (16th c.), Rijksmuseum, CC0 / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul explains that he could no longer bear being apart from the Thessalonians, so he stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy to strengthen them. Timothy has now come back with good news of their faith and love. Paul is greatly relieved and prays to see them again.

his.t: Paul says he was “left behind at Athens alone” and sent Timothy to Thessalonica (3:1-2). Acts 17:16-34 tells of his time in Athens, including the speech at the Areopagus. Acts 18:5 says Silas and Timothy rejoined him in Corinth.

Acts 16:1-3 says Timothy was a disciple at Lystra, the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father, and that Paul took him along. Paul calls him “our brother and God’s coworker” (3:2) and sends him to strengthen the church.

cus.t: Paul writes, “now we really live, if you are standing firm in the Lord” (3:8). The verb means to stand fast or hold one’s ground. He uses it for steadiness in several letters (1 Corinthians 16:13; Philippians 4:1; 2 Thessalonians 2:15).

Paul fears “the tempter” had tested them and his work would be in vain (3:5). In 2:18 he blames “Satan” for hindering his return. The Gospels use the same title for the devil who tempted Jesus (Matthew 4:3).

cu: Paul’s phrase “we were determined to be left behind at Athens alone” shows the cost of sending Timothy. The apostles suffered affliction, and Paul wanted the church not to be shaken by trials.

ot.n: The Lord will come with all his holy ones.
Satan tests Job.
The serpent tempts Eve.

im.c: St Paul Preaching in Athens, Raphael's 1515 cartoon for a tapestry. First Thessalonians 3:1 says Paul was "left behind at Athens alone" and sent Timothy to Thessalonica from there.
im.k: Raphael (1515), Victoria and Albert Museum / Wikimedia Commons

t: Live to Please God, and the Hope of the Dead
set: Paul urges the Thessalonians to keep growing in a life that pleases God: sexual purity, brotherly love, quiet work. Then he addresses a worry: some believers had died, and the church wondered what would happen to them when Christ returned. Paul says the dead in Christ will rise first, and all will meet the Lord.

his.h: Death in Greek and Roman Thought
his.t: Greek and Roman writers describe death in many ways. Epicureans held that death was the end, many expected a shadowy afterlife, and some philosophers thought the soul lives on.

Paul says God’s will is their holiness, so they are to abstain from sexual immorality (4:3). In the Roman world, men were widely allowed sex outside marriage with slaves and prostitutes, while Jewish teaching, and the church after it, held to marriage.

cus.t: The Greek word in 4:17 (apantēsis) means a meeting. Some scholars think it pictures a city’s delegation going out to greet a visiting dignitary and escort him back. Others doubt that the word was a fixed term.

Paul speaks of believers who “have fallen asleep” (4:13-15). Greek writers already used sleep for death, and Jesus used it of Lazarus (John 11:11). In these letters Paul uses it of believers, and the picture comes with waking.

cu: In the Greek world, sexual freedom was assumed for men, and Paul teaches a very different standard. Greek and Roman funeral customs included wailing and little hope of afterlife. “Cry of command… voice of an archangel… trumpet” (v.16) recalls an official’s arrival, when a city sent a welcome party outside the gates.

ot.n: The Son of Man comes with the clouds.
The trumpet at Sinai.
Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise.

im.c: The Resurrection of the Flesh, a fresco by Luca Signorelli in Orvieto Cathedral (about 1500). First Thessalonians 4:16 says "the dead in Christ will rise first."
im.k: Luca Signorelli (about 1500), Orvieto Cathedral / Wikimedia Commons

t: The Day of the Lord and Final Words
set: Paul turns to the timing of the day of the Lord, telling the Thessalonians it will come like a thief but that they are children of the day. He then gives a series of brief commands: respect leaders, live in peace, rejoice always, pray continually, give thanks, and test everything.

his.t: Rome presented its rule as bringing peace. Scholars disagree about “peace and security” in 5:3. Some hear Roman propaganda, while others hear the prophets’ warnings against false peace (Jeremiah 6:14; Ezekiel 13:10) and doubt it was a fixed Roman slogan.

Paul tells them not to “quench the Spirit” or “treat prophecies with contempt,” and to “test all things” (5:19-21). Prophecy was a gift of the Spirit in his churches (1 Corinthians 14), and what was said was to be weighed.

cus.t: “The day of the Lord will come just like a thief in the night” (5:2). Jesus used the same picture (Matthew 24:43; Luke 12:39). A thief gives no warning, so Paul tells believers to stay awake and sober (5:6).

Paul ends with “greet all the brothers with a holy kiss” (5:26), and says the same in Romans 16:16 and 1 Corinthians 16:20. A kiss was an ordinary greeting among family and friends, and the church made it a sign of its shared family life.

cu: “Peace and security” (v.3) was a slogan of the Roman empire, and Paul says sudden destruction will come on those who trust in it. “Breastplate of faith and love” and “helmet of hope” (v.8) are soldier images.

ot.n: The day of the Lord will be darkness.
God’s breastplate and helmet.
They say peace when there is no peace.

im.c: The Last Judgment, by Michelangelo (1536-41), in the Sistine Chapel. First Thessalonians 5:2 says the day of the Lord comes "like a thief in the night," and 2 Thessalonians 1:7-10 pictures the Lord Jesus revealed from heaven. Michelangelo's scene blends many biblical passages.
im.k: Michelangelo (1536-41) / Wikimedia Commons

t: Thanks and a Promise of Justice
set: Paul gives thanks that the Thessalonians’ faith is growing and their love increasing, even as they endure persecution. He tells them that God is just, and will give relief to the afflicted and repay those who afflict them when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven.

his.t: Paul praises their endurance in “all your persecutions and afflictions” (1:4). The pressure that began in Acts 17 had not ended, and the letter does not say who was applying it.
Paul says it is just for God to repay affliction to those who afflict them and to give relief to those who suffer (1:6-7). The wording of 1:8-9 echoes Isaiah (66:15; 2:10, 19).

cus.t: The Greek word translated “rest” in 1:7 (anesis) means relief or easing. Paul uses it of relief from trouble in 2 Corinthians 2:13, 7:5 and 8:13.

In 1:5 the believers are “considered worthy of the kingdom of God,” and in 1:11 Paul prays that God would count them worthy of His calling. He ties it all to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus (1:12).

cu: Persecution in a Roman city often came through social pressure and informal harassment by neighbors. Paul says their endurance is a sign of God’s coming justice and that the persecution is evidence that they are worthy of the kingdom.

ot.n: The Lord comes in fire.
Hide from the terror of the Lord.
God is feared in the council of the holy ones.

im.c: The Ascension, by Rembrandt (1636), in the Alte Pinakothek in Munich. Second Thessalonians 1:7 says the Lord Jesus will be revealed "from heaven with His mighty angels." In Acts 1:11 the angels say He will come in the same way He went.
im.k: Rembrandt (1636), Alte Pinakothek, Munich / Wikimedia Commons

set: Someone, perhaps through a prophecy or a forged letter, had told the Thessalonians that the day of the Lord had already come. Paul says that day will not come until the rebellion occurs and the man of lawlessness is revealed. He then thanks God again and urges them to stand firm.

his.t: About AD 40 the emperor Caligula ordered a statue of himself set up in the Jerusalem Temple. The governor Petronius delayed, and Caligula was killed in AD 41 before it was done (Josephus, Antiquities 18). Some readers think this memory shaped 2:4.

Paul warns them not to be shaken by a letter “as if from us” saying the day of the Lord has come (2:2), and says he signs every letter himself (3:17). Some scholars think 2 Thessalonians itself was written by someone else. Others defend Paul as the author.

cus.t: Paul says “you know what is restraining him now” (2:6) because he told them in person (2:5), and he does not write it down. Readers have proposed Roman rule, the preaching of the gospel, the Spirit or an angel, but the text does not settle it.

Paul says that because people refused the love of the truth, God sends them a deluding influence so that they believe the lie (2:10-11). Compare the lying spirit sent to the prophets of Ahab in 1 Kings 22:22.

cu: The man of lawlessness takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God (v.4). Paul’s readers may have remembered Antiochus Epiphanes (Daniel 11) and the emperor Caligula’s attempt to put his statue in the Jerusalem Temple (AD 40).

ot.n: A king who exalts himself above every god.
He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth.
A ruler who says, “I am a god.”

im.c: The Sermon and Deeds of the Antichrist, a fresco by Luca Signorelli in Orvieto Cathedral (about 1500). Later Christians linked "the man of lawlessness" (2 Thessalonians 2:3) with the figure called Antichrist, but Paul does not use that name here, and readers disagree about whom he means.
im.k: Luca Signorelli (about 1500), Orvieto Cathedral / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul asks for prayer that the word of the Lord may spread, and expresses confidence that the Lord will guard them. Then he addresses a practical problem: some in the church had quit working, perhaps expecting the Lord’s return, and were living off others. Paul instructs them to work quietly and earn their own bread.

his.t: Paul tells the church to keep away from those living “in idleness” (3:6, 11). The letter does not say why they were idle. Readers suggest excitement about the Lord’s return, dependence on patrons, or contempt for manual work.
Paul writes the closing greeting himself and calls it “the sign in every letter” (3:17). He does the same in 1 Corinthians 16:21, Galatians 6:11 and Colossians 4:18.

cus.t: In Greek and Roman cities wealthy patrons supported dependents who gave them honor and service. Some scholars think the idle believers were leaning on rich members of the church in this way. Paul tells them instead to earn their own bread (3:12).
Paul says he worked “night and day” so as not to burden them, and to give an example (3:7-9). Acts 18:3 calls him a tentmaker. The Greek word is usually understood as a worker in leather or cloth.

cu: Patrons supported clients in Greek society, and some in the church may have expected to be supported. Paul had refused such support himself and worked night and day. His rule, “If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat,” was a call to self-support, not a rule for people unable to work.

ot.n: By the sweat of your brow you will eat.
Go to the ant, you sluggard.
Guard the door of my lips.

im.c: Saint Paul at his Writing Desk, by Rembrandt (about 1629-30). In 2 Thessalonians 3:17 Paul says, "I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand," and calls it the sign in every letter of his.
im.k: Rembrandt (about 1629-30) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul had left Timothy in Ephesus to deal with people teaching different doctrines and wasting time on myths and genealogies. He reminds Timothy that the goal of the command is love, and tells his own story: once a blasphemer and persecutor, Paul received mercy.

his.t: Acts 19 and 20 say Paul spent about three years in Ephesus. In Acts 20:29-30 he warns the Ephesian elders that savage wolves would come in and that some from among their own number would twist the truth.

Acts 16:1-3 says Timothy was a disciple at Lystra, the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father, and that Paul took him along. He is named with Paul in the openings of several letters (for example 2 Corinthians 1:1 and Philippians 1:1).

cus.t: Paul tells Timothy to stop some people from devoting themselves to "myths and endless genealogies" (1:4) but does not say what these were.

Paul says some have "shipwrecked" their faith (1:19) and names Hymenaeus and Alexander (1:20). He knew the sea well: he lists three shipwrecks in 2 Corinthians 11:25, and Acts 27 tells of another. Here the word is a picture of faith wrecked.

cu: Some in Ephesus mixed the law with speculative stories and genealogies, treating religion as a puzzle for experts. Paul says the aim is a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith.

ot.n: Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom.
Commandments Paul lists in vv.9-10.
“Woe is me! I am a man of unclean lips.”

im.c: Timothy and Lois, by Willem Drost (about 1650), in the Hermitage. Second Timothy 1:5 names Timothy's grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice as the source of his faith, and 1 Timothy 1:2 calls him Paul's "true child in the faith."
im.k: Willem Drost (about 1650), Hermitage Museum / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul begins the instructions for the church by calling for prayer for all people, including kings, so that believers may live quietly. He states that God wants all to be saved and that there is one mediator, Jesus. He then addresses men and women in worship, a passage written to Ephesus.

his.t: Paul asks first for prayers for all people, including kings and all in authority (2:1-2). Jews prayed for foreign rulers (Jeremiah 29:7; Ezra 6:10), and Josephus says sacrifices for the emperor were offered in the Jerusalem Temple until they were stopped in…
Inscriptions from the cities of Roman Asia, Ephesus among them, name women who held civic and religious titles, paid for buildings and games, and were honored with statues.

cus.t: Paul wants men in every place to pray "lifting up holy hands" (2:8). Standing with the hands raised was the usual way to pray among Jews and Greeks (Psalm 28:2; 134:2), and early Christian art shows people praying this way.
Paul says women should dress with modesty and self-control, "not with braided hair or gold or pearls or expensive clothing" (2:9). First Peter 3:3 gives a similar warning.

cu: Ephesus was the city of Artemis, a goddess served by priestesses. Paul’s instructions on women (vv.9-15) have been read in different ways as either a general rule or a response to specific problems of false teaching and disorder.

ot.n: The Lord our God, the Lord is one.
The creation of Eve.
The servant gave his life as a sin offering.

im.c: Adam and Eve, an engraving by Albrecht Dürer (1504). First Timothy 2:13-14 points back to Adam being formed first and to Eve being deceived. How Paul uses that in 2:12-15 is one of the most debated questions in the letter.
im.k: Albrecht Dürer (1504), National Gallery of Art, Washington / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul lists qualifications for overseers (bishops, elders) and deacons. They are described in terms of character: self-controlled, hospitable, able to teach, not a lover of money, managing their households well. He ends with why he is writing and with an early hymn about Christ.

his.t: In Acts 20:17 and 20:28 Paul calls the same Ephesian leaders "elders" and "overseers," and Titus 1:5-7 uses the two words for the same office. Here (3:1-7) he lists what an overseer must be.

The Greek word diakonos means servant. Paul uses it of Phoebe in Romans 16:1, and Philippians 1:1 greets the "overseers and deacons" together. First Timothy 3:8-13 gives their qualifications but not their duties.

cus.t: "The husband of one wife" (3:2) is debated. The Greek says literally "of one woman a man." It may mean faithful to one spouse, no polygamy, not remarried after divorce, or not remarried after a wife's death.

Paul says a man who cannot manage his own household well cannot care for God's church (3:4-5). Churches met in homes (Romans 16:5; 1 Corinthians 16:19), and 3:15 calls the church the household of God.

cu: In a house church, an overseer was responsible for a household of believers, and so management of his own household was a sign of ability. Paul did not make the qualifications about gifts or status but about reputation.

ot.n: Priests were required to meet standards of life.
Wisdom is better than silver.
The ascended Lord, echoed in the hymn.

im.c: Saint Lawrence Distributing Alms, a fresco by Fra Angelico (1447-49). Lawrence was a deacon of Rome who died in AD 258, long after Paul, and later Christians remembered deacons for caring for the poor. First Timothy 3:8-13 names the character deacons must have but does not list their duties.
im.k: Fra Angelico (1447-49), Niccoline Chapel, Vatican / Wikimedia Commons

t: A Good Servant of Christ Jesus
set: Paul warns that in later times some will depart from the faith, forbidding marriage and certain foods. He tells Timothy that everything created by God is good and to be received with thanksgiving, and urges Timothy to be an example for believers, to devote himself to Scripture, and to watch his life and teaching closely.

his.t: Paul says some will forbid marriage and demand abstaining from foods (4:3). He does not name the group. Suggestions include Jewish food teaching and ascetic movements; some Gnostic groups of the 2nd century did discourage marriage, but that is later than the…
Paul tells Timothy, "Let no one despise your youth" (4:12). Writers of the time used words for "youth" of men well into their thirties.

cus.t: Paul tells Timothy to devote himself to "the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, and to teaching" (4:13). Synagogues read the Law and the Prophets aloud (Luke 4:16-20; Acts 13:15), and Paul expected his letters to be read aloud to churches…
Paul reminds Timothy of the gift given "through prophecy with the laying on of hands by the council of elders" (4:14), and 2 Timothy 1:6 says it came through Paul's own hands.

cu: Some early ascetic groups forbade marriage and meat as marks of holiness. Paul says this is wrong, as God created food and marriage to be received with thanks. “Let no one despise your youth” (v.12) was said of a man perhaps in his thirties.

ot.n: God saw everything he had made, and it was very good.
Moses laid hands on Joshua.
Anointing for the gospel.

im.c: Still Life with Open Bible, by Vincent van Gogh (1885). First Timothy 4:13 tells Timothy to give his attention to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation and to teaching. The painting is from the Netherlands, long after Paul, but it shows the book at the center of a community's life.
im.k: Vincent van Gogh (1885), Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul tells Timothy how to treat different groups in the church: older men and women as parents, younger as siblings. He gives detailed instructions for widows, since the church supported those without family, and for elders who deserve double honor and must not be accused lightly.

his.t: A widow in the ancient Mediterranean world often had no income of her own and depended on her family. The Old Testament names widows, orphans and foreigners as those God protects (Deuteronomy 10:18; 24:19-21), and Acts 6:1 says widows were being overlooked in…

Paul says elders who lead well are worthy of "double honor" (5:17). The word for honor was also used for payment, and in 5:18 he cites Deuteronomy 25:4 about the ox and a saying about workers deserving their wages (compare Luke 10:7). That fits support.

cus.t: No widow is to be "enrolled" unless she is at least sixty, "the wife of one husband," and known for good works (5:9-10). The letter does not say what the list was for. It may have been a roll of widows receiving support, a group with a service role, or both.

Paul tells Timothy to "stop drinking only water" and to use "a little wine" for his stomach and frequent illnesses (5:23). Wine was an ordinary drink, usually mixed with water, and ancient doctors prescribed it for stomach complaints.

cu: There was no social safety net, and a widow without family was in danger. The church kept a list of widows over sixty who had been faithful. Younger widows were encouraged to remarry. Elders who worked hard in teaching were paid.

ot.n: Do not muzzle an ox while it treads the grain.
A matter must be established by two or three witnesses.
Do not mistreat any widow or orphan.

im.c: The Prophetess Anna, by Rembrandt (17th century). Luke 2:36-37 describes Anna, an elderly widow who stayed in the temple worshiping night and day. First Timothy 5:5 describes a widow left alone who sets her hope on God and continues night and day in prayer.
im.k: Rembrandt (17th century) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul tells slaves to honor their masters, warns about false teachers who think godliness is a means of gain, and says godliness with contentment is great gain. He warns that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil, urges Timothy to flee it and fight the good fight, and instructs the rich to be generous.

his.t: Ephesus was one of the busiest ports and commercial centers of Roman Asia, and ancient writers say the temple of Artemis held deposits like a bank.

Timothy "made your good confession in the presence of many witnesses" (6:12), and Christ Jesus "gave His good confession before Pontius Pilate" (6:13). Readers have linked Timothy's confession to his baptism, his ordination or a public declaration.

cus.t: Paul tells slaves to honor their masters, and not to look down on masters who are believers because they are brothers (6:1-2). Slavery was a legal and economic fact in Roman cities, and slaves could be household managers or skilled workers.
Paul bursts into praise of "the King of kings and Lord of lords," who "dwells in unapproachable light" (6:15-16). The same titles appear for Christ in Revelation 17:14 and 19:16.

cu: Traveling teachers often charged fees and sought wealthy patrons. Paul warns that those who desire to be rich fall into temptation. His instruction to the rich to be “rich in good works” challenges the patron system.

ot.n: Naked I came from my mother’s womb.
No one takes any of their toil with them.
Give me neither poverty nor riches.

im.c: The Parable of the Rich Fool, by Rembrandt (1627): an old man checks his money by candlelight (Luke 12:16-21). First Timothy 6:9-10 warns about the desire to be rich, and 6:17-19 tells the rich not to put their hope in wealth.
im.k: Rembrandt (1627), Gemäldegalerie, Berlin / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul writes from prison, remembering Timothy’s tears at their last parting and the faith of his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice. He urges Timothy to rekindle the gift of God, to not be ashamed of Paul or the gospel, and to guard the good deposit.

his.t: Paul recalls Timothy's sincere faith, which lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (1:5). Acts 16:1 says his mother was a Jewish believer and his father a Greek, and that Timothy was a disciple at Lystra.

Paul prays for the household of Onesiphorus, who often refreshed him, was not ashamed of his chains, and searched earnestly for him in Rome until he found him (1:16-17). He had also served at Ephesus (1:18). The letter does not say where he was from.

cus.t: Paul tells Timothy to fan into flame the gift of God that is in him "through the laying on of my hands" (1:6). First Timothy 4:14 speaks of hands laid on him by the council of elders.
Paul asks Timothy not to be ashamed of the testimony about the Lord or of Paul, His prisoner (1:8), and he praises Onesiphorus for not being ashamed of his chains (1:16).

cu: “Fan into flame” (v.6) is the picture of stirring coals back to fire. In the Roman Empire, being associated with a prisoner could bring shame or danger, so many abandoned Paul. Onesiphorus was the exception, who searched for him in Rome.

ot.n: “In you I trust; let me not be put to shame.”
“Fear not, Abram.”
“Fear not, for I am with you.”

im.c: Timothy and Lois, by Willem Drost (about 1650), in the Hermitage. It is an imagined scene. Second Timothy 1:5 names Timothy's grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice as the first in whom his sincere faith lived.
im.k: Willem Drost (about 1650), Hermitage Museum / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul tells Timothy to be strong in grace and entrust what he has learned to faithful people who will teach others. He gives three pictures of faithful work: soldier, athlete, farmer. He warns about word-battles and urges Timothy to correct opponents gently.

his.t: Paul tells Timothy to entrust what he heard from Paul among many witnesses to faithful people who will be able to teach others as well (2:2). That makes four stages in handing on the message: Paul, Timothy, the faithful people, and those they teach.

Paul names two teachers who have departed from the truth by saying the resurrection has already taken place (2:17-18). First Timothy 1:20 names a Hymenaeus together with Alexander, but the letters do not say they are the same man.

cus.t: Paul asks Timothy to endure hardship like a good soldier (2:3) and says a soldier avoids civilian entanglements to please the one who enlisted him (2:4). Paul also calls Epaphroditus and Archippus "fellow soldier" (Philippians 2:25; Philemon 2).

Paul says an athlete is crowned only if he competes according to the rules (2:5). Greek games had strict rules and officials. The Greek travel writer Pausanias (2nd century AD) says athletes at Olympia swore they had trained for ten months.

cu: Soldiers had one aim: to please the commander. Athletes had to compete by the rules to win the crown. A farmer who works hard gets the first share of crops. Each pictures an aspect of faithfulness.

ot.n: The Lord knows who are his.
Depart, touch no unclean thing.
The ox who treads grain.

im.c: Ploughing in the Nivernais, by Rosa Bonheur (1849). The third picture in 2 Timothy 2:3-6 is the hardworking farmer, who should be the first to receive a share of the crops.
im.k: Rosa Bonheur (1849) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul describes how, in the last days, people will be lovers of self, money, and pleasure, with a form of godliness but denying its power. He contrasts them with his own endurance of persecution and tells Timothy to continue in what he has learned from childhood. All Scripture is breathed out by God.

his.t: Paul reminds Timothy of the persecutions and sufferings he met at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra (3:11). Acts 13:50, 14:5 and 14:19 tell of them, and at Lystra Paul was stoned and dragged out of the city. Timothy came from that region (Acts 16:1-2).

The Old Testament does not name Pharaoh's magicians (Exodus 7:11). Paul does, saying Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses (3:8). The names are found in Jewish writings outside the Bible, such as the Targums, and Origen says Paul took them from a book.

cus.t: Paul says Timothy has known the Holy Scriptures "from infancy" (3:15). Jewish writers such as Philo and Josephus say that children were taught the Law from their earliest years.

Paul says some will hold "a form of godliness" but deny its power (3:5). The phrase comes at the end of a long list of vices (3:2-4) that begins with lovers of self and lovers of money. The word "form" means outward shape or appearance.

cu: Jannes and Jambres (v.8) are names of Egyptian magicians in Jewish tradition who opposed Moses. Paul’s experiences in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra (v.11) were in Timothy’s home region.

ot.n: Pharaoh’s magicians imitated Moses.
Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the Lord delivers.
Moses, the man of God.

im.c: The rods of Moses and the magicians turned into serpents (Exodus 7:10-12), by Gerard Hoet (1728). Exodus does not name Pharaoh's magicians. Second Timothy 3:8 calls them Jannes and Jambres.
im.k: Gerard Hoet (1728) / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul gives a solemn charge to preach the word in season and out of season, because people will turn away from sound teaching. Then he says his own time is near: he has fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith. He asks Timothy to come and to bring his cloak and books.

his.t: Paul says that at his first defense no one came to his support, but the Lord stood by him and strengthened him (4:16-17). The letter does not say where the hearing was or what the charge was.

Paul says Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted him and gone to Thessalonica (4:10). Demas is named with Paul in Colossians 4:14 and Philemon 24. The letter does not say whether he left the faith.

cus.t: Paul asks Timothy to bring the cloak he left with Carpus at Troas (4:13). The Greek word for cloak is rare, and it is used for a heavy outer garment. Paul also asks Timothy to come before winter (4:21), which may be why he wants it.

Paul asks for his scrolls, "especially the parchments" (4:13). Parchments were sheets of animal skin, and they may have been notebooks. The letter does not say what the books and parchments were; suggestions include Scripture scrolls and Paul's own papers.

cu: “Poured out as a drink offering” (v.6) pictures wine poured on a sacrifice. The “crown of righteousness” is the wreath for the winner of a race. Paul’s request for his cloak and the parchments shows his needs in a cold, damp prison.

ot.n: Save me from the mouth of the lion.
The drink offering poured out.
Daniel rescued from the lions.

im.c: Paul in Prison, by Rembrandt (1627), in the Staatsgalerie Stuttgart. It is an imagined scene, but 2 Timothy speaks of Paul in chains (1:16; 2:9) and asks for a cloak, scrolls and parchments (4:13).
im.k: Rembrandt (1627), Staatsgalerie Stuttgart / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul had left Titus in Crete to appoint elders in every town. He lists their qualifications and then explains why it matters: rebellious people, especially of the circumcision party, are upsetting households.

his.t: Acts 2:11 lists Cretans among the people in Jerusalem who heard the apostles at Pentecost. Acts does not record a mission to Crete. The only visit it tells of is Paul’s ship putting in at Fair Havens on the way to Rome (Acts 27:7-13).

Paul quotes “one of their own prophets” (1:12) without naming him. Later writers such as Clement of Alexandria and Jerome name Epimenides, a half-legendary Cretan seer and poet traditionally dated about 600 BC.

cus.t: Paul tells Titus to rebuke those who pay attention to Jewish myths and the commands of men who have rejected the truth (1:14), and then says that to the pure all things are pure (1:15). The letter does not list the rules.
An elder must be hospitable (1:8). Inns in the Roman world often had a poor name, so travelers, including teachers and the helpers of apostles, depended on private homes.

cu: Crete had a long-standing reputation for liars, as the poet Epimenides said. “To the pure all things are pure” (v.15) addresses people who made much of ritual purity but had corrupt minds.

ot.n: Their worship is a human rule.
Blessing for all nations, as the church spreads.

im.c: Epimenides, a half-legendary Cretan seer and poet of the 6th century BC, in an imagined portrait from Guillaume Rouillé's book of portraits (1553). Later writers connect the saying about Cretans with him. Paul calls its author "one of their own prophets" (Titus 1:12) and does not give a name.
im.k: Guillaume Rouillé (1553), public domain / Wikimedia Commons

set: Paul tells Titus to teach what accords with sound doctrine. He gives instructions for older men, older women, younger women, younger men, and slaves. All are grounded in the gospel: the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all, training us to renounce ungodliness and live self-controlled, upright, godly lives.

his.t: Greek writers such as Aristotle set out the duties of each person in a household. Titus 2:1-10 gives short duties for older men and women, younger women and men, and slaves, and ties each to the gospel: so that the word of God will not be discredited (2:5)…

Paul says the grace of God “has appeared” (2:11) and looks for the “glorious appearance” of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ (2:13). The Greek word epiphaneia was used in the Greek world for the arrival of a ruler or a god’s help.

cus.t: Slaves are to “adorn the teaching about God our Savior” (2:10). The Greek verb kosmeo means to put in order or to decorate, and it is also used for jewelry and dress (1 Peter 3:5).

Christ gave Himself “to redeem us from all lawlessness” (2:14). The Greek verb is from the word family for a ransom price paid to free a captive or a slave. The Old Testament uses the idea for God’s freeing Israel from Egypt (Deuteronomy 7:8).

cu: This is a household code, like those in Ephesians and Colossians. Ancient writers warned that Christians threatened social order, so Paul tells them to live so that “the word of God may not be reviled.” Paul calls the church “a people for his own possession,” echoing Israel.

ot.n: Israel as God’s treasured possession.
He will redeem Israel from all his iniquities.
God will cleanse his people.

im.c: Christ Pantocrator, a sixth-century icon at Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai, one of the oldest surviving icons of Christ. Titus 2:11-14 says the grace of God has appeared and looks for the appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave Himself for us.
im.k: Unknown artist (6th century), Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai / Wikimedia Commons

t: Saved by Mercy, Devoted to Good Works
set: Paul tells Titus to remind believers to be subject to rulers, honest, and gentle. He recalls that they once were foolish and enslaved but that God saved them by mercy through the washing of regeneration. He ends with warnings against quarrels and a divisive person, and personal notes about Artemas, Tychicus, Zenas, and Apollos.

his.t: Augustus founded Nicopolis, the City of Victory, about 31-29 BC after his victory at Actium. Titus 3:12 asks Titus to come to Paul there because Paul has decided to winter there.
Titus is told to equip Zenas the lawyer and Apollos so they have everything they need (3:13). Apollos is known from Acts 18:24-28 and 1 Corinthians 1:12; 3:4-6; 16:12. Zenas is named only here.

cus.t: Titus 3:5 says God saved us through “the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit,” and not by the righteous deeds we had done.

Titus is to reject a divisive man after a first and second admonition (3:10). The Greek word hairetikos comes from a word meaning to choose, so it first meant someone who picks a party. The meaning “heretic” grew up later in church history.

cu: Cretans had a reputation for being quarrelsome. Paul tells Titus to avoid “foolish controversies” and, after two warnings, have nothing more to do with a divisive person. Nicopolis (“city of victory”) was a Roman city in northwest Greece.

ot.n: Clean water and a new spirit.
Create in me a clean heart.
Do not answer a fool by his folly.

im.c: The Baptism of Christ, by Piero della Francesca (after 1451). Titus 3:5 says God saved us through "the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit." Many readers think of baptism here, though the verse does not use the word.
im.k: Piero della Francesca (after 1451), National Gallery, London / Wikimedia Commons

t: A Slave Who Is Now a Brother
set: Onesimus, Philemon's slave, is with Paul in prison and has become a Christian through him (verse 10). Most readers think he had run away, perhaps taking something (verse 18), though the letter says only that he was parted from Philemon "for a while." Paul is sending him back with this letter.

his.t: Slaves were a large part of the Roman world. Historians' estimates vary a great deal, often putting slaves at roughly one in ten to one in five of the empire's people, and more in Italy and the big cities. The law treated a slave as the owner's property.

The name Onesimus means "useful" or "profitable" and was a common slave name. Paul puns on it in verses 10-11 and 20. Colossians 4:9 calls Onesimus "our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you," and says he is coming to Colossae with Tychicus.

cus.t: The letter does not use the word "runaway." It says Onesimus was parted from Philemon "for a while" (verse 15) and that he may have wronged him or owes him something (verse 18). Most readers take him to be a fugitive.

Paul asks Philemon to "prepare a guest room" for him (verse 22). Inns had a poor name, so travelers, including teachers and the helpers of apostles, depended on private homes. Philemon's house already holds the church (verse 2).

cu: Runaway slaves could be branded, beaten, or executed. Roman law allowed owners harsh punishments. Paul gently plays on Onesimus’s name, which means “useful,” saying he was “useless” to you, but is now “useful.”

ot.n: Judah offers to be a guarantee for Benjamin.
A Hebrew slave went free in the seventh year.
Israel was not to hand back a slave who had escaped to them from his master. The rule concerned a foreign master, and Roman law said the opposite about runaways.

im.c: Papyrus 87 (Cologne, Papyrus 12), the earliest known fragment of the letter to Philemon, usually dated to the late 2nd or early 3rd century, about 150 years after Paul. This side has Philemon 13-15, where Paul says he would have liked to keep Onesimus with him and suggests that Onesimus was parted from Philemon "for a while" so that Philemon might have him back for good.
im.k: Unknown author (late 2nd or early 3rd century), public domain / Wikimedia Commons

t: God Has Spoken by His Son
set: The letter begins without a greeting. It opens like a sermon with a majestic sentence: God spoke long ago through the prophets, but now through a Son. The writer then presents a chain of Old Testament quotations to prove that the Son is far above the angels.

his.t: In Jewish tradition the law was given through angels (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19). So the writer first shows that the Son is above the angels, then that he is above Moses and the priests who served under the law.

The letter quotes the Old Testament in its Greek form (the Septuagint) almost every time. Some quotations, such as the one in 1:6, follow the Greek wording and not the Hebrew. This fits readers who read Greek, in a city where Jews used the Greek Bible.

cus.t: To sit at the king's right hand was to share his honor and rule (1 Kings 2:19; Psalm 110:1). Hebrews says the Son sat down there after he made purification for sins.
The Greek word charaktēr comes from the engraver's tool and the mark it leaves, as on a coin or seal. The Son is the exact representation of God's being (1:3).

cu: Many Jews believed the law was given through angels (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19), so showing the Son is greater than angels was showing he is greater than the law’s mediators.

ot.n: God calls the king his Son and says he has become his Father (quoted in 1:5 and 5:5).
“Sit at my right hand.”
The Lord laid the foundation of the earth.

im.c: A page of Codex Vaticanus, a Greek Bible copied in the 4th century and kept in the Vatican Library. It shows the end of 2 Thessalonians (3:11-18) and the opening of Hebrews (1:1-2:2). In this manuscript Hebrews follows 2 Thessalonians, among the letters of Paul, although the letter itself never names its author.
im.k: Unknown scribe (4th century), public domain / Wikimedia Commons

set: After the first warning, the writer explains why the Son took on flesh and blood: to taste death for everyone, to break the power of the one who has the power of death, and to become a merciful and faithful high priest. The Son who is above the angels became lower than them for a little while.

his.t: Writers of the time, such as the Epicurean poet Lucretius, argued at length against the fear of death, which suggests how common it was. Hebrews 2:15 says that Jesus frees those who were held in slavery by this fear.
Verse 17 is the first time the letter calls Jesus a high priest. He became "merciful and faithful" by sharing flesh and blood and by being tempted, so he can help those who are tempted (2:18).

cus.t: The verb in 2:1 pictures something slipping past unnoticed, like a boat that drifts by the harbor because no one is paying attention.
The word in 2:10 (archēgos) can mean founder, leader or pioneer: someone who goes ahead and opens the way for others. It returns in 12:2.

cu: The word translated "author" of their salvation (2:10) can also mean pioneer or trailblazer: someone who goes ahead and leads others after him. Being held in slavery by the fear of death (2:15) was a heavy burden in the ancient world.

ot.n: “What is man that you are mindful of him?”
Quoted in 2:13: "Here am I, and the children God has given Me."
The seed of the woman will crush the serpent.

im.c: Papyrus 46, usually dated to about AD 200, is the oldest large copy that includes Hebrews, and so it carries chapter 2, where the Son is made like his brothers in every way (2:17). The manuscript is a book of leaves, a codex, and not a roll.
im.k: Papyrus 46, public domain / Wikimedia Commons

set: The writer compares Jesus with Moses. Moses was faithful as a servant in God’s house, but Jesus is faithful as a Son over God’s house. Then he draws on Psalm 95 and the wilderness generation, who hardened their hearts and failed to enter God’s rest, as a warning for readers.

his.t: Israel wandered forty years because of unbelief at Kadesh (Numbers 14:33-34). Hebrews 3:17 recalls those "whose bodies fell in the wilderness."
God said Moses was faithful in all his house (Numbers 12:7). Hebrews grants this, then says a builder has more honor than the house, and a son over the house more than a servant in it (3:2-6).

cus.t: The word "today" in Psalm 95 means that the time to respond is always now. The writer tells his readers to encourage one another daily "as long as it is called today" (3:13).
In Greek, a "house" can mean a household or family. Moses was a servant within the household. The Son is over it, as its builder and heir (3:2-6).

cu: Moses was held in the highest honor, so the writer first praises him as "faithful in all God's house" (Numbers 12:7). He then says a builder has more honor than the house, and a son over the house more than a servant in it (3:2-6).

ot.n: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.”
Moses was faithful in all God’s house.
The rebellion at Kadesh.

im.c: A wall painting of Moses at the burning bush from the synagogue at Dura-Europos in Syria. Moses was held in the highest honor in Judaism, so Hebrews 3 begins by praising him as "faithful in all God's house" before saying that the Son is greater.
im.k: Unknown artist (3rd century AD), public domain / Wikimedia Commons

t: A Sabbath Rest for God’s People
set: The promise of entering God’s rest still stands. The writer relates it to God’s rest on the seventh day and says there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God. He describes God’s word as living and active, and introduces Jesus as the great high priest who sympathizes with weakness.

his.t: In Greek, Joshua and Jesus are the same name, Iēsous. Hebrews 4:8 says that if Joshua had given Israel the rest, God would not later speak of another day.
Ancient Israel hoped for rest from enemies and from labor. Hebrews links the promise in Psalm 95 with God's own rest on the seventh day (Genesis 2:2).

cus.t: The word of God is said to be sharper than any double-edged sword (4:12). The Roman short sword, the gladius, was sharp on both edges and had a point.

The rare word in verse 13 (tetrachēlismena) comes from the word for "neck." Scholars explain it as a wrestler's hold that bends the head back, or as an animal's neck held back for the knife. Either way, nothing is hidden from God.

cu: The Sabbath looks back to creation. The writer says the rest promised in Psalm 95 was not fully reached under Joshua, so a Sabbath rest remains for God's people. "Throne of grace" may recall the mercy seat over the ark in the Holy of Holies, though the writer does not say so.

ot.n: On the seventh day God rested.
God swore in his anger that they would never enter his rest (quoted in 3:11, 4:3 and 4:5).
He made my mouth like a sharp sword.

im.c: A piece of Papyrus 13, a roll found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt and usually dated to the 3rd or early 4th century. Hebrews was copied on the back of an old roll that had a summary of Livy's Roman history on the front. This fragment has Hebrews 4:2-12, the passage about the promised rest and the word of God that is living and active.
im.k: Unknown scribe (3rd or early 4th century), public domain / Wikimedia Commons

t: A Priest in the Order of Melchizedek
set: The writer describes what a high priest does: represents people before God, offers gifts and sacrifices, deals gently with the ignorant, and is called by God. Jesus fits and surpasses this role. He learned obedience through suffering and is called a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.

his.t: Once a year the high priest entered the Holy of Holies with blood, first for himself and then for the people (Leviticus 16). Hebrews 5:3 says he had to offer for his own sins too.
Verse 7 speaks of prayers "with loud cries and tears" in the days of his flesh. Many readers connect this with Gethsemane (Mark 14:32-42), though the letter does not name the place.

cus.t: A picture of infants and adults.
Priests did not choose their office.

cu: Aaron's priests came from one family line. Melchizedek (Genesis 14) appears in Scripture without a genealogy, which is why Hebrews uses him as the picture of a priesthood that does not rest on ancestry (7:3, 15-17).

ot.n: Quoted in 5:6 and 7:17: "You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek."
God calls the king his Son and says he has become his Father (quoted in 1:5 and 5:5).
The Day of Atonement.

im.c: The high priest's clothing from Exodus 28, as imagined by the French artist James Tissot in a pen-and-ink sketch of about 1900. It is a modern artist's picture, not an archaeological find. Hebrews 5:1-4 and 7:26-28 compare Jesus with the high priests of Israel, who were chosen from among men, were weak themselves, and had to offer sacrifices for their own sins too.
im.k: James Tissot (about 1900), public domain / Wikimedia Commons

set: The writer urges readers to go on to maturity and warns that those who have been enlightened and then fall away cannot be brought to repentance again. He then encourages them, with confidence of better things, and points to God’s oath to Abraham as the anchor of hope.

his.t: Hebrews 6:4-8 is one of several warnings in the letter (2:1-4; 3:7-4:13; 10:26-31; 12:25-29). Readers have understood it in different ways: as a warning about believers losing salvation, about people who looked like believers but never were, or about loss of…
Mediterranean ships carried several anchors. In Acts 27:29-30 the ship carrying Paul dropped four from the stern in a storm.

cus.t: People swore by something greater. God swore by himself.
A scout who ran ahead to prepare the way.

cu: God's oath to Abraham (Genesis 22:16-17) is the writer's example of a promise that cannot fail. An anchor held a ship fast in a storm, and the anchor later became a symbol of hope on early Christian tombs. "Behind the curtain" (6:19) refers to the Holy of Holies.

ot.n: God swore by himself to bless Abraham.
The high priest goes inside the curtain.
Quoted in 5:6 and 7:17: "You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek."

im.c: A limestone anchor of the Hellenistic or Roman period, found off the coast near Paphos, Cyprus, and now in the Paphos museum. Iron-bound wooden stocks were fitted into the holes at the lower end. Anchors were a familiar sight in Mediterranean harbors. Hebrews 6:19 calls the hope we have "an anchor for the soul, firm and secure" that enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain.
im.k: Arjuno3, CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

set: The writer explains who Melchizedek was: king of Salem and priest of God Most High who blessed Abraham and received a tenth. Because Psalm 110 says the Messiah is a priest forever after his order, the Levitical priesthood was not final. Jesus is a priest forever, holy and blameless, who offered himself once for all.

his.t: Probably Jerusalem (Psalm 76:2).
They died, so the office passed on. Jesus lives forever.

cus.t: A tenth of the spoils was given to the priest.
The priesthood of Jesus was established with an oath.

cu: Tithes were paid to priests. Abraham paying a tenth to Melchizedek shows that Melchizedek was greater, and by extension the priesthood of Levi, who was still in Abraham’s body, was lesser.

ot.n: Melchizedek blesses Abraham and receives a tithe.
Quoted in 5:6 and 7:17: "You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek."
The Levites received the tithe.

im.c: The meeting of Abraham and Melchizedek, painted by Dieric Bouts for a church in Leuven (Belgium). Genesis 14:18-20 says Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brought out bread and wine and blessed Abraham, who gave him a tenth. Hebrews 7:1-10 builds an argument on this short scene.
im.k: Dieric Bouts (about 1464-68), public domain / Wikimedia Commons

set: The main point: we have a high priest seated at God’s right hand, serving in the true tent in heaven. Earthly priests serve in a copy and shadow. Jesus is mediator of a better covenant, as promised in Jeremiah 31, which the writer quotes in full.

his.t: Hebrews says priests "offer gifts according to the law" (8:4), in the present tense. Some take this to mean that the temple still stood when the letter was written.
The new covenant was promised by Jeremiah in the early 6th century BC, around the time the temple fell to Babylon (Jeremiah 31:31-34).

cus.t: Shadows show a shape without substance.
Contrasts with writing on stone tablets.

cu: The tabernacle was modeled on a heavenly pattern (Exodus 25:40). The writer treats the earthly system as a pointer to a better reality. Calling the first covenant "obsolete and aging" (v.13) may suggest that the temple was still standing but its system was passing away.

ot.n: The new covenant.
Make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.
A new heart and a new spirit.

im.c: Roman soldiers carry the temple menorah in a procession of spoils from Jerusalem, on the Arch of Titus in Rome, built soon after AD 81. Hebrews 8:13 says that what is obsolete and aging will soon disappear. After the temple fell in AD 70 the sacrifices it describes could no longer be offered.
im.k: Laurel Lodged, public domain / Wikimedia Commons

set: The writer describes the earthly tabernacle, with its lampstand, table, golden altar, and ark, and shows that it could not clear the conscience. Christ entered the heavenly sanctuary, not with the blood of goats and calves but with his own blood, securing eternal redemption.

his.t: Hebrews 9:4 lists the golden jar of manna, Aaron's staff that budded and the tablets of the covenant as being in the ark. 1 Kings 8:9 mentions only the two tablets in Solomon's time.
The ashes of a red heifer, mixed with water, were used to purify those made unclean by contact with a dead body (Numbers 19). Hebrews 9:13 says the blood of Christ does more.

cus.t: At Sinai Moses sprinkled the book and the people with blood (Exodus 24:6-8). Hebrews 9:19-21 adds that the tent and its vessels were sprinkled too.
The Greek word diathēkē means both "covenant" and "will." Hebrews 9:16-17 plays on the second meaning: a will takes effect only when the one who made it has died.

cu: The Day of Atonement was the one day when the high priest entered the Most Holy Place. “Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness” (v.22) states the principle of Leviticus 17:11. A will takes effect only on death, which gives another sense of covenant.

ot.n: “This is the blood of the covenant.”
The Day of Atonement ritual.
The life of the flesh is in the blood.

im.c: "The Scapegoat" by William Holman Hunt, painted on the shore of the Dead Sea in 1854-55. On the Day of Atonement the high priest sent a live goat into the wilderness carrying the people's sins (Leviticus 16:20-22). Hebrews 9-10 refers to the yearly ritual to show that it had to be repeated, while Christ's offering did not. (The goat that was burned outside the camp, in Hebrews 13:11, was a different animal, the sin offering.)
im.k: William Holman Hunt (1854-55), public domain / Wikimedia Commons

set: The writer summarizes: the law is a shadow, and repeated sacrifices could not perfect worshipers. Christ came to do God’s will and offered one sacrifice for sins forever. So we can enter the holy places with confidence, hold fast, and stir one another up.

his.t: The readers were publicly exposed to abuse (the word in verse 33 means being put on display, as in a theater), shared the sufferings of prisoners and had their property seized (10:32-34).

If the readers were in Rome, the earlier suffering might point to the troubles under Claudius, who expelled Jews from Rome about AD 49 (Suetonius, Claudius 25.4; Acts 18:2). This is a guess. The letter names neither the place nor the date.

cus.t: The Greek word in verse 24 (paroxysmos) means to provoke or spur on. It is also used of sharp disagreement (Acts 15:39). Here believers are to provoke one another to love and good works.
Some had given up meeting (10:25), perhaps out of fear, since being seen with a persecuted group could cost a person dearly.

cu: Early house churches met together for mutual encouragement. The writer says some have made a habit of not meeting together (10:25), perhaps out of fear. Their earlier suffering included public abuse and confiscated property.

ot.n: Quoted in 10:5: "Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but a body You prepared for Me."
Quoted in 10:38: "My righteous one will live by faith."
Vengeance is mine; the Lord will judge his people.

im.c: Another piece of Papyrus 13, with Hebrews 10:8-22. The passage says that Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for all time and invites the readers to draw near to God with a true heart, with hearts sprinkled clean and bodies washed with pure water.
im.k: Unknown scribe (3rd or early 4th century), public domain / Wikimedia Commons

set: This is the great chapter on faith. Faith is the assurance of things hoped for. The writer lists examples from Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Rahab, and many others, showing that faith trusts God’s promise even when it cannot see the outcome.

his.t: Abraham lived in tents and never owned the land except a burial plot (Genesis 23). Hebrews 11:13-16 says the faithful were looking for a better country, a heavenly one.
Verses 35-38 speak of people tortured, mocked, stoned, sawn in two, killed with the sword, and living in caves. Many readers link 11:35 to the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 6-7.

cus.t: Noah built the ark on dry land, in obedience to a warning about things not yet seen (11:7).
The walls fell after the people had marched around them for seven days (11:30). Excavators have disagreed for a century about what the Late Bronze Age city looked like at that time.

cu: Many of these figures were seen as heroes in Jewish history. The writer emphasizes that they were strangers and exiles looking for a heavenly city. "The world was not worthy of them" (v.38) turns the usual view of success upside down.

ot.n: Abraham offering Isaac.
The Passover.
The fall of Jericho.

im.c: "The Sacrifice of Isaac" by Caravaggio, painted about 1598. Hebrews 11:17-19 says Abraham offered up Isaac by faith, reasoning that God was able even to raise the dead.
im.k: Caravaggio (about 1598), public domain / Wikimedia Commons

set: Surrounded by this cloud of witnesses, the readers are to throw off every weight and run with endurance, looking to Jesus. God disciplines those he loves. The writer contrasts the terrifying mountain of Sinai with the heavenly Mount Zion, and warns not to refuse the one who speaks, for our God is a consuming fire.

his.t: Esau sold his birthright for a meal (Genesis 25:29-34) and later found no way to change what he had done, though he sought the blessing with tears (12:16-17).
At Sinai the people begged that no further word be spoken to them (Exodus 20:19; Deuteronomy 5:25), which Hebrews 12:19 recalls.

cus.t: Greek foot races were run in a stadium before crowds. The writer pictures a runner who lays aside every weight, with a "great cloud of witnesses" around him.
