The word paideia means the whole upbringing of a child. A Roman father held legal authority over his children, and discipline was a sign that a child was accepted as his own (12:5-11).

cu: Stadium races were a familiar image, with spectators filling the stands. Esau’s trading of his birthright for a meal (v.16) is a picture of a short-term choice with a lifelong cost. Discipline by a father was a sign of acceptance.

ot.n: Quoted in 12:5: "My son, do not take lightly the discipline of the Lord."
Sinai with fire and trumpet.
I will shake the heavens and the earth.

im.c: The stadium at Ephesus. Footraces in stadiums watched by crowds were familiar across the Greek-speaking world, and Hebrews 12:1 pictures believers running a race with "a great cloud of witnesses" around them.
im.k: Olos88, CC0 / Wikimedia Commons

set: The writer gives a series of short commands: love the brothers, show hospitality, remember prisoners, honor marriage, keep life free from the love of money, remember leaders, and do not be led away by strange teachings. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.

his.t: Timothy has been released (13:23). The letter does not say which Timothy this is. If it is Paul's coworker, the writer belonged to his circle, which would fit the letter's language and thought.
The phrase "those from Italy send you greetings" (13:24) can mean Italians who are with the writer away from Italy, or believers in Italy. So it does not settle where the letter was sent from or to.

cus.t: Roadside inns had a bad name, so travelers, including teachers and the helpers of apostles, depended on private homes. Some have "entertained angels without knowing it" (13:2), as Abraham did at Mamre (Genesis 18) and Lot at Sodom (Genesis 19).
The writer says worship takes the place of animal sacrifice: the fruit of lips that give thanks to his name, doing good, and sharing (13:15-16).

cu: "Outside the camp" (13:11-13) refers to the sin offering burned outside the camp on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:27). Jesus suffered outside the city gate, so believers are to go out to him, bearing his reproach. Some have "entertained angels without knowing it" (13:2).

ot.n: Quoted in 13:5: "Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you."
Quoted in 13:6: "The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid."
The sin offering is burned outside the camp.

im.c: Papyrus 126, a small 4th-century fragment now in Florence, with Hebrews 13:12-13: Jesus suffered outside the gate, so let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach.
im.k: Unknown scribe (4th century), public domain / Wikimedia Commons

t: Trials, Wisdom, and Doing the Word
set: James writes to scattered Jewish Christians, many of them under pressure. He opens with a surprising call to count trials as joy, because testing produces steadfastness. He then urges them to ask God for wisdom, to see that poverty and riches are temporary, and to be doers of the word and not hearers only.

his.t: Paul calls James the Lord's brother and names him with Cephas and John as one who seemed to be a pillar of the church in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:19; 2:9). Josephus (Antiquities 20.200) says that a high priest named Ananus had James stoned, about AD 62.

Jewish communities lay across the Mediterranean world and beyond the Euphrates (Acts 2:9-11; Philo, Embassy to Gaius 281-283). James writes to "the twelve tribes of the Dispersion." Many take this to mean Jewish believers living outside the land of Israel…

cus.t: Mirrors were usually made of polished metal such as bronze. They gave a recognizable reflection, but a less clear one than modern glass. James uses one for a man who looks at his face and then forgets what he looked like (1:23-24).

With no father or husband to provide for them, orphans and widows were among the most exposed people of the ancient world. The Law told Israel to defend them (Exodus 22:22; Deuteronomy 10:18), and James makes caring for them part of religion that is pure…

cu: Polished metal mirrors (vv.23-24) gave a recognizable reflection, which is James's picture of a man who looks and then forgets what he saw. The Greek word for “religion” in v.27, threskeia, usually meant outward worship and ritual practice. James says that the worship that is pure before God includes caring for orphans and widows, whom the Law told Israel to protect (Deuteronomy 10:18).

ot.n: Wisdom is sought like silver, and the Lord gives it (compare James 1:5).
Job is tested and endures. James mentions him in 5:11.
Love your neighbor as yourself, the command James calls the royal law (2:8).

im.c: One side of Papyrus 23, a leaf from a codex of the letter of James found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt and dated to the 3rd century (now in the Spurlock Museum, University of Illinois). This side has James 1:15-18: desire gives birth to sin, and every good gift comes down from above. It shows that James was copied and read in Egypt by the 200s.
im.k: Unknown scribe (3rd century), public domain / Wikimedia Commons

set: James describes a gathering where a rich man in fine clothes gets the best seat and a poor man is told to stand. This favoritism contradicts the royal law of love. He then asks what good it is to say you have faith but do nothing for a hungry brother. Abraham and Rahab are his examples of faith that acts.

his.t: In Jesus' day leading people loved the best seats in the synagogues (Luke 11:43; Matthew 23:6). James uses the same kind of scene to show a church repeating the world's ranking.

Abraham was the father of the Jewish people, and Rahab was a Canaanite woman of Jericho who is called a prostitute in Joshua 2:1. James puts them side by side as people whose faith showed in what they did (2:21-25).

cus.t: Pliny the Elder (Natural History 33) says that in Rome the right to wear a gold ring marked rank: first senators, later the equestrian order. A visitor wearing one would look important, which is the point of James 2:2.
James says the rich oppress the poor and drag them into court (2:6). Debt and lawsuits were common, and the Law warned against taking advantage of the poor (Exodus 22:25-27; Deuteronomy 24:12-15).

cu: The word translated “meeting” in v.2 is synagoge, so James is describing a gathering of Jewish believers. Seating showed rank (Luke 11:43 speaks of those who love the best seats in the synagogues). The stories of Abraham offering Isaac and of Rahab hiding the spies were well known, and James uses both as examples.

ot.n: Abraham believed God, quoted in 2:23.
Abraham offers Isaac on the altar (2:21).
Rahab hides the spies (2:25).

im.c: One side of Papyrus 20, a leaf from a codex of James found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt and dated to the 3rd century (now in Princeton University Library). This side has James 2:19-3:2, from the end of the argument that faith without works is dead to the first warning about teachers.
im.k: Unknown scribe (3rd century), public domain / Wikimedia Commons

set: James warns that teachers will be judged strictly, and turns to the tongue: small like a bit in a horse’s mouth or a rudder on a ship, but able to set a forest on fire. No one can tame it. He contrasts earthly wisdom, marked by jealousy and selfish ambition, with the wisdom from above.

his.t: Teaching was honored work in the early church (1 Corinthians 12:28; Acts 13:1). James warns that those who teach will be judged more strictly (3:1), and he ties the warning to the tongue.

The word "hell" in 3:6 is Gehenna, from the Hebrew name of the Hinnom Valley just south of Jerusalem. In the Old Testament the valley was linked with child sacrifice (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31-32), and later Jewish writers used its name for the place of…

cus.t: A horse was steered by a bit in its mouth, and a ship by a steering oar at the stern. James uses both as pictures of a small part that directs a large body (3:3-4).
James asks whether a fig tree can grow olives, a grapevine figs, or a salt spring produce fresh water (3:12). Jesus also used trees and their fruit to show what a person is like (Matthew 7:16-20).

cu: Teachers were highly honored, so many wanted the role. A bit and a ship's steering oar were everyday tools, and fire in dry woodland could spread fast. The phrase in v.6 that some Bibles render “the course of his life” is literally a wheel of birth or origin (trochos tes geneseos). Scholars debate what it means, and it probably refers to the cycle or course of life.

ot.n: They sharpen their tongues like a serpent; the poison of vipers is on their lips (compare James 3:8).
Death and life are in the power of the tongue.
People are made in God's likeness (James 3:9).

im.c: The back of the Papyrus 20 leaf, now in Princeton University Library. It has James 3:3-9, the passage about the bit in a horse's mouth, the ship's rudder and the tongue that no one can tame.
im.k: Unknown scribe (3rd century), public domain / Wikimedia Commons

set: James asks where wars and fights come from and answers: from desires waging war within. He calls friendship with the world enmity with God, and urges his readers to submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, and humble themselves. Then he warns against judging a brother and against boasting about tomorrow.

his.t: James traces fights among believers to desires that war inside them (4:1-3) and warns against speaking against one another (4:11-12). He does not say what the fights were about.

James imagines traders who say they will go to a city, spend a year there, do business and make a profit (4:13). Roman roads and Mediterranean sea routes made such journeys common for people with money to risk.

cus.t: The Greek word atmis means vapor, steam or smoke. Hosea 13:3 uses similar pictures for things that quickly vanish: morning mist, early dew, chaff and smoke. James says that life is like this (4:14).
To cleanse the hands and purify the heart, and to be wretched, mourn and weep (4:8-9), is the language of repentance in the prophets (Isaiah 1:15-17; Joel 2:12-13).
The prophets often described Israel's unfaithfulness to God as adultery (Hosea 2:2-5; Jeremiah 3:6-10; Ezekiel 16). James uses the same picture for believers who make friends with the world.

cu: The prophets described Israel's unfaithfulness to God as adultery (Hosea 2:2-5), and James uses that picture for believers who befriend the world (v.4). Merchants of the day planned trips of a year to make a profit (v.13), and James says that life is a mist.

ot.n: Quoted in James 4:6 in its Greek form. The Hebrew speaks of scoffers and of favor for the humble.
All flesh is grass and quickly fades. Compare the mist of James 4:14.
Israel's unfaithfulness pictured as adultery. Compare James 4:4.

im.c: A Roman fresco of a merchant ship named the Isis Giminiana, now in the Vatican Museums (about AD 200-250). It is later than James, but it shows a cargo ship of the kind that carried traders around the Mediterranean. James 4:13 pictures merchants who say they will go to a city, spend a year there and make a profit.
im.k: Joel Bellviure, CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

t: Patience and the Prayer of Faith
set: James denounces rich people who have hoarded wealth and withheld wages. He then calls believers to patience until the Lord’s coming, like a farmer waiting for rain. He gives instructions for prayer for the sick, praying elders, anointing with oil, and confession, with Elijah as an example.

his.t: The Law said a day laborer must be paid before sunset (Deuteronomy 24:14-15; Leviticus 19:13). James says the wages that were held back are crying out (5:4), as Abel's blood did (Genesis 4:10).
First Kings 17-18 tells how Elijah prayed for drought and for rain. James says it did not rain for three and a half years (5:17), and Luke 4:25 gives the same figure.

cus.t: Olive oil was used on wounds (Luke 10:34), and the Twelve anointed many sick people with oil (Mark 6:13). James tells the elders to pray over the sick person and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord (5:14).
The early rain of autumn softened the ground for planting, and the late rain of spring filled out the grain (Deuteronomy 11:14; Jeremiah 5:24). A farmer could do nothing to hurry them.
In Jesus' day people backed their words with oaths by heaven, the temple or the altar (Matthew 5:33-37; 23:16-22). James repeats the command to let a plain yes and no be enough (5:12).

cu: Farmers in Israel counted on the early rains of autumn, which let them plant, and the late rains of spring, which filled the grain (Deuteronomy 11:14). Oil was used for healing (Luke 10:34), and the Twelve anointed the sick with oil (Mark 6:13). “Do not swear” (v.12) repeats Jesus' teaching (Matthew 5:34-37).

ot.n: Elijah announced that there would be no rain (James 5:17).
The Lord restores Job. James 5:11 points to this outcome.
Love covers all offenses. Compare James 5:20.

im.c: A pottery fragment from the 7th century BC, found in 1960 at a Judean fortress near Yavne-Yam on the coast and now in the Israel Museum. In it a field worker complains to the commander that an official took his garment after he finished his harvesting, and asks for it back. It is some six centuries older than James, but it shows a harvester appealing for justice, as the workmen do in James 5:4.
im.k: פעמי-עליון, CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

set: Peter writes to believers in five provinces of what is now Turkey. They are “elect exiles,” chosen by God but strangers in their own towns. He starts with praise for a living hope through Christ’s resurrection and an inheritance that cannot fade, and urges them to be holy as God is holy.

his.t: Peter writes at a time when Christians faced growing hostility.
Roman provinces in modern Turkey.

cus.t: Gold was purified in fire and tested.
An unblemished animal was required.

cu: “Gird up your minds” (v.13) is a picture of tucking up long robes to run. “Ransomed” (v.18) refers to the price paid for a slave. The Lamb without blemish echoes the Passover and the Temple offerings.

ot.n: “You shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy.”
The word of the Lord endures forever.
An unblemished lamb for Passover.

set: Peter urges his readers to desire pure spiritual milk, and describes them as living stones being built into a spiritual house, a royal priesthood. Then he instructs them how to live as foreigners in a hostile world, submitting to authorities, and gives Christ’s example in suffering to slaves.

his.t: Roman temples were built of cut stone, and Peter says the church is God’s temple.
Household servants had little protection.

cus.t: The first stone laid determined the building’s lines.
Public respect was central to Roman society.

cu: Roman citizens were required to honor the emperor. Peter says, “Honor everyone… fear God. Honor the emperor.” House slaves could suffer harsh treatment from masters, and Peter points to Christ, who did not retaliate.

ot.n: “Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone.”
The stone the builders rejected.
The suffering servant who bore sins.

set: Peter addresses wives, including those with unbelieving husbands, and husbands. Then he turns to all believers: be of one mind, do not repay evil for evil, and always be ready to give a defense for the hope that is in you. It is better to suffer for doing good than for doing evil, as Christ did.

his.t: Eight people were saved through water.
Whether to the dead, to fallen angels, or to Noah’s generation is debated.

cus.t: Fashion of wealthy women.
The Greek word apologia is the origin of “apologetics.”

cu: A wife who converted to Christ in a Roman household could face tension because her husband expected her to follow his gods. Peter advises quiet, gentle conduct as a witness. The reference to Noah’s flood and baptism (vv.20-21) links salvation through water.

ot.n: “Whoever would love life and see good days, keep your tongue from evil.”
Noah and the flood.
Do not fear what they fear.

t: Do Not Be Surprised by Fiery Trials
set: Since Christ suffered in the flesh, Peter urges believers to arm themselves with the same mind and stop living for human passions. Former friends are surprised that they no longer join in wild living. Fiery trials are not strange, but a share in Christ’s sufferings, and a cause for rejoicing.

his.t: Used in Antioch (Acts 11:26) and in Nero’s time as a charge.
Social events usually included idol worship.

cus.t: Greek and Roman parties.
The same word is used of refining.

cu: Pagan social life centered on feasts, drunkenness, and idol worship. Believers who stopped joining in were slandered. “The household of God” (v.17) is judged first, as in the prophet Ezekiel.

ot.n: Love covers all offenses.
If the righteous are repaid on earth, how much more the wicked?
The Spirit of the Lord rests on him.

set: Peter, a fellow elder and witness of Christ’s sufferings, urges the elders to shepherd the flock willingly, not for gain, and not lording it over them. He tells the younger to submit and everyone to clothe themselves with humility.

his.t: Probably Rome, a code name for the capital.
John Mark, who traveled with Paul and later with Peter.

cus.t: Daily routine of leading, feeding, and guarding the flock.
A greeting of love.

cu: A shepherd led, fed, and protected his flock. Roman officials were often called “shepherds of the people.” Peter reminds elders that Jesus is the Chief Shepherd. The “unfading crown of glory” is a wreath that does not wilt like athletes’ garlands.

ot.n: Shepherds who feed themselves versus the Good Shepherd.
“Cast your burden on the Lord.”
God gives grace to the humble.

set: Peter writes as one who knows his death is near. He urges his readers to add virtue, knowledge, self-control, steadfastness, godliness, brotherly affection, and love to their faith. He reminds them that he and the other apostles were eyewitnesses of Christ’s majesty on the holy mountain.

his.t: Jesus foretold it (John 21:18). Tradition says Peter was crucified under Nero.
The transfiguration, often tied to Mount Tabor or Hermon.

cus.t: A tent as the body, a picture also used by Paul.
Venus at dawn announces the day.

cu: Lists of virtues were common among Greek moralists. Peter’s list begins with faith and ends with love. “Putting off of my body” is a tent image (v.14), as Paul used.

ot.n: “You are my Son.”
“My chosen, in whom my soul delights.”
A star shall come out of Jacob.

set: Peter warns that false teachers will secretly bring in destructive heresies, denying the Master who bought them. Using Old Testament examples (fallen angels, Noah’s flood, Sodom and Gomorrah, Lot), he shows that God knows how to rescue the godly and keep the unrighteous under punishment.

his.t: A prophet-for-hire who loved wages from wrongdoing.
Judged by fire; Lot and his daughters escaped.

cus.t: Disappointing to travelers in a dry land.
Impressive but useless.

cu: Balaam’s pursuit of money (v.15) is the model for false teachers who exploit others. The picture of a dog returning to its vomit and a pig to the mud (v.22) quotes Proverbs 26:11.

ot.n: The sons of God and the daughters of men.
Sodom and Lot.
Balaam and Balak.

set: Peter writes this second letter to stir up their sincere minds. Scoffers will ask, “Where is the promise of his coming?” Peter reminds them that God made the world by his word and judged it by water, and will judge it by fire. A day is as a thousand years to the Lord. His patience is salvation, and he calls them to holy lives.

his.t: Peter says some twist them, treating them as Scripture.
A key picture of judgment.

cus.t: Unexpected arrival.
The basic parts of the universe.

cu: Jews and Christians awaited the day of the Lord. Peter’s “thief in the night” echoes Jesus’ words (Matthew 24:43). The elements melting with fire resembles Stoic ideas of a cosmic fire, but Peter says it ends in new heavens and a new earth.

ot.n: A thousand years are like a day.
New heavens and a new earth.
The flood.

t: The Word of Life and Walking in Light
set: John opens like a testimony: what we have heard, seen, and touched concerning the Word of life. His purpose is fellowship with God and each other. He then declares that God is light, and says that those who claim fellowship while walking in darkness lie, but those who confess sin are forgiven.

his.t: John says the apostles heard, saw, and touched Jesus.
Some taught that the material world and the body were evil, and denied the incarnation.

cus.t: The word koinonia means a shared life.
A Hebrew idiom for conduct.

cu: Some false teachers claimed to be without sin or to have special knowledge. John answers with plain tests. “Walking” is a Hebrew way of speaking about the way one lives. The “blood of Jesus” cleansing from sin draws on the sacrifices of Leviticus.

ot.n: “The Lord is my light and my salvation.”
The cleansing from sin.
“I acknowledged my sin to you.”

set: John writes so that his readers will not sin, but if anyone does sin, they have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. He gives the test of keeping God’s commandments, especially the old and new commandment to love. Then he warns about loving the world and about antichrists who left the community.

his.t: Teachers who left the community and denied Christ.
Early Christians lived in the expectation of the end.

cus.t: Greek paraklētos: a legal helper.
A symbol of the Spirit’s presence.

cu: “Little children,” “fathers,” and “young men” (vv.12-14) may refer to stages of faith. The “last hour” was a common phrase for the end times. “Anointing” (v.20, 27) refers to the Holy Spirit, and a Christian’s shared knowledge of the truth.

ot.n: Love your neighbor as yourself.
A king who speaks against the Most High.
Great peace have those who love your law.

set: John marvels at the love the Father has given us in calling us children of God. He contrasts the children of God with the children of the devil, and says the mark of the children of God is love. The model is Christ, who laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.

his.t: The first murderer, a model of envy.
The verbs in 3:6, 9 are present tense: continuing in sin.

cus.t: The language of sacrifice.
Material resources.

cu: Cain’s murder of Abel (Genesis 4) is the model for hatred. In an age without social welfare, “the world’s goods” meant concrete help for someone in need. The “heart” (vv.19-21) as the seat of conscience.

ot.n: Cain and Abel.
Do not hate your brother in your heart.
Create in me a clean heart.

set: John tells his readers to test the spirits, since many false prophets have gone into the world. The test is whether they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. Then he writes the most famous statement about God’s love: God is love, and we love because he first loved us.

his.t: Itinerant prophets claimed spirit-inspired knowledge.
The view that Jesus only seemed to have a body.

cus.t: Assaying metals.
Common among ancient people.

cu: The Greek world was full of prophets and spirits, so John gives a clear test. “Propitiation” (v.10) draws on the language of the sacrificial system. The idea of perfect love casting out fear (v.18) relates to fear of judgment.

ot.n: God set his love on Israel.
Atonement.
His steadfast love endures forever.

set: John ties together love, obedience, and faith. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and whoever has been born of God overcomes the world. The letter ends with its purpose: that you may know that you have eternal life, and with confidence in prayer and a warning against idols.

his.t: Some false teachers said Christ came by water only. John says water and blood.
Temples and statues surrounded Ephesus.

cus.t: Legal testimony of two or three.
Boldness to approach God.

cu: “Water and blood” (v.6) may refer to Jesus’ baptism and death, countering teachers who said the divine Christ left before the cross. The “sin that leads to death” (v.16) is a debated phrase. “Keep yourselves from idols” would have been vivid in Ephesus.

ot.n: Two or three witnesses.
Defiant sin.
If I regard iniquity, the Lord will not hear.

set: In a short note, the elder writes to “the elect lady and her children” (probably a church) rejoicing that some are walking in truth. He reminds them of the commandment to love one another, and warns them about deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. They should not welcome such teachers.

his.t: They moved between churches, with or without letters.
The same people described in 1 John 2:18-19.

cus.t: “Grace, mercy, and peace” combine Greek and Hebrew greetings.
He prefers to talk face to face rather than write (v.12).

cu: Traveling teachers relied on hospitality in homes. To welcome someone was to support their work, so John says welcoming a false teacher shares in his evil works. A letter this short would fit on a single papyrus sheet.

ot.n: Love your neighbor.
Teach me your way, that I may walk in your truth.

set: The elder writes to Gaius, a beloved friend, praising him for his faithfulness and hospitality to traveling brothers. He then warns about Diotrephes, who loves to be first, refuses the elder’s authority, and puts out those who welcome the brothers. He commends Demetrius.

his.t: A church leader who rejected the elder’s authority.
Perhaps the carrier of the letter.

cus.t: Hosting missionaries was a duty.
Letters and visitors confirm a person’s character.

cu: Traveling teachers depended on hospitality, since inns were poor and costly. Refusing to host them meant refusing the elder’s representatives. “Sending them on their way in a manner worthy of God” (v.6) meant supplying food, money, and companions.

ot.n: Turn from evil and do good.
Abraham’s hospitality.

set: Jude had meant to write about their common salvation, but had to urge them to contend for the faith. Certain people had crept in unnoticed, turning God’s grace into licentiousness and denying Jesus.

his.t: James and Jude are listed among the brothers of Jesus (Mark 6:3).
A Jewish work of the third century BC onward.

cus.t: Fellowship meals with the Lord’s Supper.
Promising rain but producing none.

cu: Jude draws on Jewish tradition. The book of 1 Enoch, widely read in Judaism at the time, is quoted in v.14-15. The dispute about Moses’ body may come from the Assumption of Moses. “Love feasts” (v.12) were shared meals in the early church.

ot.n: Israel in the wilderness.
Sodom and Gomorrah.
Korah’s rebellion.

set: John, exiled on the small island of Patmos in the Aegean, is in the Spirit on the Lord’s day when he hears a loud voice and turns to see Jesus among seven golden lampstands. Jesus is dressed as a priest and king, with eyes like fire, and tells John to write what he sees and send it to seven churches.

his.t: Under Domitian emperor worship was pressed in Asia.
A rocky island used as a place of exile and a Roman outpost.

cus.t: Seven-branched lamps stood in the Temple.
A title of God in Isaiah.

cu: Rome used remote islands to exile people. “The Lord’s day” is a very early name for Sunday, the day of Christ’s resurrection. The imagery of the Son of Man draws on Daniel 7 and 10 and Ezekiel 1.

ot.n: One like a son of man coming with the clouds.
A lampstand all of gold.
“I am the first and I am the last.”

t: Letters to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, and Thyatira
set: Christ speaks to the first four of the seven churches. Each letter names the city, begins with a description of Christ, praises and criticizes, and ends with a call to hear and a promise to the one who overcomes. They describe the real pressures each city faced.

his.t: A proud city that remained loyal to Rome, with a strong Jewish community.
The provincial capital with a temple of Augustus and a great altar.

cus.t: Thyatira’s guilds held dinners at pagan temples.
A jury’s white stone meant acquittal.

cu: Pergamum was a center of emperor worship and had a great altar to Zeus. Thyatira was a trade-guild town where participation in guild feasts meant eating food offered to idols. “White stone” (v.17) may refer to an admission token or a judge’s verdict of acquittal. Smyrna had a large Jewish community that was hostile to Christians.

ot.n: The tree of life in the garden.
Balaam’s counsel and Israel’s idolatry.
Jezebel and her influence.

t: Letters to Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea
set: Christ completes his letters. Sardis has a name for being alive but is dead. Philadelphia has little power but has kept his word and will have an open door. Laodicea is lukewarm and boasts of its wealth, but Christ stands at the door and knocks.

his.t: A major earthquake struck Sardis in AD 17, and the city was rebuilt with Roman help.
After an earthquake in AD 60 the city refused imperial aid and rebuilt itself.

cus.t: Hierapolis had hot springs and Colossae cold fresh water. Laodicea’s was lukewarm.
Laodicea was famous for a medical school and an eye ointment.

cu: Sardis had twice fallen to surprise attacks because its guards slept. Laodicea was a banking, textile, and medical center with poor water, brought by an aqueduct, which arrived lukewarm. Christ’s offer of gold, white garments, and eye salve answers the city’s riches, black wool, and eye ointment.

ot.n: The key of the house of David.
The book of life.
The Lord reproves those he loves.

set: John looks and sees an open door in heaven. A voice invites him up, and he sees a throne with one seated on it, surrounded by twenty-four elders on thrones, a sea of glass, and four living creatures who never cease to say, “Holy, holy, holy.” The elders cast their crowns before the throne.

his.t: Asian cities had temples to the emperor.
Jewish visions of God’s court were common.

cus.t: Victory wreaths and kingly crowns.
A level pavement of crystal.

cu: Roman emperors were worshiped as lords and gods, with titles such as “Lord and God.” Here the elders cast their crowns before the one true Lord, a claim that in John’s day challenged the empire. The rainbow around the throne recalls God’s covenant after the flood.

ot.n: The Lord seated on a throne, “Holy, holy, holy.”
The four creatures and the throne.
The rainbow as covenant sign.

set: In the right hand of the One on the throne is a scroll sealed with seven seals. No one in heaven or on earth can open it, and John weeps. Then one of the elders says that the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered. John looks and sees a Lamb standing, as though slain, and all heaven worships him.

his.t: Wills were sealed by seven witnesses.
Jewish writings expected a lion-like conqueror.

cus.t: Instruments and prayers of the saints.
A song of salvation.

cu: A scroll sealed with seven seals resembled a Roman will, which needed seven witnesses’ seals. John hears “Lion” and sees a “Lamb,” a pairing that shows how Jesus conquers by sacrifice. The “new song” is a theme of praise in the Psalms.

ot.n: Judah is a lion’s cub, and the scepter will not depart.
A shoot from the stump of Jesse.
Like a lamb led to the slaughter.

set: As the Lamb opens the first six seals, four horsemen ride out on white, red, black, and pale horses, bringing conquest, war, famine, and death. The fifth seal reveals martyrs under the altar crying, “How long?” The sixth brings an earthquake and cosmic upheaval, and people hide from the wrath of the Lamb.

his.t: Ancient cities regularly suffered grain shortages.
Christians had already been killed under Nero and Domitian.

cus.t: Given to the faithful dead.
A prophetic image from Isaiah 2:19.

cu: Famine prices in the third seal (a day’s wage for a quart of wheat) show severe shortage. The Parthian horsemen of the east were known as mounted archers. The oil and wine not to be harmed may reflect the Roman edict on grain under Domitian.

ot.n: Four chariots with colored horses.
The sun darkened and the moon turned to blood.
How long, O Lord?

t: The Sealed and the Great Multitude
set: Before the final seal, four angels hold back the winds while another seals the servants of God on their foreheads. The number is 144,000 from the tribes of Israel. Then John sees a countless multitude from every nation, in white robes with palm branches, who have come out of the great tribulation and washed their robes in the…

his.t: Dan is omitted and Manasseh included, a difference from earlier lists.
Celebrated with palm branches and shelters.

cus.t: Used in joyful processions.
A symbol of cleansing.

cu: Sealing was a mark of ownership and protection, like the mark placed on the foreheads of the faithful in Ezekiel 9. Palm branches were used at the Feast of Tabernacles and to welcome kings. Twelve times twelve times a thousand is a symbolic number of completeness.

ot.n: A mark on the foreheads of those who grieve.
They shall not hunger or thirst.
The twelve tribes.

set: When the Lamb opens the seventh seal, there is silence in heaven for about half an hour. Then seven angels are given seven trumpets. An angel with a golden censer offers incense with the prayers of the saints. The first four trumpets strike a third of the land, sea, rivers, and sky.

his.t: Hail, water turned to blood, and darkness were Egyptian plagues.
The eruption in AD 79 may have shaped imagery.

cus.t: Offered at the altar before the Lord.
Used for war and worship.

cu: Trumpets signaled the arrival of God’s presence at Sinai and called armies to battle. The plagues echo the plagues of Egypt, in which God judged Pharaoh to free his people. Wormwood is a bitter plant.

ot.n: The plague of hail and fire.
The Nile turned to blood.
Wormwood and poisoned water.

set: At the fifth trumpet, a star falls to earth with the key to the shaft of the abyss. Smoke rises and locusts with scorpions’ stings torment people for five months. At the sixth trumpet, four angels bound at the great river Euphrates are released with an army of 200 million cavalry, killing a third of mankind.

his.t: Rome’s eastern enemy, who defeated Roman armies at Carrhae.
Devoured crops and caused famine.

cus.t: Painful but not usually fatal.
The lifespan of a locust swarm.

cu: The Euphrates was the boundary of the Roman Empire, beyond which lay the Parthians, feared horse-archers. Locust plagues devastated Mediterranean lands and were a standard picture of judgment (Joel 1-2). The “abyss” was the prison of evil spirits.

ot.n: The locust army of the day of the Lord.
The plague of locusts.
The Lord’s sword on Leviathan.

set: A mighty angel wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head and a face like the sun, stands with one foot on the sea and one on the land, holding a little scroll. Seven thunders speak, but John is told not to write them.

his.t: Ezekiel and Jeremiah also received a message by eating or touching.
The giant statue astride a harbor may be echoed by the angel’s stance.

cus.t: The usual sign of swearing.
A symbol for the sweetness of God’s word.

cu: Eating a scroll is a prophet’s act of taking a message into himself. The raised hand is the gesture of an oath. “Mystery of God” (v.7) is a secret plan now to be completed.

ot.n: Ezekiel eats the scroll.
The man in linen swears by him who lives forever.
Sweeter than honey.

t: The Two Witnesses and the Seventh Trumpet
set: John is given a measuring rod to measure the temple and the altar, but not the outer court, which is given to the nations for 42 months. Two witnesses prophesy for 1,260 days, are killed, left in the street of the great city, and then raised after three and a half days.

his.t: If written after AD 70, the temple reference is symbolic.
The length of Antiochus’s persecution and a pattern of limited time.

cus.t: Coarse cloth worn for mourning and repentance.
A dishonor in the ancient world.

cu: Measuring is a prophetic act of marking out what God will protect. The “great city” where their Lord was crucified (v.8) is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, so its meaning is symbolic. Forty-two months, 1,260 days, and “time, times, and half a time” are the same period of three and a half years, a number from Daniel 7:25 and 12:7.

ot.n: The two olive trees and lampstands.
A time, times, and half a time.
The nations rage, and the Lord’s anointed reigns.

set: A great sign appears in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars, about to give birth. A great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns waits to devour her child.

his.t: Greek and Roman stories like Leto and Python.
Some think Nero’s memory lies behind the later beast.

cus.t: A picture of escape and care (Exodus 19:4).
The dragon’s attempt to sweep the woman away.

cu: The imagery recalls ancient stories of a pregnant goddess pursued by a monster, which John reshapes. The woman is understood in different ways, as Israel, Mary, or the church. The red dragon’s heads and horns appear again in the beast of chapter 13.

ot.n: The seed of the woman will crush the serpent.
He will rule them with a rod of iron.
Michael the great prince will arise.

t: The Beast from the Sea and the Beast from the Earth
set: From the sea rises a beast with ten horns and seven heads, which receives power from the dragon and is worshiped by the world. A second beast, from the earth, performs signs and makes people worship the first beast, requiring a mark on the right hand or forehead without which no one can buy or sell.

his.t: Temples and priests of Rome and the emperor filled Asia.
A legend that Nero would return.

cus.t: Slaves and soldiers were marked or branded.
Trade guilds required participation in pagan rites.

cu: The beast recalls Rome, which demanded worship of the emperor. In Asia, there were temples to Rome and the emperor, and coins carried claims of divinity. Letters have numerical values in Hebrew and Greek, which is why the number 666 may be a name; “Nero Caesar” in Hebrew letters adds to 666, though some manuscripts have 616.

ot.n: Four beasts rise from the sea.
The image of Nebuchadnezzar that all must worship.
Signs on hand and forehead.

set: John sees the Lamb standing on Mount Zion with the 144,000 who have his name written on their foreheads. Angels announce the gospel, the fall of Babylon, and judgment on those who worship the beast. A voice says, “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.” Then the earth is harvested like grain and grapes.

his.t: Rome was called Babylon in Jewish and Christian writing.
Used to tread grapes.

cus.t: The first part of the harvest offered to God.
A curved harvesting blade.

cu: Grain harvest and grape vintage were common pictures of judgment (Joel 3:13). The winepress is trodden outside the city. “Babylon” is a code name for Rome.

ot.n: “Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe.”
The winepress of God’s wrath.
“Fallen, fallen is Babylon.”

t: The Song of Moses and the Lamb
set: John sees another great and marvelous sign: seven angels with the seven last plagues. He sees those who conquered the beast standing beside a sea of glass mingled with fire, singing the song of Moses and the Lamb. The temple in heaven is opened, and the angels come out with the bowls of wrath.

his.t: Moses and Israel sang after crossing the sea.
The tabernacle in the wilderness.

cus.t: Instruments of praise.
The clothing of priests and the pure.

cu: Singing on the shore recalls Israel after the Red Sea (Exodus 15). The “tent of witness” is the tabernacle. Smoke filling the temple (v.8) echoes Exodus 40:34 and Isaiah 6:4, when God’s glory filled the sanctuary.

ot.n: The song of Moses.
All nations shall come and worship.
The glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle.

set: A voice from the temple tells the seven angels to pour out the bowls of God’s wrath. Painful sores, blood in the sea and rivers, scorching heat, darkness, and the drying of the Euphrates follow. Spirits like frogs gather the kings to the place called Armageddon. When the seventh bowl is poured out, a voice says, “It is done!”

his.t: A fortress city that guarded the pass through the Carmel ridge.
He diverted the Euphrates to enter the city (539 BC).

cus.t: Unclean animals in the Law, and a plague in Egypt.
Unexpected arrival.

cu: Har-Megiddo means “mountain of Megiddo,” the site of many ancient battles in the Jezreel Valley. The drying of the Euphrates echoes the way the river was diverted for Cyrus to take Babylon. “Like a thief” is a call to watchfulness.

ot.n: The plagues of Egypt.
The Lord will dry up the River.
Kings fought at Megiddo.

set: One of the bowl angels shows John the great prostitute seated on many waters, who sits on a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns. She is drunk with the blood of the saints and called “Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes.” The angel explains that the seven heads are seven hills and also seven kings.

his.t: Rome was proverbial as the city of seven hills.
Seven kings may correspond to a series of emperors.

cus.t: Costly dyes for the wealthy.
A cup of wine in a pagan rite.

cu: Rome was well known as the city on seven hills. Prophets used the image of a prostitute for cities and nations that traded in power and idolatry (Nahum 3:4; Isaiah 23:16-17). Roman coins show the goddess Roma seated on seven hills.

ot.n: Nineveh, the prostitute with her charms.
Babylon was a golden cup in the Lord’s hand.
Tyre as a prostitute.

set: An angel with great authority announces, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!” A voice from heaven calls God’s people to come out of her. The kings, merchants, and sea captains mourn the destruction of the city that made them rich.

his.t: Rome’s demand for luxury goods shaped trade routes.
The empire depended on enslaved labor.

cus.t: A heavy stone for grinding grain.
They stand far off for fear of her torment.

cu: Rome imported luxury goods from across the world. The list of cargo (vv.12-13) matches goods that came to the capital, and ends with “bodies and souls of men.” The dirge follows the form of prophetic laments over Tyre in Ezekiel 27.

ot.n: The lament over Tyre’s trade.
The fall of Babylon.
A stone thrown into the Euphrates.

t: The Marriage Supper and the Rider on the White Horse
set: A great multitude in heaven shouts “Hallelujah!” over the fall of Babylon. The marriage supper of the Lamb is announced, and the bride is clothed in fine linen, which is the righteous deeds of the saints.

his.t: Rome’s triumphs showed victory over captured enemies.
Hebrew “praise the Lord,” found only in this chapter in the New Testament.

cus.t: A joyful feast lasting days.
The clothing of the pure.

cu: A Roman triumph involved a conquering general in a chariot. Here the rider has a robe dipped in blood, the armies of heaven follow him, and the weapon is a sword from his mouth, which is the word. The “supper of the great God” (v.17) is a grim feast for birds.

ot.n: The warrior with garments stained.
He will rule the nations with a rod of iron.
Your Maker is your husband.

t: The Thousand Years and the Great White Throne
set: An angel binds the dragon for a thousand years and throws him into the abyss. Those who were beheaded for their testimony come to life and reign with Christ for a thousand years. When the thousand years are over, Satan is released and gathers Gog and Magog for battle, but fire from heaven consumes them.

his.t: Pre-, post-, and amillennial views each appear in church history.
Symbolic of hostile nations in Jewish tradition.

cus.t: Heavenly records of deeds.
A picture of final separation.

cu: This passage is one of the most discussed in Scripture and gives rise to three main readings: premillennial (Christ returns before the thousand years), postmillennial (after), and amillennial (the thousand years is symbolic of the present age). Believers have disagreed on this since the early church.

ot.n: Gog and Magog.
The Ancient of Days and the books opened.
The book and the resurrection.

t: A New Heaven and a New Earth
set: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, for the first have passed away and the sea is no more. The holy city, the new Jerusalem, comes down out of heaven prepared as a bride. A loud voice says that God will dwell with his people and wipe away every tear.

his.t: Ezekiel’s vision of a restored city stands behind the structure.
Babylon the prostitute is replaced by Jerusalem the bride.

cus.t: Twelve jewels recall the high priest’s breastplate (Exodus 28).
Ancient cities shut gates at night. This one never does.

cu: The city’s dimensions are perfect cubes, like the Most Holy Place, so the whole city is God’s dwelling. “No more sea” does not mean the end of the ocean but of the chaos and evil the sea represented. The twelve gates are named for the tribes of Israel and the foundations for the apostles.

ot.n: “I will create new heavens and a new earth.”
He will swallow up death forever.
“I will walk among you and be your God.”

t: The River of Life and “Come, Lord Jesus”
set: The angel shows John the river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, with the tree of life on either side, whose leaves heal the nations. There is no more curse. God’s servants will see his face.

his.t: The first book of the Bible begins in a garden. The last ends in a garden city.
Ancient books often ended with such curses.

cus.t: Belonging to God, in contrast with the mark of the beast.
An invitation by the Spirit, the Bride, and the hearer.

cu: The tree of life returns from Genesis 2-3, now in the city. “Seeing his face” was something no one could do in the old covenant (Exodus 33:20). The warning at the end (vv.18-19) echoes Deuteronomy 4:2 and was a standard warning to copyists.

ot.n: The tree of life and the river in Eden.
A river flowing from the temple, with trees for healing.
“Come, everyone who thirsts.”
